Summary

A workshop was held in Saly, Senegal, on 9–10 November 2022 to develop a prospective study model for exploring the income and environmental impacts of the livestock value chain and potential changes in practices within these systems. The model will also be able to analyse potential synergies when multiple practices are implemented and the potential trade-offs between competing goals. The goal of this model is to better understand the strengths and challenges in livestock systems and serves as a test bed to study the ability to improve local capabilities, manage climate risk, mobilize financing and shape policies directly related to the Livestock and Climate (LCSR) and Sustainable Animal Productivity (SAPLING) initiatives of the CGIAR as well as the Accelerating Impacts of CGIAR Climate Research in Africa (AICCRA) project. Twenty-six participants, many of whom have strong modelling experience, convened to better define the problems to be studied by the model, develop model structures, further develop structures of areas of interest (feed, land use and the carbon cycle) and detail a work plan.
vi
1. Background

It is estimated that up to 1.3 billion people worldwide are employed in livestock value chain activities, with 600 million directly producing livestock (Herrero et al. 2013; Thornton et al. 2006). However, climate change and increasing populations have made this a more precarious activity in terms of its impact on feed, crop, water availability, productivity, disease, reproduction and biodiversity, as well as its contribution to climate change (Rojas-Downing et al. 2017).

With such high proportions of populations involved in livestock activities, especially in developing countries, ensuring the socioeconomic and environmental sustainability of livestock systems is of the utmost importance, including the introduction of adaptation options as well as reduction of environmental impact.

Although many models exist at farm level, including production models, bio-economic models and risk management, there have been relatively few value chain-level models (Greiner et al. 2014). Conducting analysis at the value chain level will better inform decision-makers, policymakers and industry actors to shape their actions and policies to improve the economic livelihoods of livestock farmers, the sustainability of livestock systems, and the overall economic outlook of the country.
It is in this context that the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) proposes the Livestock Integrated Assessment Model (LIAM), which has three broad goals:

Understand livestock value chain activities, their role and their impact on climate, including constraining factors along the value chain (environmental and value chain constraints) as well as opportunities.
Assess the income and environmental impact of the implementation of different practices (e.g. changes in feed practices, cattle mobility, manure management, transportation and storage).

3. Analyse potential synergies when implementing multiple practices together (increased desired impact over implementing them alone) while also identifying trade-offs between competing goals (improved income over increased environmental impact).

This model helps to better understand the strengths and challenges in the livestock system and serves as a test bed to study the ability to improve local capabilities, manage climate risk, mobilize financing and shape policy, which are directly related to the Livestock and Climate (LCSR) and Sustainable Animal Productivity (SAPLING) initiatives of the CGIAR. LCSR seeks to address the climate double burden of adapting livestock agri-food systems to climate change
while reducing greenhouse gas emissions. SAPLING seeks to increase livestock production through the adoption of resilience-enhancing, low-emitting technologies.

This model will first be applied to the beef and dairy value chains in Senegal. Livestock is a key component in the Senegalese economy and is one of the priority sectors of the Plan Sénégal émergent (ANSD 2020), the national planning roadmap. Thus, it is important to enhance the environmental and socioeconomic sustainability of livestock systems, notably while introducing adaptation options and reducing the environmental impact, all within the context of climate change, which exacerbates shocks. This application is completed within the Senegal cluster of the AICCRA (Accelerating Impacts of CGIAR Climate Research in Africa) project and relies on its strong network of partners. The AICCRA project seeks to sustainably improve food security as well as farmer and producer incomes through the implementation of profitable, diversified and resilient value chains.
2. Workshop particulars

It is in this context that a modelling workshop was convened, gathering modelers with diverse backgrounds to develop structures and key elements of the model. The two-day workshop took place from 9–10 November 2022 at Hôtel Neptune in Saly, Senegal, with the following defined objectives:
Define the problem(s) to be studied with the model: considering other tools available and the challenges faced by the livestock sector, what questions can a system dynamics-based model address?
Develop a model structure: building on the currently available expertise, define a suitable model to address the defined problems. Which areas of the model require a further level of detail?
Develop specific model structures further: with the identified areas of the model that require a further level of detail, design the concept of the model and identify sources of data.
Detail a work plan: define set projects and targets over the next year of the project, including target countries, data collection and model building.
Twenty-six participants attended the workshop, including four who participated in certain sessions online. See Annex 1 for the agenda and Annex 2 for the list of participants.
3. Session summaries
Introduction and background presentations

On the first day of the workshop, the morning session consisted of introduction of the participants, including a discussion on how each of them was involved in modelling and what type of modelling they were engaged in. The participants brought a broad range of modelling experience, including varied domains such as emissions, land use and forage, although some no longer had modelling as their primary activity. This diverse group of participants had a lot in common and set the tone for the rest of the workshop.

Sirak Bahta (ILRI) then made a presentation on the objectives of the meeting, and the modelling needs within the CGIAR initiatives, livestock master plans and AICCRA. The Livestock Master Plans, which are country-level projects providing guidance on livestock sector strategies and investment plans over the course of 15 and 5 years, respectively, have a growing need for integrated modelling of livestock production systems that can robustly analyse different scenarios and combinations of best practices that would enable the promotion of the sector, improving food security and nutrition, reducing poverty and promoting economic growth while also taking into account the environmental impact of activities. As a part of an offering of models, which includes household- and farm-level analysis, along with macroeconomic analysis at the sector and national level, the work proposed here would help to address the emissions and environmental impact along with economic trade- offs stemming from different scenarios projected in the livestock production systems.

Derek Chan (ILRI) presented the case of beef and dairy value chains in Senegal, where increased competition for lower quality and quantities of biomass and water is occurring. Many adaptation options are being discussed, including shifts to more intensive production systems, coupled with the development of feed varieties improved using regionally sensitive climate information services. In order to properly analyse the potential impacts and trade-offs of such changes, an integrated model is being proposed, with the inclusion of different modules in order to study the interactions between them. These modules are herd dynamics, beef and dairy value chains, beef and dairy demand, manure management, feed decision- making and consumption and pasture consumption and regrowth. The study will also include the effect of these interactions on land use, water use and soil quality, measuring their impact on household income and livelihoods and emissions along with the effect that the adoption of practices and climate assumptions have on the model (see Figure 1). The model also includes a user-friendly interface, which targets decision-makers to test different scenarios.

The session then continued with select participants presenting their research and models in order to provide a basis for what modelling already exists and to inform the workshop discussions. Below is a summary of their presentations:

Charles Mensah (ILRI) presented preliminary results from a study that prioritizes the many implications that climate change (including temperature increases, changes in rainfall quantity and variability, increases in carbon dioxide concentration, as well as floods, drought and heatwaves) has on the different nodes of livestock value chains, including feed availability and disease.

Ricardo Gonzales-Quintero (Alliance Bioversity International - CIAT)'s presentation explained why and how environmental impacts should be included in the modeling toolkit used for the Livestock Master Plans. His presentation covered the environmental impact and natural resource use of feed consumption, including climate change, water use, land use, non-renewable energy use, eutrophication and acidification, while also taking into account herd composition and energy requirements.

Hatem Belhouchette (International Centre for Advanced Mediterranean Agronomic Studies [CIHEAM]) presented a dynamic agricultural household bio-economic simulation model (DAHBSIM). It is a dynamic model that takes into account the interactions between crop and livestock activities on the farm as well as their emissions and calculates farm-level income, costs and risk.

Emerta Aragie (International Food Policy Research Institute, IFPRI) presented the linked economic and animal systems (LEAS) model, which combines herd dynamics, computable general equilibrium (supply and demand for animal products) and microsimulation models (tracking changes in income and prices for food), with the goal to study both demand and supply while linking it to the livestock system.

Mike Graham (ILRI) presented his work in linking the data collected through the Mazingira Centre with the global livestock environmental assessment – interactive (GLEAM-i) model to estimate the impact on emissions of herd and feed interventions, which allowed for the scaling up of Mazingira data to the national level.

Alioune Ndiaye (Practical Action) presented his approach to measuring the impact of climate change on pastoral and agropastoral systems, which includes the regression of livestock revenues on livestock prices and production as a function of labour, capital, climate conditions (including precipitation, temperature and geography) and socio- economic characteristics.

Rein van der Hoek (ABC) presented results from trade-off scoring exercises conducted in SAPLING countries that asked interviewees to assess the impacts of innovations along the lines of productivity, economics, the environment, the human condition and social impact. Preliminary results found generally positive impacts of proposed innovations on productivity and economics but less agreement on environmental impact.
3.2. Model development and identification of key modules

After the presentations from the experts, discussion began around potential use cases of a system dynamics model, sectors that could be focused on in particular and how to carry out this analysis. The participants identified the following sectors as important to explore: further land use change, demand for livestock products, natural resources (land, soil, water, pollution and biodiversity), land use management, socio-environmental outcomes of interventions and innovations (strategic innovation framework). These were their proposals when asked how to conduct the analysis:
Encourage thinking in terms of livestock systems (e.g. extensive cattle production systems)
Be able to include interventions such as vaccines, feed and forage interventions, policies and subsidies
Asymmetrical distribution, so that the model is sensitive to socioeconomic and geographic differences, including resource availability and access
Demographic dynamics as well as population policies
Geospatial, market price, climate, income variability, import vs. export and sensitivity to climate change data should be included.
3.3. Scoping key model sectors

From the earlier discussion, three modules were chosen to be studied in further detail by the participants. In groups, workshop participants were asked to develop a preliminary module structure for each theme and describe what questions should be addressed. The three modules identified were feed, land use and the carbon cycle.
3.3.1. Feed

The proposed feed structure includes four categorizations of feed: natural feed, crop residue, grown forage and purchased feed. Rainfall availability, soil quality, land availability (including degraded and undegraded land), seed availability (including price) and input availability affect the relative quantities and quality available of the four categorizations of feed. Seasonality (rainy and dry seasons) as well as climate shocks may affect this as well. The types and quantities of feed consumed depend on the energy and protein requirements of the herd (breeds, age, sex and species), the system they are brought up in (extensive, semi-intensive or extensive), or whether milk production is a goal. Water consumption and availability should also be taken into account. Manure production has the potential to be another income stream or to be reused directly on the land. Productivity and emissions can then be calculated as a result of these activities.
3.3.2. Land use

The land-use group decided to take the resource-use perspective, where there are actors each with their demand for natural resources (land, water and biodiversity), so we model to see how everyone’s needs can be satisfied without depleting the natural resources in future generations. In their model, the feed module would affect the cropland, grazing land and natural land (forest and wetlands). Tenure security and mobility affect grazing land, and the latter is affected by surface and groundwater availability. The availability of grazing land reduces overgrazing, which encourages grassland productivity, which feeds into the carbon module. Additionally, the herd module feeds into overgrazing and overgrazing reduces biodiversity.
3.3.3. The carbon cycle

This group mapped the movement of carbon from crops and produced by the herd in the soil. Major feedback included the generation of feed that improved the livestock population, which increased manure production leading to more carbon in the soil. These are moderated by the availability of labour, livestock demand, feed prices and availability and climate.
3.4. Reflection and next steps
The priorities were discussed within groups:
Partners: increase cooperation, including identifying key implementation partners and capacity development opportunities.

Model use: conduct ex-ante assessment of SAPLING and other innovations at the value chain, country or regional levels. Define the limitations, usefulness, relevance and complementarity with other models.

Impact assessment: demonstrate the value of the model through social impacts (gender and social inclusion), environmental impacts (greenhouse gas emissions and carbon) and economic impact (profitability and livelihoods) of interventions.

CGIAR initiatives: engage SAPLING and LCSR country teams in order to identify the priorities/demand and interest in the application of a model, and adapt to the context countries, in particular, those shared between LCSR/SAPLING (Kenya, Tanzania, Ethiopia and Mali). Also consider including linkages to wider CGIAR outcomes. Next steps: define and fill the data gaps.
On the model:
Model objectives and questions: justify the reason for the model, objectives and questions. What agency is represented in the model (decision-making unit)?
Model structure: define the system boundaries, including the scale of modelling, while remaining realistic.
Scenario development: develop scenarios to be simulated and implemented, including scaling strategies, then test the model in different scenarios.
Model validation: validate the model in a specific context (conditions and production systems), possibly through a baseline analysis.
User interface: develop the user interface further to improve accessibility.
Concerning the modules:
Harmonize modules with other modules: identify the intensity and direction of possible linkages and validate links and structures cross-module.
Specify the interaction with other models, especially making sure that the model is inclusive of food demand and supply.

Finalize the conceptual model interdisciplinary team and translate it into a stock and flow diagram. Input data (from different sources) and parametrize, test and validate. The validation should occur with other stakeholders and experts.
On the feed module: Develop a method to determine feed intake and requirements.

Lessons learned from ‘livestock master plan’ development and implementation
Steve Staal, Sirak Bahta, Joseph Karugia and Isabelle Baltenweck
Key messages
Introduction

Since 2014, ‘livestock master plans’ (LMPs) developed by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and partners have been used as a reference for gov-ernment plans and strategies in livestock sector de-velopment, and to guide investment in livestock sector areas (e.g. value chains and infrastructure) in various countries. The main lessons to emerge from the uptake of LMPs include the need to
• involve more stakeholders during development of the LMPs,

The livestock sector, despite comprising on average 40% of agricultural gross domestic product (GDP), suf-fers from underinvestment. For example, only about 5% of overseas direct investment (ODI) to developing countries goes to agriculture, and less than a tenth of even that low investment is directed towards livestock development.

In sub-Saharan Africa countries, which have substan- tial livestock industries, national agricultural priorities typical focus on staple crops and livestock develop-ment remains systematically underfunded compared to its economic importance in these countries.
• hold target consultations with investor groups
• align budgeting with national systems
• establish data collection and monitoring systems
• ensure institutionalization of the LMP, and
• contextualize LMPs for local use.

To address this issue, an expanding area of ILRI sup- port to public policy has been the development, with partners, of national LMPs. These LMPs provide analy-sis, information and capacity to set priorities within national livestock development strategies to generate public and private investments. The LMP development process combines quantitative analytical tools with consultative
Lessons learned from ‘livestock master plan’ development and implementation
and partnership exercises and uses both international experts and national capacity to jointly develop plans.
This brief presents evidence on the uptake of LMP out- puts in four countries – that is, how much were the LMPs recommendations taken up and how can we im-prove the process?
About livestock master plans

A livestock master plan (LMP) is a five-year sector investment plan. It includes both investment anal- ysis and a budget—including a financial and a human resource budget that guide the develop-ment of a country’s sustainable livestock sector. It is meant to positively impact the economy of the country or state in which it is carried out and to achieve the development objectives of the people and government. These include reducing poverty, increasing the revenue that the sector contributes to either state or national income, and improving food and nutrition security by including a strategy to increase animal-sourced food consumption and exports.

Road maps with specific visions, targets, chal-lenges, strategies, and proposed investments in technology and policy interventions, with ex-pected outputs, outcomes and impacts are mapped out. Through joint effort among interna-tional and national experts, the LMP develop-ment process also builds the analytical capacity of government analysts to carry out data-driven and fact-based analyses for quantitative livestock sector planning.
The LMP provides government policymakers, pri-vate investors, and development partners with re-liable quantitative facts on:
• The current contributions and constraints of the livestock sector.
• The potential of the sector to contribute to national development objectives.
• Priority livestock commodities and value chains and proposed investment options (com-bined technologies and policies).
• Projections of how better targeted invest-ment in livestock can improve economic perfor-mance and improve lives in the sector.
More information: https://www.ilri.org/livestock-master-plans.

To date, ILRI in partnership with the French Agricultur-al Research Centre for International Development, CIRAD, and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and national partners has supported the
development of LMPs in Ethiopia, Rwanda, Tanzania and the Indian state of Bihar. New LMP exercises are currently being conducted in Od-isha State (India), Kenya and the Gambia.

We conducted lesson learning evaluations in the countries where the LMPs have had more than one year to demonstrate impact to assess the success of these exercises and to refine them to increase future impact. The findings from Ethiopia, Rwanda, Tanzania and Bihar (India) are presented here.
LMP assessment methodology

In each country site, some variation of the follow-ing steps was conducted, which comprised both the collection of secondary data and information, as well as in-depth consultations with key stake-holders in the livestock industry.

1. Collect background information in order to a) review and document evidence as to how well the LMP projection targets were achieved, such as in livestock industry trends, and b) to identify key stakeholders for consultation.

2. Establish contact with key livestock officials and other key stakeholders and conduct the con-sultation with stakeholders. These include public officials, non- governmental organizations (NGOs), farmer and donor representatives and private sector actors.
3. Validate the assessment findings with stakeholders and identify ways forward for im-proved implementation of LMPs.

Table 1: Details on the assessment process, a summary of the results of the assessment and finally areas for im-provement.

Ethiopia LMP assessment process The Ministry of Agriculture recommended and facilitated contacts with a number of key stake- holders in the Ethiopian livestock industry. Three consultation meetings for public/government officials, NGOs/donors, and private sector, respectively, were held in 2021, followed by a final validation workshop. Overall results of the Over 60% of the stakeholders had heard of the LMP, and had mixed levels of awareness of its assessment contents. Livestock industry data from both the Government of Ethiopia (GoE), the Ethiopia Central Statistical Agency (CSA) and FAOSTAT show that the projected increases in livestock industry production from the LMP were largely unachieved. Data on public investment in livestock were not easily obtained, but various sources suggest that the LMP contributed in particular to new World Bank/GoE livestock investment of USD132 million (http://projects.worldbank.org/P159382?lang=en), new donor project financing of USD75 million, and new private-sector investments of USD200 million. The analytical results and projections from the LMP were incorporated directly into the GoE Growth and Transformation Plan 2015–2020, which was a key national planning document. In that way, the LMP played an important national planning role. The LMP was perceived to have contributed to the dairy industry particularly through investment in breeding services and infrastructure, and because of strong private co-investment in the dairy value chain. Other perceived benefits included establishment of new quarantine systems for exported animals based on a public-private partnership, new improved forage farms, and the development of new guidelines for improving animal health, welfare and surveillance in the meat value chain. Constraints to LMP implementation were perceived in the overly ambitious targets and projections, and inadequate public finance support beyond that already committed to the livestock sector. In addition, the regional structure of Ethiopian government planning, implementation and budgeting did not match the value chain structure of the LMP. Lessons for future LMPs During development of the LMP, improve coordination between federal, regional and local offices, and secure their participation in the planning. Coordinate budget preparation with the normal budget planning process, not in par-allel, and ensure that budget needs at various levels are addressed. Ensure underlying data and typologies adequately reflect reality on the ground and have sufficient local validation. Establish data collection and monitoring system to gauge and adjust progress associ-ated with the LMP implementation. Rwanda LMP assessment process The Ministry of Agriculture and Animal Resources (MINAGRI) guided the LMP assessment pro-cess, with the director general for animal resources suggesting key stakeholders to include. Government agencies, private industry actors, and NGOs stakeholders were consulted, usual-ly in individual meetings or informal small groups. MINAGRI also emphasized the need to ob-tain farmer-level input into the process. To achieve that, focus group discussions were held with 4-6 farmer
representatives in several districts.

Overall results of the assessment Lessons for future LMPs Bihar LMP assessment process Overall results of the assessment During the LMP projections period (2016/2019), livestock populations in Rwanda re-mained mostly constant, although cattle increased by 13% according to government estimates. Milk production increased by 11% and non-poultry meat by 22%. NGOs and donors indicated that they used the LMP to justify and support proposal de-velopment and relied on some of its projections for the livestock sector. Private actors such as feeds manufacturers said they were aware of the LMP, but had not used it. Government officials (MINAGRI and RAB, the animal resources department) indicated much more familiarity with the LMP, particularly at the central level and had made use of it. District-level veterinary and livestock officials were aware of it. Officials indicated that they use the LMP as a guide in developing sector strategies, projects and activities for Rwanda’s livestock sector. They consider the LMP as the ref-erence and guide for all activities that the ministry plans to carry out. The MINAGRI and RAB confirmed that the Strategic Plan for Agriculture Transformation Phase 4 (PSTA4) was developed using the LMP as a guide with the PSTA4’s information and the road map provided by, and similar to that of, the LMP. The PSTA4 is the implementation plan of the National Agricultural Policy (NAP), which is the agriculture sector’s main strategy document under Rwanda’s National Strategy for Transformation. The LMP also was used to do a livestock sector analysis that provides a comprehensive wider picture for each sub-sector. Stronger involvement of livestock actors at various levels in the LMP development and planning process. The assessment was based on interviews with staff from the Department of Animal and Fisher-ies Resources, Directorate of Animal Husbandry, the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) and the Bihar Veterinary College. The Bihar LMP was to be implemented over five years starting in 2019 to improve the livestock sector in the state but this was delayed because of the COVID-19 pandemic. Thus, this assessment was conducted rather early in the implementation stage, to see if any follow up is needed. One direct impact of LMP is the ‘Digitalization of Livestock Management System (DLMS)’, which is a comprehensive administrative and management system being taken up by the Department of Animal and Fisheries Resources. It is now part of the National Livestock Mission and is an extension of the LMP itself. When the government of Bihar presented the LMP to the National Livestock Mission, they readily agreed and approved it. Bihar will be the first state in India to implement the DLMS under the National Livestock Mission. Under DLMS, all livestock development programs in the state will be available online. The special secretary also informed that the new phase of the World Bank project, developed as part of Kosi River Flood Rehabilitation, has livestock components that were inspired by the LMP. Budget was allocated for piggery development in six project districts, which was not there earlier, and new goat farms, layer farms, broiler farms and a frozen semen station, which were also based on LMP recommendations, have been funded by the government. This was especially needed as there has been some development in the dairy and poultry sub-sectors because of private investment but not in piggery and goatery.
Discussions with private sector actors revealed they had yet to use the LMP

The government is currently implementing a new program ‘Saath Nichai’ (seven determination), whose components include livestock development. Under Saath Nichai, entrepreneurship development is included targeting livestock entrepreneurs rearing goats and pigs who receive about 50% subsidy as incentive. This may be considered an LMP effect promoting private sector investment.

Lessons for future LMPs Tanzania LMP assessment process Overall results of the assessment Targeted consultations with investor groups should be a requirement in the LMP devel-opment process. After the LMP is developed, operational plans should be prepared to guide LMP im-plementation with roles for LMP team members to ensure that they are involved in insti-tutionalizing it the system. Many of those who participated in the Bihar LMP process now work in different departments and are not involved in its implementation. At the beginning of LMP development, an LMP project cell should be formed within the department of agriculture for the development and implementation of LMP for five years with an active monitoring and evaluation component. Data collection is required at regular intervals to know the status of the livestock sector at the grassroots level such as cost of production, milk price, disease status, adherence of breeding policy etc. It is important to include more stakeholders in the development of the LMP, including private sector actors. There is a need to prepare brief supplementary booklets e.g., on dairy, meat and eggs, drawing content from the main LMP document, for easy reference and action by different stakeholders. The findings from the interviews carried out are clustered into three stakeholder groups: gov- ernment ministries, departments and Local Government Authorities (LGAs); private sector and NGOs. Interviewees demonstrated knowledge and familiarity with the contents and goals of the master plan although there was less awareness of it by LGAs. Interviewees, however, reported lower levels of knowledge about the implementation status of the plan. Government (ministries, departments and LGAs): The Tanzania livestock master plan (TLMP) is commonly used as guide by investors on where to invest in the livestock sector. The understanding of the TMLP among government stakeholders that were consulted varied. Several interviewees who participated directly in the TLMP’s development had a clear understanding of the master plan and its targets, while those whose participation was limited had a moderate understanding it. In some instances, only a few department heads demonstrated a thorough understanding of the TLMP’s vision and goals. The level of awareness of the TLMP at the LGAs-level is relatively low with only 30% of interviewees reporting being aware of the plan. As a result, the TLMP is not frequently referenced by the LGAs in the development of their district agricultural plans. They usually refer to the governing party CCM (Chama Cha Mapinduzi) manifesto, the National Development Strategy, and Agricultural Sector Development Programme (ADSP) II priorities. It should be noted that several of the government stakeholders interviewed reported that they were not sufficiently involved in the formulation of the TLMP but were instead engaged at the launch stage of the plan. Private sector: 50% of the interviewed private sector respondents had heard about the TLMP but had limited knowledge of how it was being implemented in their respective sectors. It was evident that the private sector is interested in the TLMP, but most of the actors did not know how the TLMP’s impact is being measured. However, some of the private sector stakeholders indicated that they have worked in close collaboration with the government to address challenges hindering investments in the livestock sector. NGOs : About 90% of the interviewed NGO respondents were aware of the TLMP and its objectives
because most of them were involved in the TLMP process since its inception. But their participation
in the implementation of the TLMP has been minimal. For example, 80% of the respondents reported
that they have never received an update or report on the TLMP’s implementation progress from the
ministry.
Lessons for future LMPs
All the key sector players must be identified and effectively represented in the TLMP’s
implementation and a budget set aside to effectively resource implementation.
The Ministry of Agriculture should create a system to track and report on the implemen-tation of the
TLMP. This should be underpinned by a robust data collection and moni-toring system for effective
monitoring.
The government should coordinate the TLMP’s implementation. This should start by government
first appointing a team to specifically bring together the different players and resources needed to
ensure key TLMP deliverables are met.

Lessons for future LMP development and implementation

In several countries the LMP was confirmed as having contributed directly to national livestock development plans. It was also seen as a reference point for the de- velopment of projects, strategies and planning docu- ments. In some cases, the LMP contributed to specific investments in infrastructure of sub-sector projects. In the case of Bihar, the administrative and manage-ment system was taken up by the state government.
Key lessons include:
Involve more stakeholders during development of the LMP: This will ensure coordination between fed- eral, regional and local offices and secure their partic- ipation in the planning.
to track and report on the implementation of the TLMP. This should be underpinned by a robust data collection and monitoring system for effective monitor-ing.
Ensure institutionalization of the LMP: Operational

plans are needed to help institutionalize LMPs in dif- ferent countries, with involvement of LMP team mem- bers. An LMP project cell, or bureau, could be formed within the relevant ministry for the development and implementation of the LMP for five years with an active monitoring and evaluation component.
Contextualize LMPs for local use: In more

decentral-ized countries, it is important that local government administrators are aware of the LMP and it is appro-priateness for use in their own planning systems. This was seen in both Ethiopia and Tanzania where the LMP was not appropriate for local level use.

Assessing the environmental impacts of livestock   production using the CLEANED approach
KEY MESSAGES
By Emmanuel Mwema, Gwladys Boukpessi, Rein Van der Hoek, An Notenbaert

· CLEANED calculates the environmental footprint of livestock systems and value chains in terms of land requirements, productivity, economics, soil impacts (e.g., erosion, N balance), greenhouse gas emissions (GHGe) and water impacts.

· Livestock production activities significantly impact the climate and environment, such as land and soil, water and biodiversity. This tool allows users to assess these impacts and how they would change through the introduction of new technology or an altered livestock production model.

· The tool is easy-to-use and keeps data input requirements to a minimum. Input data is related to the livestock production system and not necessarily the whole farm. The rapid results from the tool provide evidence (in quantitative terms) for decision-making and planning purposes.
INTRODUCTION
CLEANED officially stands for Comprehensive Livestock Environmental Assessment for improved Nutrition, a secured Environment and sustainable Development along livestock value chains.

It is a desktop application tool that quantifies the environmental footprints of livestock systems and value chains. In contrast to its long name, it is designed to provide rapid results in a data scarce environment. With a few clicks of a button, it calculates the land and water requirements, soil health impacts, carbon sequestration and greenhouse gas emissions (GHGe) associated with different types of livestock enterprises and estimates positive or negative changes as a result of different intervention scenarios. The tool is most useful in the design and planning phase of projects, initiatives or programs that look into farm level interventions because it allows users to understand impacts and trade-offs, and to better design sustainable livestock systems.
· Results generated from the tool can help policy makers, scientists, project managers and development partners design sustainable livestock intensification pathways.

THE CHALLENGE

Globally, livestock production generates more than 40% of agricultural GDP and is among the fastest growing agricultural sectors. Livestock are important agents for nutrient cycling, especially through converting forages and crop residues into manure. In the developing world, the sector improves livelihood resilience.

However, livestock and associated feed production poses a threat to ecosystems through GHGe, land degradation and deforestation, water pollution and depletion, nutrient mining and erosion, as well as biodiversity loss. As demand for livestock products continues to rise, there is a pressing need to develop interventions to reduce the environmental footprint of livestock production. According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), production of animal protein is expected to grow by around 1.7% per year between 2010 and 2050, with meat production projected to rise by nearly 70%, aquaculture by 90% and dairy by 55%.

The CLEANED tool was therefore designed specifically to help users plan the most sustainable interventions. It assesses the trade-offs in different contexts and from divergent livestock management practices.
WHAT ARE THE BENEFITS OF USING CLEANED?

Its simplicity, minimum data entry, flexibility and adaptability for local systems all make CLEANED an excellent decision- making tool during various stages of planning farm-scale interventions. By quickly evaluating the impacts of a wide range of interventions, users are able to select sets of promising interventions to be discussed and assessed further. The rapid ex-ante assessment allows users to find better intensification pathways that result in reduced environmental footprints. Results from the tool can be scaled to regional and national levels thus reducing unnecessary costs and time.

Production of animal feed often has the biggest environment impact in livestock farming systems. CGIAR researchers are working with farmers in East Africa to identify appropriate forage feed varieties that can provide benefits with minimal natural resource use.

HOW CLEANED WORKS

CLEANED has been designed to adapt to a poor data environment. It is especially suited for developing countries where relevant data to assess environmental impacts can be scarce. In such cases, data is collected locally from secondary data sources and through expert opinion for use in the assessments. This differentiates CLEANED from other existing tools that are generally knowledge- intensive and require significant time and input data.
Use of the tool involves two processes:
1. Collecting and inputting the baseline data—farm location, seasons, livestock production systems, feed baskets, farm inputs, amount of precipitation etc.

2. Data analysis and generation of reports for different scenarios of how the livestock production systems might change. The user has two pathways to follow; either to run calculations on the desktop interface1 using Run program icon or proceed to R software calculations. The output is the same on either of the pathways.

Resources used in the entire CLEANED process include costs for building technical capacity for users, data collection/field survey and time to carry out the assessments and generating reports (typically between two and four weeks). Where input data is readily available, assessments usually take a maximum of five working days.

1) The purpose of the desktop interface is to run the R model and is meant for users without R or Java Script Object Notation (JSON) knowledge. The results tab in the CLEANED Desktop application shows the results of the assessments.

WHO IS THE TOOL BUILT FOR?

The tool can be applied to a wide range of projects and can be used by anyone interested in livestock enterprises including scientists, students, development partners, policy makers and project managers. Researchers from the CGIAR Research Program on Livestock have used CLEANED in various countries around the world, such as:
• In the southern highlands of Tanzania – the tool was used to assess the environmental impacts of improved feeding as a livestock intensification pathway in smallholder farms.
• In Western Kenya – the non-governmental organization Send a Cow (SAC) partnered with the International Center for Tropical
Agriculture (CIAT) to use the tool to assess the land requirement for a dairy cow in western Kenya under different feeding regimes and explored the trade-offs of these feeding strategies.
• In Nicaragua – in collaboration with FAO, CLEANED was used to assess the environmental impact of intervention scenarios to guide public and private investments (see case study below).

• In Ethiopia – at a workshop led by the Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI), the tool enabled participants to appreciate the tradeoff between increasing production and productivity, and maintaining or reducing environmental impact.
CLEANED can integrate data from multiple sources–from farmers, experts, NGOs, researchers and local governments–which is practical in countries where data availability is limited.

CONCLUSION

As the global population continues to increase, so will the demand for livestock products. Although livestock production provides livelihoods for billions of people around the world and contributes to food and national security, it also negatively affects land, water, and biodiversity resources. In addition, livestock production and associated fodder production contribute to global warming and pollution. According to the most recent Intergovernmental Panel for Climate Change (IPCC) estimates, the FAO determined that global livestock production accounted for 14.5% of all anthropogenic GHGe’s . CLEANED was developed to produce rapid multi-dimensional environmental impact assessments of livestock transformation in mixed crop-
livestock farming systems in developing countries.

The CLEANED tool provides an alternative to other tools and approaches for assessing environmental impacts of crop and livestock value chains, that are generally more knowledge- intensive, require significant time and data input, and usually only assess short-term impacts at field and farm scales. CLEANED allows users to assess impacts of new technologies or system interventions. This helps to ensure that initiatives aiming to improve incomes and food security in livestock value chains have a minimum environmental footprint, while lifting people out of poverty.
CASE STUDY: Strengthening Sustainable Dairy and Beef Value Chains in Nicaragua
A swathe of degraded pastureland in Nicaragua. Photo Alliance Bioversity and CIAT/Rein Van der Hoek

Nicaragua’s livestock sector is the largest in Central America with 200,000 smallholder farmers generating 75% of their income from dual-purpose (milk and meat) cattle farming. The productivity and product quality of Nicaraguan smallholder cattle farmers is affected by a lack of sufficient infrastructure, combined with often sub-optimal production practices. Inadequate pasture management has caused soil degradation and feed deficiencies, issues which have been exacerbated by climate change. New approaches are needed to improve environmental integrity.

The CLEANED approach was applied by the Livestock and Fish CGIAR Research Program, in partnership with local partners Instituto Nicaragüense de Tecnología Agropecuaria (INTA) and Universidad Nacional Agraria (UNA), to carry out a rapid, ex-ante assessment of

Permanent link to cite or share this item https://hdl.handle.net/10568/155114 External link to download this item https://www.tropentag.de/abstract.php?code=VZkPs1QH DOI Abstract/Description Socio-ecological systems are based on the perspective of humans in nature. Natural systems produce ecosystem services for human beings, while social systems intervene in natural systems with positive (environmental benefits) and negative externalities. Livestock production takes place in a natural ecosystem, with human intervention. Accordingly, in livestock farming there exist both ecosystem services and environmental benefits. Our objective is to identify the main ecosystem services and environmental benefits present in livestock farming and propose an integral valuation strategy. We conducted an extensive literature review, established a working group with experts from the field, and conducted applications of proposed methods in the field. Based on this, we identified and prioritised seven ecosystem services and three environmental benefits for valuation, namely, food service, feed service, carbon storage and sequestration, microclimatic regulation, soil fertility, habitat for species, aesthetic appreciation, methane emissions reduction, water footprint reduction, and land use reduction. Our integral valuation strategy consists of the implementation of three valuation methods, i.e., ecological valuation, economic valuation, and social valuation. Our main result is the design of ten integral valuation strategies ready to be piloted in the field. These strategies will be fundamental for the economic and environmental assessment of different interventions in livestock farming and will complement traditional cost-benefit and financial viability analyses. We have currently implemented these strategies in three studies in Colombia to evaluate the reduction of methane emissions in silvopastoral systems with improved pastures and the reduction of the carbon footprint in meat and milk production. Our findings show favourable outcomes when the environmental values are captured. The integral value of ecosystem services and environmental benefits will provide crucial support for informed decision-making on specific restoration initiatives, considering the project's objectives and the potential return on investment. The level of chronic malnutrition among children in Rwanda remains high. Only 30% of children aged 6-23 months consume a diet that meets the minimum dietary diversity requirements, while just 47% achieve minimum meal frequency. Furthermore, 38% of children under five years are stunted according to the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda. Under the Feed the Future Innovations Labs for Livestock Systems research project, the Enhancing milk quality and consumption for improved income and nutrition in Rwanda project has been working to improve child nutrition in the country through the Gabura Amata Mubyeyi (which means parents, give milk ) intervention. The intervention focuses on using social behavioural change communication to promote animal-source foods consumption, particularly the drinking of milk among Girinka households. Three Stones International, the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and Research Triangle International (RTI), liaised with the nationally appointed officers and technical working groups for approval of the developed messages, images and counselling cards. They were also shared with the team tasked with updating the nationwide counselling package used by community health workers. This approach allowed for integration of the intervention counselling cards into the existing national maternal and child nutrition (MIYCN) programs and related activities implemented by community health workers. The Gabura Amata Mubyeyi intervention was implemented between February and September 2019, reaching about 3,500 mothers in Ruhango and Nyabihu districts on average per month. Social behaviour change communication intervention materials intended to improve animal-source foods consumption were designed in collaboration with Rwanda s National Early Childhood Development Program, which coordinates nutrition activities in the country. The materials consisted of five counselling cards, one poster, and one brochure translated into Kinyarwanda for effective language reach to the locals. A counselling card specifically dedicated to the promotion of animal-source foods did not exist in the previous national MIYCN counselling package, which was developed in 2011. Revised national counselling cards were developed with a message titled Your baby needs animal-source foods during stakeholder design workshops in which Three Stones International, the project implementing partner, shared the tested messages from the Gabura Amata Mubyeyi intervention, promoting animal-source foods for young children. These updated counselling cards were validated at the national level through the National Child Development Agency and have now been adopted into the national community health workers curriculum. One of the newly developed counselling cards promoting animal-source food consumption (photo credit: National MIYCN counseling cards). Much debate between the project team and stakeholders went into the discussion on the appropriate time to introduce cow s milk to young children, before it was agreed to continue emphasizing that cow s milk be started at 12 months. Specific messages on this and the importance of hygiene, safe handling and storage of fresh cow s milk were also developed. The intervention counselling cards were designed with culturally appropriate messages and images targeting the pregnant and lactating women with children under five years of age. Their key messages focus on: 1) the importance and benefits of animal-source foods and milk consumption; 2) the appropriate quantities of animal-source foods and cow s milk to be consumed by pregnant and lactating women and young children; 3) the appropriate time to introduce cow s milk and animal-source foods to young children; 4) recognizing cow s milk allergy or animal-source food intolerance symptoms and treatment; and 5) the importance of hygiene, food safety and storage of fresh milk. The key messages, images and counselling cards were also developed with a gender sensitive lens that promotes the inclusion of mothers, fathers and caregivers in the initiative and translated into Kinyarwanda. A counselling card depicting both men and women participating in feeding their children (photo credit: Three Stones International). From the selected model families of the Gabura Amata Mubyeyi intervention, it was evident that inclusion of men in the counselling card images showing them engaging in child nutrition activities led to positive behaviour changes at home. The inclusion of husbands in nutrition education sessions led to greater understanding of the importance of animal-source foods and mothers found it easier to discuss their household nutritional needs and priorities with their husbands. The men too were delighted to acquire new knowledge. Following the successes registered in the course of the project, behaviour change messaging targeting mothers, fathers and caregivers has emerged as a key means to increase animal-source food consumption, especially milk, at the household and community level. Communicating compelling messages that promote the consumption of animal-source food through various channels (interpersonal and print) results in behaviour change that increases diet diversity and reduces child stunting. About SAPLING

CGIAR’s Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender inclusion (SAPLING) is working in seven countries focusing on livestock value chains to package and scale out tried-and- tested, as well as new, innovations in livestock health, genetics, feed and market systems. SAPLING aims to demonstrate that improvements in livestock productivity can offer a triple win: generating improved livelihoods and nutritional outcomes; contributing to women’s empowerment; and, reducing impacts on climate and the environment. Its seven focus countries are Ethiopia, Kenya, Mali, Nepal, Tanzania, Uganda and Vietnam.
Acknowledgements

This work was conducted as part of the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity. CGIAR research is supported by contributions to the CGIAR Trust Fund. CGIAR is a global research partnership for a food-secure future dedicated to transforming food, land, and water systems in a climate crisis.
Background to training

An exploratory study conducted by the CGIAR’s Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender inclusion (SAPLING) work package 2 in March–April 2023 in Masaka, Mukono and Wakiso districts in Uganda showed nutrition knowledge gaps for both men and women livestock farmers. Results also revealed socio-cultural norms based on beliefs that hinder consumption of some animal-source foods (ASFs) for some members of the society, particularly children and women. For instance, some cultures hinder consumption of ASFs such as eggs, pork and certain types of fish for pregnant women. SAPLING in collaboration with stakeholders co-designed a social behaviour change communication (SBCC) intervention that goes beyond the provision of nutrition education to improve nutrition knowledge but also focuses on addressing norms to demystify consumption of ASFs by children and women of childbearing age. The intervention was implemented by health workers, specifically the village health teams (VHTs) through a cluster-randomized controlled trial design with three study arms in Mukono and Masaka districts as follows:

1. T0 - One third of the clusters (villages) were randomly assigned to receive nutrition information provided only to women using adapted Ministry of Health's Maternal Infant and Young Children Adolescent Nutrition (MIYCAN) counselling cards.
2. T0+T1: - One third of the clusters were randomly assigned to receive nutrition information provided to both men and women using MIYCAN counselling cards.

3. T0+T1+T2: The remaining one third of the clusters were randomly assigned to receive nutrition information provided to both men and women using MIYCAN cards and a gender transformative intervention targeting men and women to address social norms associated with consumption of livestock derived foods particularly for women and children.

Health workers and traditional leaders selected to implement the SBCC interventions were trained to deliver the interventions for the specific study arms. They were trained in maternal and child nutrition and optimal practices for inclusion of animal-source foods in healthy diets, as well as social norms messaging to demystify consumption of ASFs by women and children.
Location and modality
The training was held in three locations: Maple Leaf Hotel, the sub-county offices in Masaka District, and in two primary schools in Mukono District.
Dates
The training was implemented from 6–10 August 2024.
Who conducted the training
A cascade model of training delivered in three tiers was implemented to provide training to trainers – from the national, sub-county and village levels as follows:

4. International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) staff trained 5 national trainers comprising 3 officers from the Ministry of Health Nutrition Division and 2 senior Buganda Kingdom officials from Mukono and Masaka districts for 2 days,
5. The Ministry of Health and Buganda Kingdom officials trained 175 subcounty health assistants from the Mukono and Masaka districts health offices for three days, and
6. Subcounty health assistants trained 752 village health teams and traditional leaders for two days, with backstopping from the Ministry of Health officials and the Buganda Kingdom officials.
Objectives of the training

The overall training goal was to enhance the capacities of traditional leaders and health care workers in maternal and child nutrition and optimal practices for inclusion of animal-source foods in diets. The objective of the training was to capacitate the village health teams (VHTs) and sub-county health assistants (supervisors of VHTs) on the tools, materials and approaches to be used for the gendered social behaviour change communication (SBCC) interventions to households and caregivers aimed at; (i) enhancing nutrition knowledge of healthy diets, and (ii) mindset change on social norms that limit consumption of animal-source foods as part of healthy diets, especially for young children and women of reproductive age.
Training agenda
The training was conducted over eight days (Annex 1).
Training participants

All village level health care workers, specifically VHTs from Mukono and Masaka districts were profiled to obtain basic information to enable selection of those to be trained to participate in the implementation of the SBCC intervention. Introduction

CGIAR started a series of initiatives to implement its 2030 research and innovation strategy. One of these is the ‘Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender inclusion (SAPLING)’ an initiative implemented by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), the International Centre for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) and the Alliance of Bioversity International & International Centre for Tropical Agriculture (ABC-CIAT). The aim of SAPLING is to enable 800,000 livestock producers – especially women and youth in seven countries to engage in inclusive value chains and achieve sustainable productivity gains resulting in improved livelihoods. Uganda is one of the seven countries identified as a focus country for SAPLING given the importance of livestock in the livelihoods of its people and the commitment of public and private actors to transform food systems through sustainable livestock development. In Uganda, SAPLING aims to improve livelihoods of livestock producers and other actors in the pig, dairy and beef value chains.
Work package 2 of SAPLING focuses on innovations and practices for consumption of livestock derived foods as part of diverse diets. Its objectives are to:

o Co-create innovative models and approaches for social behaviour change communication to influence behaviour on diets – inclusion of livestock-derived foods (LDFs) in diverse diets, and consideration of food safety
o Design and pilot a decision support framework and tools to identify context specific bottlenecks in LDFs’ consumption, and overall food security and identify options to address the constraints.

Work package 2 has a strong gender focus and aims to generate evidence on how social norms influences and impacts on nutrition outcomes and explore approaches to engage men to support food and nutrition decisions.

The team followed a systematic process in identifying, co-creating and implementing a social behaviour change communication (SBCC) intervention aimed at influencing behaviour in diets and food safety practices. The following four step process was followed:
1. Diagnostic studies implemented in 2022/2023
2. Stakeholder co-creation workshop
3. Piloting of the SBCC interventions
4. SBCC roll out

Diagnostic studies to identify barriers to food and nutrition security and LDFs

A food systems framework commonly referred to as Food Systems, Environments, Nutrition: Structured Evidence (FoodSENSE) () was developed by SAPLING Work package 2 to guide identification of food and nutrition security bottlenecks from a food systems perspective. The findings from its implementation in Masaka, Mukono and Mpigi districts identified key challenges affecting the four food security pillars namely, availability, access, utilization and stability in the food system. The challenges were related to poor market access for nutrient dense foods, food price fluctuations occasioned by seasonality, poor storage and processing infrastructure; negative social and cultural norms that restricted consumption of nutritious foods especially for women and children; limited knowledge on nutrition and food handling; and limited enforcement of existing policies on food safety and hygiene in the markets (Caulfied et. al, 2023).

A further exploratory qualitative study was implemented in Masaka and Mukono districts in 2023 through focus group discussions (FGDs) and key informant interviews to identify the binding constraints to consumption of LDFs especially among children and women of reproductive age. The districts are in the central region of Uganda and dominated by people of the Buganda ethnicity. Together, the two districts are home to about 800,000 people, with between 15-20% of these being children under the age of 5, the major focus of our nutrition intervention. The districts were selected because, despite the high level of livestock ownership, consumption of LDFs remains low. This has resulted in high prevalence of malnutrition

in children, with data from the 2016 DHS showing stunting to be higher by about 2% relative to the rest of the country (Uganda Bureau of Statistics, 2018). We also considered factors such as the lack of community- based nutrition programs that target consumption of LDFs. A map depicting the two districts is presented in Figure 1.

Limited basic knowledge of nutrition and social norms were identified as key barriers. Two social norms that limit the consumption of LDFs by women and children were discovered to be; (i) men frequenting pork joints located along the streets, where they eat diets rich in LDFs, and then go home to eat the food they provide to the rest of the family, (ii) while women generally share LDFs prepared in the household, specific parts of livestock (especially chicken) are traditionally given to particular household members (Ahmed et. al., 2023). A follow up household baseline survey was implemented to collect household level data and benchmark baseline values of indicators for nutrition outcomes of interest prior to the social behavior change communication intervention. It is against this background that three SBCC modules were identified as focus points to address the constraints around nutrition knowledge and social norms limiting the consumption of LDFs.
Module 1 - Mismatch between prevalence and perception of norms

A very active and important strand of social norms literature is the study of the differences between actual and perceived prevalence of norms, and how researchers have exploited these in interventions aimed at countering them. The most famous and one of the first of these studies relates to female labor force participation in Saudi Arabia (Bursztyn et al., 2020). To study this in our context, we asked respondents a series of questions relating to their views on widely prevalent social norms as part of the household baseline survey. Using a Likert scale, the participants were asked to ‘state whether they strongly agree, agree, are neutral, disagree, or strongly disagree to given statements’. We also asked how many people out of ten in the villages would agree with their response (perceived prevalence). From the first set of questions, with responses from a 5-point Likert scale, we constructed a series of variables that are assigned ‘1’ if the respondent ‘strongly agreed’ or ‘agreed’ with the statement. For the second set of statements on perceptions of the prevalence of these norms, we obtained the average number of people out of 10 from their village they perceived to support their position. These results, both the first and second set of questions, are decomposed to obtain the share of respondents (percentage).
The results reveal differences between perceived and actual prevalence, both among and between men and women as presented in Figures 2 to 4.

Given the large discrepancies between actual and perceived beliefs, we aim to bridge the divide through SBCC, and by so doing, move actual practice closer to individual beliefs rather than perceptions. Through this, we will correct the beliefs of those who practice these norms because they perceive others in the community to practice them. In this second module of the social norms’ intervention, we focus on the inequality in food distribution and consumption. We provide evidence of its prevalence and stress how it impacts the outcomes of children and women, especially pregnant women. We also stress the fact that to ensure better education outcomes for the children and their future well-being, some LDF proteins cooked at home should be given to them. This is relevant because parents invest a lot of resources in their children’s education. From our data, this is about UGX 1.2 million per year for households with a child in high school. If parents expect children to do well in school, they should provide better nutrition for them at a young age.
Module 3 - Men eating outside the household

Within the ethnic groups in central Uganda, it is generally accepted that men eat outside their homes in street restaurants and male-centered socialization events. Data from our FGDs showed that about 50% of male respondents had eaten food from outside the home in the past 7 days, compared to less than 10% of women. This has led to a situation where men are mostly well nourished while providing limited nutritious diets to their families.

For this module we aim to design an intervention to address norms regarding men eating outside their homes and selling most of the livestock instead of leaving some for household consumption. We suggest eggs as cheap, but effective alternatives for proteins. We show that the cost of eggs for household members is cheaper than that of men consuming LDFs outside their homes.
Stakeholders’ co-creation workshop

A two-day stakeholder co-creation workshop was held in November 2023 to discuss the planned SBCC intervention and to co-create the SBCC messages and brainstorm, on appropriate delivery models. Participants comprised of representatives from the Ministry of health- nutrition department, local government – district health officers, community health teams, cultural leaders, nutrition department of national universities and non-government organizations. The workshop process was guided by the following objectives;
1. To craft effective messaging toward addressing norms limiting the availability of LDFs to children and mothers.
o The need to address norms limiting the availability of LDFs to children and mothers.
Identify key components of effective messaging for such behavior change.
o Create compelling and tailored messages that resonate with the social and emotional needs of the targeted audience.
o Conduct user testing to refine messaging based on feedback.
2. To identify which group of people are best placed to deliver the social norms’ intervention
3. Craft an effective and catchy brand name for the campaign.
4. To determine what is the best format to deliver the interventions.

Emily Ouma, the Uganda country lead for SAPLING and the lead for Work package 2. She gave a presentation on the objectives under work package 2 of SAPLING. Hardi Ahmed, a PhD student from the University of Alicante in Spain under SAPLING, presented an overview of the nutrition intervention study in Uganda. He presented the results from the exploratory study (Ahmed et al. 2023). The workshop participants were split into three groups to discuss and provide input into the results presented.

In each group, participants explored reasons why people behaved in the manner they did regarding LDFs. The process was more investigative, asking ‘why’, and participants were encouraged to share their stories.

This was done by synthesizing information gathered during the empathizing stage and defining the social norms and behaviors to be addressed. Participants developed two or three problem statements that captured the challenges and opportunities identified during the empathy stage and presented and discussed them in plenary. They identified which of the statements clearly articulated the emotional challenges, issues, and opportunities associated with the findings presented during the empathy stage. Ideation stage

The problem statements generated in stage 2, empathy maps etc. were presented to the groups to think of creative ways to counter the social norms to address the key needs, challenges, and concerns that had been crafted in the problem statement. Open, divergent, and creative thinking was encouraged to generate a wide range of ideas to address the key findings from the earlier design phases. The main point of interest was dealing with the challenges raised in the problem statement. Participants were encouraged to build on each other’s ideas to create more comprehensive and innovative ideas for messaging to effectively counter social norms. Avenues to explore included workshops, video presentations, role-playing activities, community cooking demonstrations, hospital-based campaigns, etc. Using flip charts/boards and sticky notes, each group posted all the ideas that they generated. Workshop participants then together moved around the room and reviewed the lists generated by the groups as shown in Table 2. The three ideas with the highest votes, listed in chronological order, were selected as the ideal fit for further exploration. We all need LDFs, not only the men. • Prepare a skit that compares two families. In family 1, the father eats all the LDFs, and the children and women are malnourished and in poor health; in family 2, the father shares with the rest of the family, and they are healthy. The key message is that all members of the family need to have LDFs as part of their diets. Group 2 • Communal level: I understand that based on our societal norms, men are entitled to the most nutritious parts of LDFs. While the role of men in the household is important, they do not need that amount of LDFs to be healthy. As a result, let us ensure that children and women in your household also receive more of the LDFs for better health. • Household level: The mentor asks households to tell him/her how they distribute food, and he/she will try to explain the norm in practice: why they are distributing food the way they are and why they need to change. • Institutional level: Your institutions hold a lot of influence on how people in the community behave. Children and women of childbearing age in your community do not receive enough protein to promote better lives, and this is because men are allocated the most nutritious parts of meat. To promote the future of your community, you need to nudge men towards allocating more livestock source proteins to other family members. Group 3 • Stunting, underweight, poor growth rates in children, and poor performance in school are a result of lack of LDFs in diets. Men should change their ways and be involved in planning the family diets and ensure the provision of LDFs to improve child nutrition, academic performance, and health for current and future generations. • Men, you are the engines of the home. As you partake of the LDFs think of the young future engines, boys and girls, that require proteins from LDFs to be strong and healthy. • Engage in backyard livestock farming (rabbitry, poultry, pigs) first and foremost for food and nutrition security at home and the surplus for financial income. • Billboard: Ladies and gentlemen, let us help each other to prepare delicious balanced meals that include LDFs for all family members so that we have healthy, intelligent future
generations.
