ICT for dairy data capture from farms

The rapid expansion of ICT alongside mobile based solutions for “paperless” exchange of information has catalyzed a transformation for information sharing in the smallholder farming systems of Africa (World Bank, 2011). The challenge within countries, Ethiopia included, is to adapt and expand critical infrastructure to support ICT adoption which includes mobile telecommunications networks and cloud computing facilities. ICT-enabled services can use multiple platforms (eg radio, e-tools, short message services) to provide information for various actors in the dairy value chain. Through the ADGG Program, mobile phone-based solutions have been adapted to capture and transmit data on performance of dairy cattle to the centralized national databases hosted on a cloud-based data platform (ADGG Data Platform). The ADGG data platform collates and synthesizes farm information and subjects it to various analyses using advanced analytical tools. Results from analyses are used to develop targeted feedback information that are then shared with farmers and extension service providers, to respectively inform their management and service delivery planning or decisions. Initial feedback information includes herd assessment, and individual animal and herd performance benchmarking. The platform has also developed electronic training resources that provide valuable information on breeding
management practices in dairy herds (ADGG Dairy Tool).

Dairy herds and animals registered by ADGG, PAID and Luke projects have been harmonized into one national dairy cattle database. Total number of dairy herds, dairy cattle with pedigree and test-day milk records and test-day milk data registered in the digital ADGG platform are more than 72,000, 116,000 and 279,000, respectively. The data can be accessed via the Ethiopia
country landing page (see Figure 3). This program is piloted in 98 districts in Amhara, Oromia, SNNP, Sidama and Tigray regions and Addis Ababa city administration.

ICT based extension and feedback

ICT based farmer-feedback systems have been developed and deployed to assist farmers improve their cows’ productivity based on performance data collected from their herds. SMS based feedback system following the “cow’s gestation calendar and dairy production management” support messages were reaching smallholder dairy farmers through digital extension. Farm data on milking and calving, AI service, feeding and other records, received from the farm through the ADGG platform is then synthesized and feedback shared with producers in the form of short text messages through their mobile phones. More than 8,890,258 education SMS messages and 162,456 instant feedback SMS messages based on cow gestation dates have been provided to farmers by ADGG in the last four years. The SMSs’ have been translated into and delivered in three local languages (Amharic, Tigrigna and Afan Oromo). Information received by farmers guides their adoption of improved cow management practices which will ultimately lead to
sustained productivity gains, income, nutrition, and poverty reduction.

Investors and service providers including cooperatives can also leverage on the platform’s agility and robustness to better aggregate information on product quantities and demands for inputs in different areas. The public sector needs to have requisite policies in place that encourage innovation around ICT to enable the use of ICT services to promote improvements while at the

same time protect the smallholder producers from complex challenges when exposed to large global actors, and secure smallholders’ ownership of data and appropriate data access rights. Appropriate, locally accessible, affordable, and smart tools and applications are required to inform timely decision making and to improve herd and system’s productivity and profitability. Viability and sustainability of the dairy industry in sub-Saharan Africa, hinges on the integration of ICT tools that help increase accessibility of extension services by farmers. This is because of the highly fragmented nature of smallholder dairy herds, they can’t all be reached by the public extension service and such limited access to extension services and support significantly hamper the sector’s overall performance. Inadequate access to technical advice and services reduces the ability of farmers to address everyday challenges resulting in poor performance of the herd. Development and deployment of ICT based services would facilitate improvements in farm production and profitability, animal health, animal welfare, and the environment and at the same time create access to technical and market information that leads to improvement in efficiency and productivity gains along the dairy value chains (Mwantimwa, 2019). Moreover, the use of ICT holds considerable potential to make agriculture more attractive to the youth because of their receptiveness to ICT tools, making it easier for them to access dairy information and services (Nuer, 2018). Obstacles that hinder dairy farmers from accessing agricultural information using ICT tools include availability of electricity, internet connectivity and its ability to deliver timely agricultural information and feedback. Thus, advancement of policies and legislations by the government to enhance the adoption and use of ICT technologies in dairy farming are necessary
to transform the dairy sector in the country.
Use of genomics technology for dairy genetic evaluation

Genomic selection has become the method of choice for identifying genetically superior sires and dams in developed countries due to the accelerated rate of genetic progress mostly because of the reduction in generation interval and increased prediction accuracy. In genomic selection animals can be selected accurately early in life, based on their genomic predictions. Furthermore, it is much more suited for selection of traits that are difficult or expensive to measure: such as fertility, disease resistance, methane emissions, and feed conversion traits (Hayes et al., 2013). Garcia-Ruiz et al. (2016) reported that genetic gains for milk, fat, and protein yields for registered cows in the USA were 50, 2.2, and 1.6 kg per year before genomic selection was

adopted but increased by over twofold to 109, 6.0, and 4.1 kg per year after genomic selection was introduced. The enabling factors for the huge success in genomic selection in developed countries include the availability of well-established infrastructure for routine data capture systems and conventional genetic evaluation. In addition, the existence of well-developed dairy breeding companies has significantly contributed to this success. These companies routinely undertake and/or contribute to the design of the genotyping strategy for widely used dairy bulls and the associated cost (Mrode et al., 2019). However, in developing countries, most of the dairy production occurs in small holder systems, where herd sizes are small and with little or no routine systems for capturing performance and pedigree data (Kosgey and Okeyo, 2007). The use of genomic information for genetic evaluation and determination of the breed composition of crossbred animal using admixture analysis (Strucken et al., 2017; Marshall et al., 2019), parentage identification and prediction of the genetic merit of animals using the genomic relationship matrix for genotyped animals present unique opportunities for mitigating the limiting data infrastructure in developing countries. In situations where only a proportion of the dairy cows are genotyped, the genotypic information can be combined with pedigree information using the Single Step GBLUP (ssGBLUP) approach (Misztal, et al., 2009) to undertake
prediction of the genetic merit for all animals.

In Ethiopia, ADGG has applied genomic technology to genetically evaluate and determine breed composition of crossbred animals kept under small and medium dairy production system. Hair samples were collected from crossbred cows and bulls for genotyping. The samples were genotyped, and genotype information was combined with phenotypic data collected through the ADGG platform to estimate genomic estimated breeding value (gEBV) and thus select bulls and cows with higher genetic merit for breeding. The estimation of gEBV was based on a pilot data from 3,802 cows with 53,955 test day records and a pedigree consisting of 113,447 records. Genotypic data were available on 5,146 animals which were genotyped with the GeneSeek Genomic Profiler (GGP) Bovine 50K chip. About 47,843 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were returned from the laboratory and after the usual edits, 40,581 SNPs were available for analysis. These were imputed to the Illumina HD chip (686,052 SNPs) using a reference population consisting of crossbred cattle from a previous East Africa Dairy Genetics Gain
project and several European Holstein-Friesian, Jersey, Guernsey, and Ayrshire purebred animals (Aliloo et al., 2018).

Initially, genetic parameters for milk yield were estimated from the same pilot data consisting of 3226 cows and 53147 test day records using ASReml (Gilmour et al, 2009) with ssGBLUP. For the parameter estimation, cows were required to have at least three test day records in a lactation, a minimum age at first calving of 18 months and days in milk was restricted to between 4 and 500 days. Data from all lactations were used but lactation greater than 1, were set to 2. The model fitted was:
Milk = HY + PYm + age.lac + fixed-lactation-curves(calving-season) + breed + htd + pe + animal

Where HY- herd-year of calving, PYm = production year-month, htd = herd-test-date, age.lac = age effects as interaction with lactation and fixed lactation curves consisted of Legendre polynomials and Wilmink function, pe and animal represents the permanent environment and additive animal genetic effect. The H matrix used in the ssGBLUP procedure consisted of 5169 animals with 4719 having only pedigree information and 450 of these with genotypes. The variances obtained from the model for the animal genetic, pe, htd and residual effects were 2.631, 4.264, 1.339 and 6.805 respectively and the heritability estimate was 0.17±0.03.

Similar edits applied for the estimation of genetic parameter were used for the genomic prediction except that cows with one test day records were included in the analysis. Thus 3802 cows with 53955 test day records were used for the genomic prediction. The genotypes on 5146 animals were included in the analysis, although only 609 of these cows also had test day records. All genotyped animals with no records were included in the genomic prediction analysis, so these animals can obtain predicted gEBV. The ssGBLUP procedure implemented therefore involved an H matrix consisting of 21724 animals with a weight of 5% on the A matrix in forming G22 matrix. The MiX99 software (Lidauer, et al. 2016) was used in the analysis to predict the gEBVs of animals and their reliabilities.

The animals were selected following the guideline developed by the ADGG project (https://portal.adgg.ilri.org/sites/default/files/ADGG_ETH_BULLCOW_sel_GUIDE_2020.pdf). The gEBVs of bulls ranged from -3.88 to 4.35Kg with a standard deviation of 0.84, implying that some of the top bulls available for selection are 4 to 5 standard deviations above the average bull, indicating that genetic progress can be made through using these the top bulls. Similarly, corresponding values for cows were -3.86 and 4.22 and 0.80 respectively. Top bulls and cows ranked on the estimates of gEBVs were made available for farmers.

Capacity building and awareness training

Building research and development infrastructure enables NAGII and regional livestock offices to effectively implement their genetic improvement plan. To this effect, the ADGG program equipped NAGII with high-capacity server (8 TB storage and 256 GB memory) to collect and store data. Besides, four Combo Lacto-Scan machines are procured to capture milk compositional traits and somatic cell count and each piloted district was provided with 100 motorbikes, 92 tablets, 15 laptops, printed plastic ear tags and heart girth measurement flexible tapes to enable smooth data collection and reporting and ensure uninterrupted monitoring of farms.

Work has also been done to strengthen the human and infrastructural capacity of the national system to collect field data, manage, analyze, and provide feedback to smallholder farmers. A total of 120 performance recoding agents (PRAs) are recruited and trained from 98 districts and large-scale farms from project regions on national dairy animal identification, importance of performance recording and data capturing using the ODK tool. PRAs visit dairy farms at least once a month, during which they advise the dairy farmer to whom they are assigned and capture new performance records. A critical component of the program, included, awareness creation, through trainings, which were organized and delivered to farmers, regional, zonal and district livestock office experts focused on merits of animals’ identifications and keeping the history of individual animals to improve genetics, increase productivity and profit.
The capacity of 15 Ethiopian experts in quantitative genetics was enhanced through tailored training courses on data management, related statistical analyses, and hands-on genomic

breeding value predictions exercises. The data generated from the national herd performance recording system is being used for related research by five MSc and two PhD students’ in writing their theses. Forty-five days full-fledged AI training was delivered to 15 PRAs in collaboration with the PAID project. AI kit and motorcycles were procured and distributed to all trained PRAs to ensure sustainability of data capturing and AI service provision to smallholder farmers.
First dairy cattle virtual parade

The first dairy cattle animal parade was held virtually on March 30, 2021, in the presence of dignitaries from the MoA, ILRI and BMGF and with the participation of senior government officials, farmers’ representatives, researchers, development workers from domestic and international organization, private firms, research institute, and universities. The top ranked animals were exhibited and, six farmers (two out of the six are women), who owned three best bulls and cows were recognized and awarded. The purpose of the award is to motivate dairy farmers to participate in national animal identification, record keeping and genetic improvement activities actively and continuously. Further information on the first dairy animal parade event can be accessed from published articles in both hard copy and online using the following links: https://www.ilri.org/news/building-sustainable-livestock-genetics-improvement-system-food-secure-ethiopia and https://www.capitalethiopia.com/featured/ministry-of-agriculture-eyes-to-triple-dairy-production/

Ethiopia’s sub-humid highlands face a critical challenge in balancing agricultural productivity with land degradation. This study explores the effectiveness of soil and water conservation practices (SWCPs) in addressing this challenge. We investigated the interaction effects of types of SWCPs, landscape positions, and location on Teff (Eragrostis teff) and wheat (Triticum aestivum) yield. In addition, we assessed the economic viability of SWCPs using cost-benefit analysis with farmer-funded and cost-sharing scenarios. The results indicated that yield was significantly affected by the interactions between factors like SWCP type and landscape position. Soil bunds consistently increased crop yield across diverse locations and landscapes, indicating superior erosion control benefits. Lower landscape positions on foot slopes benefited most from SWCP implementation. Teff yield increased by 188 % and wheat yield by 181 % under soil bunds. The cost-benefit analysis confirmed the financial viability of SWCPs, particularly for Teff (NPV = 4499.35 USD, IRR = 50 %, and BCR = 1.51) and wheat (NPV = 544.35 USD, IRR = 16 %, and BCR = 1.06) grown on lower landscapes with farmer-funded investment scenarios. Positive return on investment was observed in both scenarios, with cost-sharing offering greater economic benefits for farmers. These findings highlight the importance of an integrated approach to SWC implementation for achieving multiple Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by enhancing food security, improving farmer incomes, and promoting sustainable and productive landscape man- agement practices. Future research should explore the long-term sustainability of SWCPs, their adaptation across diverse agroecological zones and landscapes, the incorporation of various crops, the broader socioeconomic impacts, and the development of effective extension programs for wider adoption by farmers.

1. Introduction

Soil erosion is a critical environmental and agricultural challenge across the globe, particularly in sub-humid ecosystems like those found in East Africa such as Ethiopia [1–3]. This erosion reduces land productivity and negatively impacts downstream ecosystems and infrastructure [4]. Implementing SWC practices has been demonstrated as a powerful tool for mitigating soil erosion in some regions of the world. Studies in Ethiopia [5,6] have shown that SWC practices like terracing, mulching, and stone bunds significantly reduce soil erosion rates, improve soil moisture content, and enhance agricultural productivity.

Ethiopia’s subhumid highlands are a critical agricultural region facing a significant threat from severe soil erosion. This vulner- ability arises from various factors, including high and concentrated population, high annual rainfall, steep terrain, and inappropriate land management methods [7]. Estimates of annual soil loss under various land use patterns range from 30.4 to 122.3 t ha! yr} [s], exceeding established sustainable limits for Ethiopia, varying from 2 to 18 t ha! yr™! [9]. This erosion significantly degrades soil fertility, reduces crop yield, and negatively impacts agricultural productivity and ecosystem services [10].

Soil and water conservation practices (SWCPs) have emerged as a promising strategy to address soil erosion and enhance agri- cultural sustainability [7]. Existing research demonstrates a positive impact of SWCPs on soil fertility and crop yields. Studies have shown improvements of soil quality [11,12], with a notable example from Debre Mawi reporting a 32.15 % improvement of soil quality due to SWCP implementation [13]. Similarly, significant yield enhancements have been observed, with terraced farms in the Anjenie watershed achieving yield increases of 94 %, 205 %, and 125 % for Teff, barley, and maize, respectively, compared to non-terraced fields [14]. However, the effectiveness of SWCPs is known to vary depending on several factors, including geographic location [15, 16], the specific type of SWCP implemented [17,18], landscape position, and the type of crop being cultivated [15,16]. Although
landscape position plays a crucial role in Ethiopian agriculture, its influence on SWCP efficacy remains understudied [5,19].

While existing research highlights the negative economic impact of soil erosion and the benefits of SWCPs, a deeper understanding of the interactions between geographic location, SWCPs, landscape position, and economic outcomes is needed. This knowledge gap hinders the optimization of these practices for local contexts and advances to better soil and water conservation technologies based on their impacts on yield. This research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining interactions between location, types of SWCP,

Therefore, this study investigates the impact of soil and water conservation practices (SWCP) on grain yield, profitability, and/or return on investment (ROI) in the subhumid tropical highland ecosystem of Ethiopia. Recognizing the potential variability in pro- ductivity gains due to crop type, landscape position, and specific SWC structures, the research aims to: 1) quantify the effects of SWCPs on Teff and wheat grain yield; 2) analyze the economic gain variation of SWCPs (e.g. cost-benefit analysis); and 3) identify existing impacts of interactions between SWCP type, landscape position, and location on grain yield and economic outcomes.

By considering both agronomic and economic factors, this study provides valuable insights for optimizing soil and water con- servation strategies and promoting sustainable land management practices in the subhumid ecosystem, ultimately contributing to rural livelihoods and economic viability and agrifood systems improvement in the region in general and the study area in particular.
2. Methods
2.1. Study area description

This research was conducted in three watersheds of the northwestern Ethiopian highlands. This zone is characterized by tepid thermal regimes (mean annual temperature of 16–21 ◦ C) and moist moisture regimes (average growing season length of 121–180 days). The watersheds are Aba Gerima (582 ha), Debre Mawi (597 ha), and Debre Yakob (299 ha) (Fig. 1(A–E)). A table summarizing each watershed’s major climatic data is presented in Table 1.

All three watersheds share several key common characteristics. They exhibit a similar range of slope gradients, with the dominant slopes falling within the 2–15 % range. Also, all watersheds cultivate wheat and Teff as primary crops, and Nitisols and Vertisols are the most dominant soil types, although their proportions vary. Notably, soil and water conservation structures in the form of stone and soil bunds were implemented in all three watersheds between 2013 and 2014 under the Water and Land Resource Center supporting
program.

On the other hand, the watersheds also exhibit some key differences. The topographic orientation and coverage of landscape positions (upper, middle, and foot slopes) differ across the watersheds. Aba Gerima has the greatest proportion of the lower landscape, while Debre Yakob has the most extensive middle landscape. Upper landscape coverage is also most significant in the south and southwest areas of Debre Yakob. The specific proportions of Nitisols and Vertisols vary. Debre Yakob has the most diverse soil composition, with Nitisols (28 %), Luvisols (38 %), Regosols (33 %), and Vertisols (1 %). In contrast, the upper parts of Debre Mawi and Aba Gerima are dominated by Nitisols, with increasing Vertisol presence in the lower landscapes.
2.2. Methodology
2.2.1. Treatments and crop selection

This study examined the combined effects of location, soil and water conservation practices (SWCPs), and landscape units on the grain yield of two dominant crops, Teff (Eragrostis teff) and wheat (Triticum aestivum) in a tepid sub-humid ecosystem. A pre-experiment survey identified dominant crops and soil and water conservation practices (SWCPs) within the three watersheds. Teff and bread wheat, the most dominantly grown crops, were chosen for a landscape yield response study. The soil and water conservation structures were extracted from Google Images, verified on the ground, and categorized into three management conditions. These include non- conserved, soil bund, and stone bund areas. The soil and stone bunds were constructed 10 years ago. Fig. 2(A–D) illustrates the appearance of soil and water conservation structures during and after that period.

The landscape units of the watersheds were derived from the landscape map of Ethiopia [20], derived basically from the geo- morphology map produced by the International Soil Research Center (ISRC) at 50m resolution in 2019. The classification considers relief intensity, elevation difference, topographic index, slope gradient, and position in the landscape. Using these thematic layers, the study sites were classified into three distinct landscape units: upper, middle, and lower positions. This classification was verified through a field survey and adjusted to align with the actual field conditions and the proposed experimental design. The spatial dis- tribution of these three landscape positions across the three study watersheds is illustrated in Fig. 3(A–C), which was used to guide the
selection of experimental plots.
Therefore, experimental treatments were formed from a combination of location, SWC practices, and landscape units to assess their
effects on the yield of two major crops. In the three study watersheds (Aba Gerima, Debre Mawi, and Debre Yakob), three SWCP

2.2.2. Experimental setup and design

The experimental setup was designed to assess the impact of various factors on crop productivity in the context of the three wa- tersheds. As mentioned, the study incorporated soil and water conservation practices (non-conserved, stone bund, and soil bund),

A three-way factorial design with nested replicates was employed to evaluate the combined effects of location, SWCPs, and landscape position on crop yields. Each watershed served as a spatial location (n = 3). Three landscape units (upper, middle, and lower landscape positions) were identified within each watershed. Three SWC practices (non-conserved, soil bunds, and stone bunds) were implemented within each landscape unit. Plots were randomly assigned within the study watersheds to receive one of the nine treatment combinations (3 SWCPs x 3 landscape units). Each treatment combination was replicated three times, resulting in a total of 27 potential treatment plots per watershed. However, due to the absence of certain treatment combinations in specific watersheds on the ground, a total of 114 data plots were established (Table 2). The treatment combinations that appeared on the ground were 14, 16, and 8 for Aba Gerima, Debre Mawi, and Debre Yakob respectively with 3 replications (Table 2). The landscape units and types of SWCPs were mapped in the ArcGIS environment. However, the crop plots were selected at the farm level through a ground survey. The relevant response variable (crop yield) was collected at the end of the growing season and analyzed using three-way ANOVA to assess the main and interaction effects.
2.3. Yield data collection and main assumptions

To facilitate statistical analysis and interpretation, 17 and 21 treatment combinations were used for Teff and wheat respectively, resulting in a total of 38 unique treatments each replicated three times. Among these, 22 treatments represented treated fields with soil and water conservation practices (SWCPs), whereas 16 represented untreated control fields.

For each treatment within SWCP-implemented fields, a 4 m2 steel quadrant was cast at three distinct positions: base (lower part of the area between two bunds), middle, and upper section (upper part of the area between two bunds) within the bunds. These positions were marked and delineated using wooden pegs and nylon ropes to ensure precise sampling area demarcation. To account for potential land area loss due to SWCP structures, harvests from the three bund positions were combined and extrapolated to represent a standard 12 m2 area, replicating this process three times per treatment. By adopting this strategy, the collected data accurately reflects yield within bunded fields. Considering an estimated 7 % land loss (or effective cropped area of 0.93 ha per 1 ha) due to SWCPs [16,21], all results were converted and reported directly as tone per hectare for consistent analysis and interpretation.
2.4. Financial viability of soil and water conservation investments

The central hypothesis we aim to test here is whether the costs outweigh the benefits when investing in soil conservation measures, as often is suggested, but about which the empirical evidence base is ambiguous. This study investigated the 10 years (2014–2023) impacts of soil and water conservation (SWC) practices on Teff and wheat yields and economic returns. We focused on two common SWC interventions, soil and stone bunds, implemented across the three identified landscape units. The study aims to provide comprehensive insights into their effectiveness over 10 years, from a period when the watersheds were treated with soil and water conservation practices through the project implemented by the Water and Land Resource Center (WLRC) and the local agriculture
departments up to 2023.

For conserved plots, yield data for 2014 was obtained by averaging the respective control plot yield based on landscape position. Subsequently, yield differences observed in 2023 were linearly interpolated to estimate yield for the intervening years (2015–2022) in conserved plots [22]. The annual income was calculated by annual yield gain multiplied by the respective market price (Table 3). The sum of the 10-year annual income from each treatment was used for income calculations.

The financial study uses the current price discounted based on the average discount rate. Economic data at the farm level were collected using farmer interviews, and market surveys (Table 3). This data encompassed SWC implementation costs, crop production expenses, and prevailing market prices for Teff and wheat. Specific assumptions were made to maintain consistency across treatments: an average of 1 Km SWC structure per hectare of land, established work norms for SWC practices (150 and 250 person-days per hectare or 6 m for soil bund and 4 m for stone bund per person day) for constructing soil bunds and stone bunds, respectively) [23]. Fertilizer and seed rates were estimated based on local extension recommendations.

A comprehensive cost-benefit analysis (CBA) was conducted to assess the financial implications of implementing the two main SWC measures in three landscape units compared with no conservation efforts. The financial viability of each approach was evaluated using economic parameters like Net Present Value (NPV), Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR), and Internal Rate of Return (IRR), considering an average discount rate of 11.50 % [24] to overcome inflation.

The economic benefits of different soil and water conservation (SWC) practices were assessed using gross margin analysis. This analysis considers crop yield data, production costs, and market prices (Table 3) to calculate the gross margin for each SWC practice. Return on investment (ROI) was then estimated by dividing the net gain (gross margin minus the cost of implementing the SWC practice) by the initial investment cost. To explore the economic feasibility under different financial circumstances, two scenarios were considered. The first scenario assumes that farmers or the community have already implemented all SWC measures. This might involve community mobilization efforts where farmers collaborate to build bunds on each other’s fields, contributing labor in exchange for reciprocal help. The second scenario assumes that farmers only cover 10 % of the total SWC investment, with the remaining 90 % subsidized through programs like food-for-work (FFW) or cash-for-work (CFW). Regardless of the scenario, the long-term maintenance of the SWC practices remains the responsibility of the farm owner.
2.5. Statistical analysis

The R statistical software package [25] was employed for all data analyses. Crop yield data from the three-way factorial experiment (location × SWC practice × landscape unit) were subjected to normality tests (e.g., Shapiro-Wilk test) to confirm adherence to a normal distribution [26,27]. The data satisfied the normality assumption, and subsequent analyses proceeded with a three-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) using the general linear model (GLM) procedure at a 5 % significance level ((α = 0.05). The Least Significant Difference (LSD) post-hoc comparisons were used to separate means and identify significant differences among treatment combina- tions for each measured response variable (e.g., crop yield).

For comparisons between treated and untreated farmlands, a one-way ANOVA was conducted [25] to assess statistical differences. Inter-bund variability in crop yield at the base, middle, and upper sections between successive bunds was analyzed using descriptive statistics, including means, standard deviation, and coefficients of variation (CV). Similar statistical comparisons using appropriate tests were performed to evaluate economic parameters such as Net Present Value (NPV) and Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR).

3.2. Effects of soil and water conservation (SWC) on teff and wheat yield

There was a significant (p < 0.01) difference in the yield of Teff and wheat crops grown in treated (soil bund and stone bund) and untreated plots within a sub-humid ecosystem (Table 5), irrespective of the type of structures and landscape units. The results revealed a significant increase (p < 0.01) in mean Teff yield (188 %) and mean wheat yield (181 %) for plots with SWC practices compared to untreated controls. This finding suggests that SWC practices in general can substantially enhance crop yields regardless of the specific structure type or landscape unit within this ecosystem.
3.3. Effects on teff yield
3.3.1. Main effects of location, landscape, and SWCPs

Significant differences in Teff yield were observed among locations, landscape units, and types of SWCPs (p < 0.001) (Table 4). The highest average Teff yield (1.73 t/ha) was recorded for Debre Yakob, followed by Debre Mawi (1.46 t/ha). The lowest yield (0.85 t/ha) was observed in Aba Gerima, highlighting potential spatial variations in environmental factors impacting Teff production. Among the three landscape positions, the lower landscape position recorded the highest average yield (1.44 t/ha), followed by the upper position (1.17 t/ha). The middle landscape position exhibited the lowest yield (0.93 t/ha), where this unit is dominated by steeper terrain as compared to other landscape units. These findings dictate the importance of considering topographic variations within fields for optimizing Teff management. In the same manner, the yield of Teff varied based on the types of SWCPs. Soil bunds offered the highest average yield (2.07 t/ha), followed by stone bunds (1.33 t/ha). Untreated fields recorded the lowest average yield (0.58 t/ha) (Fig. 4). This highlights the significant potential of SWC practices, particularly soil bunds, in enhancing Teff productivity.
3.3.2. Interaction effects of location, landscape position, and SWCP

A significant (p < 0.001) three-way interaction effect of location, landscape position, and SWCP on Teff yield was observed (Table 4). This finding suggests that the impact of SWC practices on Teff yield depends on both the spatial location and the specific
landscape unit within a particular watershed.

Soil bunds enhance Teff yield across landscapes. The highest mean Teff yields were obtained in the lower landscapes treated with soil bunds at Debre Mawi (2.98 t/ha) and Debre Yakob (2.78 t/ha) (Table 6). These yields were statistically superior to all other treatment combinations but statistically similar to each other. This finding highlights the potential of soil bunds for enhancing Teff yield regardless of the specific landscape position within these watersheds. For Aba Gerima watershed, the highest Teff yield (1.22 t/ ha) was obtained at the lower landscape with a stone bund.

Further analysis of Table 6 reveals variations in Teff yield across different landscapes and SWC practices. The second-highest yield (2.46 t/ha) was recorded in the upper landscape of the Debre Mawi watershed with soil bunds. This was followed by the middle landscape at Debre Mawi with stone bunds (1.93 t/ha). These results suggest that soil bunds outperform stone bunds, but the specific yield benefit may vary depending on the landscape units.

Untreated plots exhibited the lowest yields. Consistently across all landscapes within each watershed, the lowest Teff yields were observed in untreated plots (Table 6). For example, in Debre Mawi, untreated plots in the middle and upper slopes yielded only 0.43 t/ ha and 0.59 t/ha, respectively. Similarly, low yields were observed in untreated plots at Aba Gerima and Debre Yakob. This emphasizes the importance of implementing SWC practices for improving Teff yield.

Scaling Partners Platform

Second, the scaling partners’ platform, which is operating at the local level. Since early 2023, ICRISAT has expanded the partnership from demand partners (district and extension agents) to a wider scaling network including government sectors (at zone and district levels), several NGOs (Sasakawa Africa Association, Self Help Africa, People in Need, Stichting Wageningen Research Ethiopia, CRS/Catholic Sinodos, InterAid France, SNV, ERSHA, Hunde, Termpeza Limat) and universities. Through the engagement of these scaling partners, we have established a scaling partners network and developed a scaling strategy plan. 1The platform is organized into around ten innovation packages and six work packages (Fig 1). They have a role to provide feedback to the DST coordination platform and serve to facilitate vertical scaling (national) and horizontal scaling (at the district, extension agents and farmers level). The coordination of the platform is led by the agriculture offices in the zone that has a decentralised operation.

Scaling strategy plan

In 2023, scaling partners met and discussed scaling issues and developed a scaling strategy plan2. A network platform was proposed for each zone administration to operationalize the scaling strategy plan that aims to address the issues associated with scaling innovation components (Fig. 2). The platform was established to promote collaborative actions and mitigate scaling barriers. Scale partners regularly review scaling issues, develop action plans, and organize joint monitoring and supervision. The platform identified ten components of the innovation package that limit the readiness for scale innovation. This multi-sectoral participation underscored the need for a coordinated approach to address scaling issues and implement scalable fertilizer advisory solutions.

These strengths can be complemented by opportunities such as government policy, farmers’ willingness for technology uptake, scaling partnerships, community cooperation, and expansion of digital infrastructure. Scaling Partners Network Action Plan

In a recent scaling partners network workshop3 held in the southern and central Ethiopian regions, the platform developed action plans to address scaling gaps and barriers in three zones – Hadiya, Kembata, and Welaita (Table 1). These plans aim to address scaling barriers and leverage enablers within the collaborative approach to advance the fertilizer advisory system, ensuring that innovations reach a wider base of small farmers in Ethiopia. By addressing these barriers, the scaling network seeks to create an enabling environment for the widespread adoption of evidence- based fertilizer and lime recommendations tailored to the diverse landscapes of the Central and Southern Ethiopia Regional States.

Using the results of the SWOT analysis, the scaling partners developed a network strategy to overcome barriers and capitalize on enablers within the fertilizer advisory innovation package. This strategy includes concrete measures to facilitate collaboration among partners, optimize resource use, and align efforts to ensure that smallholder farmers receive accurate, timely, and location-specific fertilizer recommendations. Furthermore, the strategy emphasizes the need for continuous capacity building, data-driven decision- making, and the integration of digital tools to improve the reach and impact of fertilizer advisory services in Ethiopia. With action plans and network strategy in place, the scaling partners are well positioned to contribute to the broader goals of scaling agricultural system solutions, which seek to improve agronomic practices, improve soil fertility, and boost agricultural productivity in Ethiopia’s mixed highland regions.

Abstract
Ethiopia faces significant yield gaps in cereal production, with average yields of staple crops

falling well below their potential. A major issue is the continued reliance on blanket fertilizer recommendations that fail to account for local soil variability and environmental conditions. This paper examines the shift towards site-specific, data-driven fertilizer recommendations as a transformative strategy for Ethiopian agriculture. Through extensive use of agricultural data, big data analytics, and machine learning, the Alliance of Bioversity International, CIAT, and the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT), in collaboration with the demand partners and scaling partners, have developed and piloted site specific fertilizer decision support tools (DSTs). These tools are designed to optimize nutrient application and provide tailored agronomic solutions adapted to local conditions. The Ethiopian government’s adoption of these approaches highlights their potential to significantly boost productivity and foster sustainable farming practices. However, fragmented efforts by research institutions using separate tools, and the lack of a unified DST for national deployment, remain major challenges. To address these challenges, a harmonized DST framework has been proposed to integrate various tools into a cohesive system. This collaborative effort is reshaping Ethiopia's agricultural landscape and aligns with the government's commitment to enhancing digital extension services and delivering precise agronomic advice. The active involvement of CGIAR's Excellence in Agronomy Initiative, along with national and international research institutes, has been crucial in developing the data ecosystem, conducting analytics, creating advisory content, and validating the tools in the field. The harmonized DST framework is currently undergoing extensive field testing by the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research across 2,500 farmers' fields for major cereal crops. This initiative marks a significant departure from traditional blanket fertilizer strategies, advancing towards site-specific, data-driven agronomic guidance delivered through agile communication channels. By offering tailored, localized solutions that cater to Ethiopia’s diverse agricultural landscape, this approach aims to empower farmers and bring impact at scale while building resilience against environmental challenges. This paper underscores the importance of coordinated partnerships and the integration of innovative technologies to effectively close yield gaps and enhance food security. Ultimately, this initiative not only aims to increase agricultural productivity but also sets a precedent for similar collaborative efforts across sub-Saharan Africa, contributing to a more sustainable and resilient agricultural system capable of adapting to changing conditions and meeting future demands.
Keywords: Data-Driven Agriculture, Fertilizer Optimization, Soil Health, Nutrient management
1. Yield Gap in Cereal Production

Ethiopia is currently facing a significant yield gap in cereal production, with average yields of major crops such as maize, wheat, and sorghum well below their potential. National average yields stand at approximately 3.4 t ha-1 for maize, 2.5 t ha-1 for wheat, and 2.3 t ha-1 for sorghum (www.yieldgap.org/ethiopia; Silva et al., 2021; Debebe et al., 2022 ). For instance, wheat yields are only 26.8% of their water-limited potential, and the yields of maize and sorghum are also far below their potential, achieving just 19.7% and 29.3% of their respective water-limited potentials. Several key factors contribute to this yield gap, including poor soil fertility, inappropriate or insufficient fertilizer use, reliance on traditional agricultural practices, and exposure to environmental stressors such as drought, pests, and diseases. In addition, the adoption of improved crop varieties and modern agricultural techniques has been slow. Research indicates that optimizing fertilizer use and introducing improved crop varieties could potentially double or even triple yields (Belachew et al., 2023). However, these practices are still largely underutilized.
2. Challenges with Fertilizer Use and Recommendations

One of the major challenges in Ethiopian agriculture is inadequate fertilizer use, particularly the limited integration of organic fertilizers. Farmers typically apply only 37-40 kg ha-1 of inorganic fertilizers, which is significantly lower than the recommended rate of 100-200 kg ha-1 for optimal production (Getaneh et al., 2024). While chemical fertilizers can increase yields, their effectiveness is often limited due to insufficient quantities, poor quality, or a mismatch with soil requirements. Simply increasing application rates without addressing soil nutrient deficiencies, landscape variability, and environmental impacts can result in poor yields, nutrient leaching, and soil degradation. As a result, the dominant use of inorganic fertilizers, such as urea and DAP, has led to a significant reduction in the use of organic alternatives, which dropped markedly between 2004/05 and 2020/21 (Melak et al., 2024). This imbalance has exacerbated soil fertility problems, as many farmers overlook the importance of maintaining soil health when applying fertilizers (Doldt et al., 2023). Additional challenges, such as land degradation, erratic climate patterns, and limited agricultural extension services, further limit farmers' access to integrated nutrient management strategies (Elias et al., 2023). However, neglecting such an approach can deplete soil nutrients, reduce fertilizer effectiveness, and ultimately threaten the long-term productivity of Ethiopian agriculture, especially for cereal crops.

Efforts to improve soil fertility in Ethiopia have progressed significantly since the 1960s. Early soil testing conducted by Alemaya College of Agriculture and the Institute of Agricultural Research (IAR) revealed widespread nutrient deficiencies, particularly in nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P), which led to the adoption of chemical fertilizers such as urea and diammonium phosphate (DAP) to enhance crop yields (Zeleke et al., 2010; Woldeab & Mamo, 1991). Fertilizer research in Ethiopia began in the 1960s following soil surveys that revealed widespread nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) deficiencies. Early research focused on cereal crops like tef, wheat, and maize, leading to blanket fertilizer recommendations. Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, trials recommended varying N and P rates across agro-ecological zones, but adoption by smallholder farmers was limited due to high fertilizer prices and declining crop responses. In the 1990s, research expanded to integrated use of inorganic and organic fertilizers, although this wasn't widely adopted.

The reliance on blanket fertilizer recommendations for cereal production that do not consider the diverse farming systems, soil types, and spatial variability inherent in the landscape remains a key challenge. This approach can lead to either a zero or negative yield response to fertilizer, and generally low profitability from the fertilizer use, particularly for smallholder farmers (Vanlauwe et al., 2011; Kihara et al., 2016; Tefera et al., 2020). These generalized prescriptions for large areas, although intended to increase nutrient input, often result in a broader environmental impact due to inorganic fertilizer pollution in agricultural landscapes (Kihara et al. 2020; Rodriguez, 2020). For instance, national average recommendations do not consider variations in soil fertility and climatic conditions, which results in mismatches between crop nutrient needs and the actual application (Abera et al., 2022). The ""one-size-fits-all"" nature of these recommendations reduces fertilizer use efficiency, hinders crop productivity, and contributes to environmental degradation, such as soil degradation and water contamination. Over the past five decades, these blanket strategies have not achieved significant productivity gains (Getaneh et al., 2024; Gutema et al., 2024). Consequently, farmers continue to experience inconsistent yields and reduced profitability and face long-term risks to soil health. While localized fertilizer strategies have demonstrated potential for improving yields, many farmers still rely on outdated practices of generalized fertilizer recommendations due to a lack of site-specific agro-advisory services (Kenea et al., 2024) that resulted in low efficiency, nutrient imbalances, and inconsistent crop yields across different farming regions.
3. Shifting to Site-Specific Fertilizer Recommendations

Due to the low agronomic effectiveness and poor economic efficiency of blanket fertilizer applications, efforts have been made to improve fertilizer recommendations. One such initiative is the Optimizing Fertilizer Recommendations for Africa (OFRA) project, which developed agro- ecological zone (AEZ)-based fertilizer recommendations for Ethiopia, using data from a limited number of sites (Kaizzi et al., 2017). While this AEZ-based approach provided more tailored recommendations than blanket applications, it did not fully account for the many micro-level factors influencing crop responses to nutrients. As a result, the recommendations could still lead to either suboptimal or excessive fertilizer applications. Another approach attempted to examine the impact of local-scale topography on yield responses to fertilizers, which led to the development of landscape-based recommendations (Amede et al., 2020).

The Ethiopian Soil Information System (EthioSIS), established in 2012 under the Ethiopian Agricultural Transformation Agency (ATA), marked a significant advancement in fertilizer source recommendations by developing maps based on macro and micronutrient levels. This initiative aimed to move beyond uniform fertilizer guidelines by tailoring recommendations to the specific nutrient needs of various regions. To validate these soil fertility maps, the National Agricultural Research System (NARS) conducted extensive on-farm trials. The data generated by EthioSIS enabled the government, research institutions, and donors to prioritize soil health and enhance fertilizer efficiency. In response, the Ministry of Agriculture (MoA) and ATA developed the Soil Health and Fertility Roadmap in 2011 and 2012 to address key soil fertility challenges and transform the agricultural sector. However, previous efforts to segment recommendations based on broad agroecological zones have not adequately addressed micro-level variations in soil and landscape conditions. This mismatch between crop nutrient needs and actual fertilizer application has resulted in many areas remaining unresponsive to fertilizer applications due to deficiencies in specific nutrients (Erkossa et al., 2022). Identifying nutrient pools in the soil alone is insufficient for reliable fertilizer recommendations, as both soil-related and non-soil-related factors influence nutrient uptake. Current methods do not fully integrate the effects of soil,
climate, topography, and nutrient pools, indicating a need for more precise, site-specific fertilizer recommendations (Abera et al., 2022; Erkossa et al., 2022).

The introduction of data-mining techniques and machine learning offers significant potential for optimizing fertilizer use by enabling site-specific recommendations. However, in Ethiopia, data remains fragmented and often inaccessible, limiting data-driven decision-making. To address this, in 2018/2019, a group of volunteer researchers formed the Coalition of the Willing (CoW website), an informal collective aimed at consolidating decades of scattered agricultural data into a national soil and agricultural database. Through voluntary data-sharing initiatives, CoW has successfully centralized nearly 40,000 crop response data points and approximately 20,000 legacy soil profile data points, now accessible via a portal managed by the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR). This centralized resource is vital for generating tailored fertilizer recommendations using advanced data analytics and machine learning, significantly enhancing soil health and agricultural productivity. Promoting data-sharing policies and fostering collaboration among multidisciplinary teams are key to accelerating the development of these site-specific recommendations.

The Coalition of the Willing’s initiatives, leveraging big data and advanced data-mining techniques, have played a crucial role in creating data-driven, context-specific fertilizer recommendations, helping to improve agricultural productivity and land management (Desta et al., 2021). This data informs innovative and targeted fertilizer recommendations tailored to Ethiopia's rapidly evolving landscapes. So, the growing need for integrated, site-specific nutrient management can be supported by comprehensive datasets that allow machine learning algorithms to identify key relationships between fertilizer application, soil conditions, weather, and crop yields, which marks a major shift from the blanket fertilizer recommendations of the 1970s to more precise, sustainable strategies (Abera et al., 2021; Liben et al., 2024).

Since 2020, CGIAR’s Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) initiative, through its Fertilizer Ethiopia and Digital Green use cases, has pioneered a co-design approach aimed at developing digital agronomy solutions with a primary focus on optimizing fertilizer rate recommendations. This co- design process involves close collaboration with local stakeholders, including smallholder farmers, agricultural researchers, policymakers, and private sector partners. By integrating diverse perspectives, the approach ensures that the solutions are not only scientifically sound but also practically applicable and aligned with the real-world needs of farmers and the agricultural ecosystem. One of the key strengths of this initiative lies in its ability to leverage legacy crop response data—historical data from previous trials and research on how crops respond to various fertilizer applications under different conditions. These data sets are invaluable as they provide a solid foundation for understanding the relationships between fertilizer rates, soil conditions, crop types, and environmental factors. This historical knowledge is then augmented with modern analytical tools, including machine learning and big data analysis, allowing for more precise, data-driven recommendations.

The development of these digital agronomic solutions follows a structured seven-step methodology to ensure rigor and accuracy at every stage. This comprehensive methodology ensures that the solutions developed are not only scientifically robust but also practical and scalable. By passing through the seven-stage gates, each step of the process undergoes stringent checks for technical validity, ensuring that the solutions are ready for deployment at scale. This structured approach mitigates risks, improves user adoption, and ensures that the solutions deliver tangible benefits in terms of yield improvement, resource efficiency, and economic sustainability for farmers (https://www.cgiar.org/initiative/excellence-in-agronomy)

Through the Digital Green and Fertilizer Ethiopia use cases, CGIAR's EiA initiative is transforming traditional fertilizer recommendations into dynamic, data-driven, and context- specific solutions that adapt to the complexities of local farming conditions. This shift from generic, blanket recommendations to tailored, site-specific strategies represents a significant advancement in agronomy, helping farmers make better-informed decisions that enhance productivity, improve soil health, and increase overall sustainability in the agricultural sector

The Alliance of Bioversity International, the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) with its NextGen Agroadvisory, of the Digital Green use case and the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT) with its landscape-targeted fertilizer advisory tool of Fertilizer Ethiopia use case were pivotal in developing tailored fertilizer recommendations aimed at increasing agricultural productivity in Ethiopia. These institutions have focused on knowledge-based decision-making to support the country's agricultural transformation efforts. By using machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI), these efforts integrate diverse datasets—such as weather patterns, soil properties, and land management practices—to develop decision tools that predict site-specific agronomic inputs, including fertilizers. These SSFR approaches optimize nutrient application by tailoring it to specific field or landscape conditions. The result is higher crop yields, greater nutrient use efficiency, increased profitability for farmers, and minimized environmental impacts from improper fertilization (Liben et al., 2024).

The methods represent a transformative solution for Ethiopian agriculture, offering a data- driven, tailored approach to fertilizer use that effectively enhances productivity and sustainability. This shift from a ""one-size-fits-all"" approach to site-specific fertilizer recommendations represents an important evolution in soil fertility research in Ethiopia, acknowledging the complexity of local environments and leading to more effective and sustainable nutrient management practices. The transition to site-specific fertilizer recommendations continues to evolve, leveraging new data-driven approaches and technologies to improve soil health, boost nutrient use efficiency, and mitigate the environmental impacts of fertilizer use (Silva et al., 2021).
4. Prominent DSTs for Site-Specific Agronomic Solutions
4.1. NextGen DST for Seasonal and Site-Specific Fertilizer Recommendations

The NextGen DST was developed in Ethiopia through a collaborative, multi-phase process designed to address the limitations of blanket fertilizer recommendations. It emerged from a partnership between national and international organizations, with the Alliance of Bioversity International and the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) spearheading its development. The Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR) played a critical role by contributing valuable data on soil fertility, crop responses, and on-farm trial results. The Ministry of Agriculture (MoA) aligned the tool with national strategies and facilitated its dissemination through the Extension Division. Key demand partners, such as Digital Green, and private sectors, such as LERSHA were key in delivering the NextGen DST to farmers via digital platforms. Additionally, the ""Coalition of the Willing"" (CoW) provided vital data on crop responses and other variables, enriching the tool's knowledge base. This collaborative approach ensured that the NextGen DST was comprehensive, data-driven, and tailored to the specific needs of Ethiopian agriculture (Desta et al., 2021; Liben et al., 2022).

A key aspect of the NextGen DST's development was the use of a vast repository of legacy data spanning over five decades of research on crop responses to fertilizers in Ethiopia. This data, combined with environmental covariates such as soil properties, weather patterns, and topography, was analyzed using machine learning algorithms to generate tailored, site-specific fertilizer recommendations. The NextGen DST was also designed to integrate seamlessly with other agricultural platforms, including the process-based QUEFT model, which simulates crop growth and nutrient uptake for more accurate fertilizer recommendations. Additionally, it connects with the Ethiopian Digital AgroClimate Advisory Platform, providing climate forecasts and informing key decisions on planting dates, fertilizer application, and harvesting. Given the challenge of soil acidity in Ethiopia, ongoing efforts aim to incorporate features that provide spatially explicit lime application guidance, helping to mitigate soil acidity and enhance soil health.

The NextGen DST underwent comprehensive validation trials in 2021, involving 277 farm plots across various agro-ecological zones and soil types in Ethiopia. These trials aimed to evaluate the tool's effectiveness against national recommendations and traditional fertilizer practices. The results consistently showed that the NextGen DST's site-specific fertilizer recommendations (SSFR) led to substantial wheat yield increases of 16% to 25%, with improvements observed in 72% to 75% of the fields compared to national recommendations and local practices. Additionally, nitrogen use efficiency improved by 30%, and water use efficiency ranged from 0.58 kg to 0.83 kg of grain per hectare per millimeter of water, demonstrating more sustainable resource utilization. Economically, SSFR provided significant profitability advantages, with average profit increases ranging from $469 to $669 per hectare per season (Liben et al., 2024). Further validation in 2023 by the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR) on 25 experimental sites across four districts reinforced these findings. Grain yield increases due to SSFR ranged from 7.5% to 57%, while biomass increases varied between 5.5% and 45%. The trials confirmed the tool's ability to enhance nutrient and water use efficiency. Economic analysis also highlighted the cost-effectiveness of SSFR, delivering the highest net benefits across all districts and yielding substantial marginal rates of return, making it a financially viable approach to improving wheat production in Ethiopia (Liben et al., 2024).

The DST piloting by key partners has benefited farmers across Ethiopia and demonstrated strong interest and demand for the technology. The promising results from the validation trials prompted collaborative efforts to pilot and scale the NextGen DST across Ethiopia. Digital Green, with its expertise in digital agricultural extension, played a key role and the SSFR advisory disseminated by Digital Green reached approximately 11,171 farmers, with more than 3,000 implementing the recommended practices during the 2022 pilot phase (Tamene et al., 2023). This was further expanded to reach an additional 52,421 farmers in 2023 (Tamene et al., 2024), including maize piloting in 2024 that reached a total of 3,190 farmers in three maize- growing districts, bringing the total to 63,592 wheat and maize farmers in 18 districts in three regions. Of these, 10,880 are willing to implement the practices. The MoA's Extension Division also piloted the DST within Agricultural Commercialization Clusters (ACCs), and reached over 600 farmers through this initiative, demonstrating the government's commitment to scaling up the technology. Private sector entities like LERSHA further expanded the reach by piloting the DST bundled with credit and insurance services, offering a holistic solution to farmers. while the advisory has been piloted with over 8,000 farmers via LERSHA in 2024. With a close partnership with the key demand partners, the total number of farmers reached until 2024 is more than 72,800. To effectively reach farmers, the NextGen DST recommendations were disseminated through various channels or digital platforms, including Mobile apps (Telegram Chatbots), IVR, video-mediated messages, SMS messages, and online platforms like the
NextGen WebApp provide easily accessible information to demand partners, extension advisors and farmers.

Training and support from extension agents are crucial in bridging the gap between technology and its practical application on farms. Exchange visits and radio broadcasts have proven effective in reaching broader audiences and showcasing the benefits of the Decision Support Tool (DST) in real-world scenarios. Despite challenges such as high fertilizer costs and shortages, many farmers are eager to adopt the site-specific fertilizer recommendations (SSFR) provided by the NextGen DST. In 2024 alone, nearly two thousand additional farmers adopted SSFR, bringing the total number of adopters to over ten thousand. This enthusiastic response highlights the perceived value of the DST in enhancing fertilizer use efficiency and improving yields and profitability. Farmer field days and feedback mechanisms were instrumental in gathering insights and promoting adoption, with testimonials from farmers and extension workers consistently underscoring the superiority of DST recommendations compared to local standards or traditional practices.

The NextGen DST in Ethiopia serves as a successful case study in leveraging data-driven approaches to address critical agricultural challenges. Its collaborative development, rigorous testing, and impressive results have garnered significant attention from the Ethiopian government. The Ministry of Agriculture has recognized its potential by considering the integration of the NextGen DST as a core component of a harmonized DST in the national extension system. This marks a pivotal step towards broader adoption and the possibility of transforming agricultural practices nationwide. The piloting of the NextGen DST for wheat has already set the stage for its expansion to other key crops like maize, teff, and sorghum, offering farmers across different cropping systems access to tailored fertilizer recommendations. The DST’s adaptable framework also positions it for replication in other countries, potentially revolutionizing agricultural practices across Africa. As the NextGen DST continues to evolve with new features, data, and partnerships, it promises to enhance agricultural practices and improve livelihoods, both in Ethiopia and beyond. Its success underscores the power of data- driven tools in advancing fertilizer efficiency, increasing crop yields, and promoting sustainable farming practices.
4.2. Landscape-based Site Specific Fertilizer Recommendation

The Landscape-Specific Fertilizer Advisory (LSFA) of ICRISAT was developed to address the limitations of traditional blanket fertilizer recommendations in Ethiopia, which failed to consider the diverse factors affecting crop yields across the diverse agricultural landscapes in Ethiopia. The primary goal of LSFA is to provide a more precise, data-driven approach to fertilizer management that enhances nutrient use efficiency, boosts agricultural productivity, and minimizes environmental impacts across landscape positions. The initiative began in July 2013, led by ICRISAT in collaboration with regional and national research partners focusing on fertilizer application tailored to key landscape features such as hill slope, mid-slope, and foot slope positions (ICRISAT, 2023a). Unlike blanket recommendations, LSFA effectively addresses differences in soil fertility, cropping systems, soil depth, and climate. Although farmers traditionally adjusted fertilizer use based on observations, such as soil depth and water capacity, these adjustments lacked scientific validation, resulting in inefficient nutrient use. LSFA was thus developed as a digital advisory tool using data from multi-location crop trials, soil maps, climate data, and landscape positions, with machine learning applied to generate site and crop-specific decision rules for targeted fertilizer recommendations (Desta et al., 2023).

The development of LSFA was a collaborative effort involving the Ministry of Agriculture, local agricultural offices non-governmental organizations, the National Agricultural Research System (NARS), universities, private service providers, input suppliers, the Ministry of Agriculture, and. This multi-sectoral collaboration ensured that LSFA was practical and relevant for smallholder farmers in Ethiopia (ICRISAT, 2023a). LSFA uses a landscape segmentation approach to manage soil fertility variability. By dividing landscapes into homogeneous segments based on soil type, topography, and moisture, LSFA delivers targeted fertilizer recommendations for each landscape position, allowing farmers to maximize productivity by applying fertilizers precisely according to their specific land conditions (Agegnehu et al., 2023; Desta et al., 2022; 2023). A core feature of LSFA is the integration of Decision Support Tools (DSTs) that use advanced algorithms to generate fertilizer recommendations tailored to specific crops and landscape conditions. These DSTs account for factors such as rainfall, soil type, crop variety, and landscape position (Desta et al., 2023). Additionally, LSFA includes a mobile application for farmers or extension agents to input farm-specific information and receive fertilizer recommendations via mobile apps, SMS, or printed formats. This tool provides smallholder farmers with practical and accessible information to optimize fertilizer use, enhance crop yields, and reduce resource wastage (Desta et al., 2023).

The LSFA represents a transformative solution for Ethiopian agriculture by offering a data- driven, site-specific approach to fertilizer use. By integrating scientific knowledge with practical decision-making tools, LSFA empowers smallholder farmers with accurate, actionable insights for more efficient nutrient management, increased productivity, and sustainable agricultural practices. The Landscape-Specific Fertilizer Advisory (LSFA) has proven to deliver substantial agronomic and economic benefits for tef, wheat, and sorghum cultivation in Ethiopia. By tailoring fertilizer recommendations to the unique conditions of different landscape positions, LSFA optimizes nutrient use efficiency and maximizes crop yield potential. This data-driven approach marks a significant improvement over traditional, blanket fertilizer recommendations, which often failed to consider site-specific factors (Desta et al., 2023).

The Landscape-Specific Fertilizer Advisory (LSFA) validation trials showed significant agronomic and economic benefits for tef, wheat, and sorghum cultivation in Ethiopia. The LSFA validation trials led to remarkable yield improvements for both wheat and tef. Wheat yields increased by an average of 15%, while tef yields rose by 20%, and sorghum yields increased by 29%, compared to standard extension fertilizer recommendations. These gains were even more pronounced in foot slope areas, with wheat and tef yields 23% and 56% higher, respectively, than control plots. These yield improvements translated into substantial economic gains. Wheat farmers experienced a profitability increase of $90 (ET Birr 4,383) per hectare, while tef farmers saw an increase of $1.

1. Introduction

Cereal crops are of critical importance to food security and rural livelihoods in Ethiopia, being cultivated on about 10 M ha annually and engaging nearly 16 M smallholders (CSA, 2022a). Moreover, two-thirds of the national cereal production is used for household consumption (CSA, 2022b). Tef, maize, sorghum, and wheat constitute 71% of the cereal area and 77% of the cereal production in country (CSA, 2022a) and average yields at national level more than doubled in the past two decades (Figure 1A; CSA, 2001; CSA, 2022a; Hodson et al., 2020). Yield gains occurred in tandem with area expansion (Figure 1A), translating into impressive increases in cereal production at national level (Figure 1B). Tef remains the most important staple crop in the country (Tadele & Hibistu, 2021), followed by maize (Abate et al., 2015) and wheat (Silva et al., 2021).

Past yield trends were the result of increases in fertilizer use, improved genetics, and supportive extension system among other factors (Abate 2015; Assefa et al., 2020; Silva et al., 2023a). Yet, farmers’ yields still only reach about 20-40% of what is possible with agronomic best practices (van Ittersum et al, 2016; Assefa et al. 2020; Silva et al., 2021). Such low productivity levels cannot satisfy cereal demand in the country resulting in high import dependencies. This is especially true for wheat (Silva et al., 2023a; Senbeta et al., 2023) for which imports amounted to 1.4 M t in 2022, corresponding to 865 M US$ (FAOSTAT, 2024). Current yield constraints are related to poor agronomy, including sub-optimal crop management and low input levels (Assefa et al. 2020; Silva et al., 2021), and low adoption of soil fertility management practices, but field-specific constraints are yet to be identified. Overcoming such yield constraints towards yield levels of about 50% of the water-limited yield, equivalent to doubling current farm yields, could ensure cereal self-sufficiency at the national level whereas full yield gap closure would transform the country into a net cereal exporter (van Ittersum et al., 2016).

Achieving cereal self-sufficiency is a priority for the Ethiopian government and many recent efforts were put in place to transform the country’s cereal production systems (e.g., Hodson et al., 2020; Abera et al., 2022). Yet, such efforts often do not prioritize yield constraints in farmers’ fields, which are crop- and context-dependent. We argue that research and development efforts aiming to increase cereal productivity need to be guided by technology targeting approaches which acknowledge current yield constraints and ensure that future yield gains are sustainable and profitable at the farm level. Such agronomic pathways for sustainable crop intensification can be identified through high-quality and large-n agronomic surveys powered by e.g., predictive analytics based on interpretable machine learning techniques (Nayak et al., 2024). assets are essential to monitor changes in farm practices and production levels and to derive actionable policy recommendations that recognize the diversity and heterogeneity of smallholder production landscapes.

The objectives of this study were to quantify yield gaps and identify the key yield constraints associated with them for tef, wheat, and sorghum crops across strategic production environments of Ethiopia. Our analysis builds upon agronomic surveys, including crop cuts, conducted in the 2022 Meher growing season in 10 districts for tef, 13 for wheat, and 8 for sorghum. Yield gaps were quantified as the difference between the water-limited yield (retrieved from the Global Yield Gap Atlas for wheat and sorghum and obtained through expert knowledge for tef) and the crop cut yields measured in farmers’ fields. Field-specific yield constraints were identified through an interpretable machine learning approach leveraging upon SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values (Nayak et al., 2024). Our results provide new spatially disaggregated evidence for the importance of agronomic management towards increasing smallholder productivity in Ethiopia.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Agronomic survey and crop yield estimation

Agronomic surveys with crop cut yield measurements were conducted in 10 districts for tef, 13 districts for wheat, and 8 districts for sorghum. Sample districts were identified based on the potential production and cultivated area of each crop. Within districts, three to ten kebeles (sub-districts) and five to ten villages within each kebele were selected based on the cultivated area of each crop. 15 – 50 farm fields were randomly selected within each village from the list of households who grow the crop of interest, while considering a similar proportion of male and female farm households. The number of farm fields per village was defined based on the crop yield variability in the district and proportional to the crop area coverage of the sample kebele.

Actual farm yields were measured through crop cuts conducted for tef, wheat, and sorghum at the end of the 2022 Meher growing season. Measurements were conducted on the largest field of each farm where the crop of interest was cultivated. All fields were geo-referenced and where data were poorly recorded the GPS coordinates of the household were used instead. For each crop x field combination, yields at 12% moisture content were measured from two to three randomly selected rectangular sub-plots. The sub-plots were 2m x 2m for tef and wheat and 5m x 3m for sorghum and performed across the diagonal of each field. Yield measurements were performed on a total of 1001, 1709, and 950 tef, wheat, and sorghum fields and were replicated three times for tef and wheat and two times for sorghum. Actual farm yields were expressed per ha considering the measured field area. Within-field replicates provide a measure of within-field yield variability for each of the surveyed farm fields (data not shown). Mean differences in selected crop management practices across administrative zones were assessed with analysis of variance followed by an estimation of least-square means using the emmeans R package (Lenth, 2024).

A corresponding agronomic survey was conducted in early 2023 to all households owning the fields where the yield measurements were conducted. The agronomic survey employed a standardized tool developed in ODK Collect (available here). The purpose of the agronomic survey was to collect household level data to capture information on farm(er) characteristics and crop management practices for each field where yields were measured. The survey questionnaire was structured in two modules: (1) a survey module on farm(er) characteristics and assets and major production constraints at farm level and (2) a survey module on field characteristics, detailed crop management practices, and production factors at the field level. The surveys were conducted in local languages by trained enumerators.
2.2. Secondary data sources and estimation of yield gaps

The farmer field database was augmented with simulated yield data and biophysical data from secondary data sources based on the field-specific GPS coordinates. Water-limited yield potentials simulated with the WOFOST crop model (de Wit et al., 2019) for wheat and sorghum in Ethiopia (Meher seasons between 2001-2021; van Ittersum et al., 2016) were obtained using R through an API of the Global Yield Gap Atlas (www.yieldgap.org). The Global Yield Gap Atlas follows a bottom-up protocol based on local weather, soil, and agronomic data to estimate crop yield ceilings within a spatial framework using climate zones (see Tesfaye, 2016, for further details
