What specifically, was done?

1. In every cooperative, three fertility camps were organized. In the camps, veterinarians thoroughly examined the buffaloes and provided supplements with fertility-supporting micro-minerals and also administered hormone treatments to induce estrus and ovulation in anestrus animals. Additionally, the veterinarians provided medication for endoparasite infections. Follow-up of the treatment was done by the livestock promoters to increase the effect of the medication.

2. The farmers, based on the advice of the livestock promoter, gave one kg of compound feed for each buffalo daily in addition to 500 g of corn flour, 500 g of mustard cake, and 20 g of salt at their cost. They also chopped dry/green roughages before feeding to enhance utilization and minimize wastage. 3. Farmers sowed forage seeds (arranged by the livestock promoter) on their land after the rice harvest in October. The promoter trained the farmers on silage making, which will help the farmers conserve their forage as silage to feed during the dry season.

4. The successful implementation of the bundled interventions was based on their active dissemination by livestock promoters. They were pivotal in selecting farmers, and coordinating with local government, cooperatives, and line

agencies. They organized farmer field schools and provided training on integrated nutrition and fodder production. Additionally, they used digital tools to assess nutrient gaps in buffaloes' diets and provided advice accordingly. The promoters facilitated connections between cooperatives and feed dealers. Moreover, they actively engaged in fertility management camps, identifying buffaloes with infertility issues, and informing farmers about the camps. They played a supportive role in organizing fertility camps and monitored the estrus status of buffaloes as well as the success of conception after the camp. The records of estrus and conception outcomes are maintained by the promoters in a digital application and provided to the authorities for analysis. They also record animal performance in a digital application, which forms the basis for genetic evaluation of the national livestock resources, allowing genetic improvement.

What result was observed?
A preliminary evaluation shows that the bundled technology and integrated service delivery package could impact buffalo production /reproduction in the following ways:
1. Eighty-seven percent (87%) of farmers reported an increase in daily milk production by 1 to 2 liters within a week of implementing the package.

Before implementing the nutrition package, I used to get 6 liters in the morning and 3 liters in the afternoon. Now, after adopting the package, I collect 7 liters in the morning and 3 liters in the afternoon"".
Ashamaya Tamang, buffalo farmer, Dugdha Utpadak, Sahakari Sanstha, Itahari
2. Ninety-three percent (93%) of farmers observed improvement in milk quality, particularly in increased fat content by 1%.

3. The buffaloes treated in the fertility clinic (90% out of the total presented in the camps) began exhibiting signs of estrus within five to six months after calving, in some cases within 3-4 days after treatment and actively sought male buffaloes for mating. This was a significant improvement compared to the previous situation where some buffaloes had not shown estrus for more than three years.

Previously, my buffalo didn't exhibit the behavior of seeking out male buffaloes, leading to infertility issues. I had to sell the buffalo because of this. However, after undergoing treatment at fertility clinics, the buffalo now enters estrus within 21-22 days"".
Ram Kumar Rai, buffalo farmer in Itahari
4. The positive changes in buffalo health, such as enhanced physical condition, weight, appetite, and coat quality, affirm the overall success of nutritional improvement.

How can this model be scaled up to
benefit dairy farmers in all rural
municipalities in Nepal?
To replicate the i-SAP bundled livestock technologies and services in new areas, the following factors may be considered:

1. Decision to implement SAPLING model and allocation of budget in the annual financial plan by provincial government (scaling agency), rural municipalities and dairy cooperatives (indicative budget in Table 1).

2. Selection of dairy cooperative: As it will be easy to implement the program through a farmer-based organization, it will be good to identify dairy cooperatives based on a set of criteria including good governance, quality-based milk value payment, welfare activities, farmers’ trust, proactive leadership among others. However, if promising cooperatives are not available, the program can be implemented directly by the local government through its Livestock Service Section.

3. Selection of livestock promoter: The livestock promoter is the key person linking the livestock technologies, inputs and services to farmers, therefore select a technically qualified junior technical assistant (JTA passed) local youth, preferably a lady, to be trained as a livestock promoter. Make sure that the cooperative management is included in the selection panel and they are willing to provide him/her with (i) direct access to members, (ii) space to set up

an input sales unit in the cooperative, (iii) a soft loan to start the input business, and (iv) a basic monthly incentive for the first one year till he/she gets established. However, if a suitable candidate is not available in the municipality area, an existing agro-vet or a feed dealer can be approached to deliver the same function after undergoing training by a resource organization such as a training centre, university or a research institute.

4. Training of livestock promoter: A suitable resource organization may be approached to train the selected candidates. The module-based training may be given on: (i) feeds, forages and feed improvement, extension and business skills; (ii) animal reproduction and health; (iii) genetic improvement; (iv) marketing and value chain development; and (v) artificial insemination. The training on artificial insemination is seen as a means for strengthening the business of the promoter, which may be given after one year based on performance.

5. Arrangement of fertility camps and support nutrition and genetic improvement: The cooperatives, with the support of livestock promoters, may arrange fertility camps (three per year) in their area of operation with wide publicity among dairy farmers. Local veterinarians /technicians may be involved in managing the camp with the support of experts from resource organizations. The required medicines /mineral supplements may be provided by the Livestock Service Section of the concerned municipality. The livestock promoter shall arrange concentrate feeds, forage seeds etc., from his input shop or cooperative (if they are already selling it) or a feed factory on a credit basis. The cost of inputs can be recovered later from the milk value of the concerned farmers as agreed by the cooperative. The livestock promoter shall also visit the farms and provide knowledge-based support to farmers on genetic improvement, feed balancing, feed chopping, silage making, straw treatment etc. In addition, the promoters shall support the national agencies for animal identification and data recording on animal
performance.

6. Monitoring and evaluation: Being the scaling agency, the provincial government, with the support of the resource organization shall monitor implementation of the program and advise for continuous improvement.

Commendation

A team of policymakers from the Federal, Provincial and Local government, Nepal Agricultural Research Council (NARC), the Agriculture and Forestry University and Tribhuvan University visited the project sites in Eastern Terai and was impressed with the impact of the i-SAP innovation. Dr Rewati Raman Paudel, Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development, who was in the team said ”in a short time, we can see the impact of the program on buffalo productivity and the involvement of women farmers in livestock farming is leading to their empowerment.” Dr Hom Bahadur Basnet, Dean of the Agriculture and Forestry University, opined that “simple adjustments in farming methods utilizing existing resources enabled farmers to observe tangible outcomes.” He also underscored the pivotal role of promoters in assisting farmers to enhance productivity sustainably and reduce infertility. Dr Doj Raj Khanal, Livestock Director, NARC thought that “the use of digital applications by promoters to offer feeding advice to farmers was particularly noteworthy.” All of them also gave valuable suggestions to improve the program while scaling it out in other provinces.
Conclusion

There is considerable potential to enhance dairy milk productivity through the adoption of an integrated package of techniques for fertility improvement and nutritional management by the community, through strengthening extension and advisory services as well as improved access to inputs and services using the livestock promoters. Feedback from various interactions reveals farmers' satisfaction with observed outcomes such as improved body condition scores, increased milk yield, and higher conception rates. The engagement and empowerment of women farmers, combined with nutritional

packages and reproductive management activities further enhance these outcomes. The success is attributed to the livestock promoters commitment and effective coordination with cooperatives, backed by municipalities, which serve as crucial links between farmers and municipal dairy stakeholders, facilitating feedback loops within the dairy sector.

Key messages and solutions
Knowledge on husbandry practices is needed to enhance productivity of smallholder dairy farmers
ANM approach leverages village-level agents that are a link between agro-dealers and farmers
Qualified personnel (AHAs, extension personnel, etc.) are engaged as agents of agro-dealers; agents train farmers, thus creating demand for agro-dealer products
Agents bulk orders from farmers and coordinate delivery, saving farmers time and costs of individual transactions
Agents are paid commission for volumes of sales; thus are incentivized to offer trainings that generate demand
Opportunities and benefits
For agro-dealers: Increased sales,  improved management of stock and expansion of market share, all leading to profitability.
For service providers: earning additional income from commission and strengthening business ties with farmers; value add to farmer-clients
Farmers: Improved knowledge on husbandry practices and cost savings – bulking orders (discounts) and shared transport cost
Needed: Strategic alliance between a business-focused agro-dealer & qualified service provider/extension agent with access to geographically clustered farmers – possibly via a Cooperative

Where cooperatives have with members clustered across villages that are located far from market centers where agro-dealers are found
Where service providers (AHAs, AISPs) are already linked to farmers via service provision; therefore ANM is a value add
In emerging dairy areas where farmers are beginning to appreciate the value of improved husbandry
Evidence
Evidence show that ANM approach reduces transaction costs of procuring inputs by farmers
ANM is also effective in enhancing the knowledge base of farmers on animal husbandry leading to increased productivity

About SAPLING

CGIAR’s Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) is working in seven countries focusing on livestock value chains to package and scale out tried-and-tested, as well as new, innovations in livestock health, genetics, feed and market systems. SAPLING aims to demonstrate that improvements in livestock productivity can offer a triple win: generating improved livelihoods and nutritional outcomes; contributing to women’s empowerment; and, reducing impacts on climate and the environment. Its seven focus countries are Ethiopia, Kenya, Mali, Nepal, Tanzania, Uganda and Vietnam.

This work was conducted as part of the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity. CGIAR research is supported by contributions to the CGIAR Trust Fund. CGIAR is a global research partnership for a food- secure future dedicated to transforming food, land, and water systems in a climate crisis.
Background to training

Livestock production in the Northwest Highlands (NWH) of Vietnam, particularly in Son La Province, faces significant challenges. Limited knowledge and skills among farmers in livestock production practices, particularly in feed and feeding strategies, are major constraints that impede livestock productivity1. In the Livestock CRP project (Li-chan), farmers in four villages of Chieng Chung and Chieng Luong communes, Mai Son district, were trained on feeds and feeding regimes, however, the farmer’s receptivity to knowledge was still limited due to the short project duration and other operational barriers. Acute winter (dry season) feed shortage, lack of high-quality forage varieties and limited capacity in animal nutrition techniques are pressing issues for livestock producers in the region. The reliance on traditional forage varieties, such as Napier grass, further constrains productivity, and this presents an opportunity for introducing and promoting improved forage varieties in the region.

Improved animal nutrition is fundamental in ensuring livestock productivity and efficiency. Local stakeholders play a crucial role in this domain, and empowering these stakeholders with the knowledge and skills necessary for optimal animal nutrition is essential for sustainable agricultural practices and economic development. Therefore, training of trainers (ToT) with local extension staff and veterinary officers, and training of farmers (ToFs) with women and men farmers and farmer groups is crucial to enhance knowledge and skills on animal nutrition.

The CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Improved Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) aims to transform the livestock value chains towards greater productivity, adaptation, equity, and sustainability in Son La Province in the NWH of Vietnam. This aligns with the local programs and development goals for the agriculture sector in the province. SAPLING focuses on testing and promoting locally adapted feed intervention strategies for cattle and pigs to address the feed challenges and enhance livestock performance in the region.

In 2023, the Feeds and Forages component of SAPLING (work package 1 – Technologies and practices for sustainable livestock productivity) conducted a ToT course and four ToFs to impart practical knowledge on pigs and cattle feeds and nutrition in Mai Son District, with 114 participants (24 local staff and 90 farmers). To enable a wider reach of farmers, ensure strengthened local capacity in animal nutrition, and accelerate scaling of feeds and forages interventions, a follow-up in-depth ToT was organized in 2024 and lasted 3 days from 28–30 May 2024, with participants from Mai Son and Phu Yen districts. The main purpose of the training was to equip the trainers not only with the technical knowledge in cattle and pig nutrition, but also impart skills that can be effectively transferred to farmers in Son La Province.

The 2024 ToT training took place at the Mai Son District Agriculture Service Center from 28–30 May 2024. All materials were prepared for the practical sessions including feed materials (rice straw, forage biomass, rice bran, maize meal, feed concentrates) and other materials needed (urea, probiotics, nylon bags, plastic containers) (Annex 2).

Interactive and hand-on learning methods were applied during the ToT, by using PowerPoint presentations, posters and practical demonstrations. Participants were divided into three groups for the practical

Who conducted the training

The training was led by a team of experienced staff from the National Institute for Animal Sciences (NIAS), the Northern Mountainous Agriculture and Forestry Research Institute (NOMAFSI), and the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT. Three NIAS staff were trainers for the ToT, including Associate Prof. Tran Thi Bich Ngoc, Tran Viet Phuong and Nguyen Thien Truong Giang. NIAS staff also prepared the training materials and the protocol of the training course, and the list of participants. Objectives of the training

The objective of the training was to build the capacity of local extension staff, veterinary officers, and farmers in animal nutrition by through a training of trainers (ToT) program and follow-up training of farmers (ToF) sessions. These programs focus on providing practical and theoretical knowledge on feed technologies and livestock feeding regimes for both pigs and cattle in Son La Province. Specifically, the training aimed to equip participants with skills they could transfer to local farmers to improve livestock productivity.
Training agenda
The following topics were covered in the training (full agenda in Annex 1):
• Feed and feeding regimes for cattle (https://hdl.handle.net/10568/134521)
o Feed classification (forages, concentrate, mineral)
o Feed processing: silage making (with forages, biomass maize, crop residues…), urea- treated rice straw.
o Feeding regimes for cattle in different periods (lactating cow, suckling calf, weaning calf, heifer, and fattening)
• Feed and feeding regimes for pigs (https://hdl.handle.net/10568/134553)
o Feed classification (protein feed, energy feed, mineral feed, vitamin feed)
o Feed processing: concentrate mixing, concentrate feed fermentation by probiotics.
o Feeding regimes for pigs in different periods (gilts, pregnant sow, lactating sow, grower- fattener pigs)
Training participants
The ToT had 32 participants of whom 9 were women (4 Kinh and 5 Thai ethnicities) and 23 men (2 Kinh and

21 Thai ethnicities) (Table 1). Participants included local staff from the Son La Agricultural Extension Center; Mai Son and Phu Yen Centers of Agricultural Services; extension and veterinary staff at commune level from Chiềng Chung, Chiềng Lương, Hát Lót, Mường Bon, Chiềng Mai, Mường Bằng, Chiềng Re, Phiêng Cằm, Nà Bó and Cò Nòi communes; and key farmers from the target farmer groups. These participants were selected by Sub-DAH and Mai Son Center of Agricultural Services, to become local lead trainers for farmers in their respective jurisdictions, ensuring knowledge transfer to a wider farming community.

Conclusion

The ToT training successfully engaged all invited participants over the three-day program, resulting in a significant improvement in their knowledge and skills in animal nutrition and feed technologies for cattle and pigs. Participants showed high levels of engagement and enthusiasm throughout the sessions.
Knowledge
transfer:

The training covered essential topics such as feed processing (silage making, urea- treated rice straw, and feed fermentation), feeding regimes for different stages of cattle and pigs, and forage-based feeding strategies. These topics were delivered through PowerPoint presentations and interactive group discussions, followed by practical sessions where participants could apply the knowledge in real time.
Hands-on
learning:

During the practical sessions, participants actively engaged in silage preparation, urea- treated rice straw production, feed mixing, and feed fermentation for pigs. They followed a ‘learning by doing’ approach, allowing them to confidently grasp and execute the techniques on their own.
Evaluation:

The trainees were evaluated through their participation in group discussions, practical exercises, and individual presentations. About 33% of the participants demonstrated a strong grasp of the material, delivering confident presentations and showing good communication skills. Another 50% performed well, while 17% displayed average teaching skills, largely due to a lack of prior experience in teaching despite a solid understanding of the technical material.
Forage
farms:

The participants visited local forage demo farms showcasing both improved and local forage varieties, such as Green Elephant grass (VA06), Mulato II, Mombasa Guinea, and Ubon Stylo. This visit allowed the trainees to evaluate the performance of these forages and gain practical insights into integrating them into local farming systems.

Following the ToT, SAPLING and the Mai Son District Agricultural Service Center organized 34 training of farmers (ToF) sessions from 11–22 June 2024, across nine communes. A total of 1,183 farmers participated (65.5% men, 34.5% women), representing primarily Thai and Hmong ethnic groups. These sessions extended
the knowledge gained in the ToT to a broader farmer base, covering essential feed and nutrition practices for livestock management.
Next
Next steps

The ToT program demonstrated success in building local capacity in animal nutrition, paving the way for the scaling-up of these interventions across Son La Province. However, to ensure long-term impact and sustainability, several key steps need to be taken:

• Expand ToT programs: To achieve widespread adoption of improved livestock practices, it is recommended that the ToT program be expanded to other districts within Son La Province. Local staff at the commune, district, and provincial levels who were trained during the ToT sessions will play a vital role in this expansion, acting as lead trainers and knowledge transfer agents for farmers in their respective areas.

• Strengthen follow-up support: Continuous engagement with ToT participants is essential to ensure the consistent application of the skills and knowledge acquired. Providing follow-up support and additional refresher courses will help reinforce their understanding and address any practical challenges they may face when transferring these skills to farmers.

• Broader outreach through ToFs: The success of the initial ToF sessions highlights the need for further farmer training sessions, especially targeting underrepresented groups like women and ethnic minorities. Expanding ToF programs to additional communes and villages will ensure that more farmers benefit from improved feed and nutrition strategies, thereby enhancing livestock productivity and economic outcomes across the province.

• Sustaining knowledge transfer: To maintain the momentum generated by the SAPLING project, it will be important to institutionalize these trainings within local agricultural services. By integrating animal nutrition and feed technology training into the regular programs of local extension and agricultural service centers, the project’s interventions will continue to have an impact even after the SAPLING initiative concludes.

With these next steps, the SAPLING initiative can ensure that the benefits of improved animal nutrition and feed technologies reach more livestock keepers, leading to enhanced livestock productivity and improved livelihoods across the Northwest Highlands of Vietnam.

Abstract

Livestock production in Vietnam is critical in reducing poverty and increasing income particularly for ethnic minorities in the Northwest Highlands. Improved livestock management and productivity can be achieved through better feed management and increased cultivation of improved forages, to meet animal nutrition demand. This study aimed at assessing feed intervention strategies to address context-specific feed-related challenges, mainly winter-feed shortage, for improved animal nutrition and livestock productivity in Mai Son district, Son La province, Vietnam. These interventions included promoting the uptake of improved forage varieties (grasses and legumes) and capacity building on animal nutrition techniques including feed processing and preservation, feed mix and feeding regimes for cattle and pigs. Willing farmers selected various forage varieties, were provided with seeds and planting materials to grow on their farms and guided on forage planting, management, and utilization. Local partners and stakeholders supported various activities and ensured successful implementation amidst the restrictions arising from the Covid 19 pandemic. Farmers reported increased awareness on feed technologies, increased yield, and availability of high-quality feed for their livestock, as well as challenges encountered in applying different feed-related techniques. Initial results from this study show the potential of feed and forage technologies in improving livestock productivity and lays a foundation for scaling these interventions to other regions of Vietnam.
I. Introduction

In the Northwest Highlands (NWH) of Vietnam, the main feeding system for cattle and buffalo are mainly through tended native pasture (74%), stall feeding using crop residues and free grazing on communal land and forests. Feed and forage quality is generally of low quality resulting in low livestock output. Intensifying beef cattle production has been identified as a way of increasing livestock productivity and income of smallholder livestock farmers in this region (Huyen et al., 2010). Currently, cattle production systems have begun transitioning from extensive to semi-intensive and intensive systems (Ba et al., 2015). However, to fully achieve this goal, measures need to be put into place to address constraints of animal husbandry including feed-related challenges such as winter feed shortage.

Pig production also plays an important role in the livelihoods of livestock farmers in the NWH region. In remote areas, pig production is associated with indigenous pig breeds characterized by low productivity but well-adapted to local harsh conditions and showing better resistance to diseases than improved pig breeds (Le et al., 2016). Bản pigs are mainly fed with available feed resources such as rice bran, corn, banana trunk, vegetables, and leaves. Although there is a long-standing tradition of Bản pig production, farmers have limited knowledge in feed practices for pigs which greatly affects the productivity and health of the pig herd.

Assessments carried out in 2020, in Mai Son district identified the main feed-related challenges in the region including shortage of winter feed, poor diets and low yield and poor quality of available forages (Hammond et al., 2021). Most households rely on crop residues and collected feed such as rice straw, sugarcanes tops, banana stem, maize, sweet potato etc. Some villages have communal pastures where animals can graze (Atieno et al., 2021). However, the available feed is of either of low quality or limited especially during winter. Bản pigs have a high fat content and less lean meat which lowers the market value leading to low returns to the farmers. There is limited knowledge on suitable forage types and management, feed processing and preservation (Atieno et al., 2021). The results of this assessment informed the design of feed interventions to help address these challenges. This study aims to assess locally suited feed intervention strategies for cattle and pigs, for improved animal nutrition in the Mai Son district, Son La province, located in the Northwest Highlands of Vietnam.
II. Study area

The study area is located in 2 communes (Chieng Chung and Chieng Luong) of Mai Son district, Son La province, has different types of farming systems ranging from grazing and extensive systems at the mountain tops to mixed crop-livestock systems at the bottom of the mountains, with varying socio- economic and ecological conditions (Hammond et al., 2021). The study location is divided into 4 farming system types (A, B, C1 and C2) based on accessibility i.e., distance to the main road or nearby market, and production system. Six villages were selected for interventions in the 2 communes (Table 1).
⮚ Type A – intensive systems in the lowlands with good market access and relatively better capacity for innovation.
⮚ Type B - mixed crop-livestock systems in the mid-altitudes with mainly Thai ethnic minorities
⮚ Type C1 - remote extensive system in the high altitudes, with low access to market, fragile environment, mainly Hmong ethnic group
⮚ Type C2 – remote mixed crop-livestock system in the high altitudes, with low access to market, fragile environment, mainly Hmong ethnic group

Feed intervention strategies

To propose context-specific measures on animal nutrition, feed-related challenges need to be identified. In 2020, a survey was conducted in 6 villages of Chieng Chung and Chieng Luong communes, Mai Son district, Son La province, using the Gendered Feed Assessment Tool (G-FEAST) (Atieno et al., 2021). G-FEAST was designed to identify opportunities and constraints in animal feeding practices for different household types by assessing the availability and use of local feed resources, identify challenges and constraints affecting livestock production through the gender lens, opportunities for improved animal nutrition and propose context-specific interventions on livestock feed for improved animal nutrition (Lukuyu et al., 2019a; Lukuyu et al., 2019b). The G-FEAST survey informed the design of context-specific feed interventions to be implemented in Chieng Chung and Chieng Luong communes such as promoting improved forage varieties, knowledge on better utilization of crop residues, feed processing and preparation and feeding regimes (Atieno et al., 2021).
Based on this survey, feed interventions were designed as follows:
1. Improved animal nutrition: Trainings on feed utilization, processing & preservation, and feeding regimes for cattle/buffalo and pigs
2. Improved forage varieties – Promote adoption of improved forage varieties – high yielding, high nutrient, cold-tolerant varieties.
1. Improved animal nutrition
a) Overview of topics covered and training materials

Farmers in the intervention villages were trained on different animal nutrition techniques such as feed processing and preservation, better utilization of crop residues, feed mixing and improved diets for cattle and pigs. The training was conducted from March 22-26th, 2021, one day per village and covered the following topics (more information and details of the training materials can be found at (https://bit.ly/3bHMfRH; https://bit.ly/3bEoz0N):
Training topics covered included:
i) Feed and feeding regimes for cattle and buffalo
● Feed classification (forages, concentrates, minerals)
● Feed processing: silage preparation (grass, maize, crop residue…), urea-treated rice straw
● Feeding regimes for cattle (lactating cows, suckling calf, weaning calf, heifer and fattening diets)
ii) Feed and feeding regimes for Bản pigs
● Feed classification (protein feed, energy feed, minerals, vitamins)
● Feed processing: concentrate mixing, concentrate feed fermentation by probiotics
● Feeding regimes for Bản pigs (gilts, pregnant sow, lactating sow, grower-fattener pigs)

The first session involved poster presentation with easy-to-follow illustrations. The posters were also translated to local languages (Vietnamese and Hmong) so farmers could understand and follow through. The second part of the training involved practical demonstrations on various techniques with participants taking part in preparing materials and hands-on demonstration. Feed materials were prepared for practical training sessions depending on the available feed resources in the different villages at the time of the training. Materials included banana trunk, sugarcane tops, rice straw, rice bran, cornmeal and cassava meal.
b) Farmers’ participation

About 145 farmers (70 men and 75 women) participated from the six villages of Chieng Chung and Chieng Luong communes (Table 2). Most of the invited households participated in the trainings while in some villages e.g., Buom Khoang, recorded more participants in attendance. More female participants enthusiastically participated in the hands-on practical sessions including preparation on silage and urea-treated rice straw, feed mixing and feed fermentation. The training approach used was interactive and allowed participants to actively participate and freely ask questions and seek clarifications. Some farmers took notes and videos of the training sessions.

c) Follow up on uptake of feed technologies

Six months after the training while conducting monitoring of farmer-led forage trials (section 2), follow-up interviews were done with 49 farmers who were also growing introduced forages, to assess the uptake of the animal nutrition techniques from the training. Out of 49 farmers interviewed, 17 reported already applying one or more of the techniques they had learned in the training. The farmers also reported benefits from applying feed techniques such as reduction in labour and time for feed preparation. For instance, some farmers now prepare enough silage and store for a longer time as compared to before the training. Cattle prefer to eat more of the silage. Farmers preparing fermented pig feed using probiotics reported they no longer need to cook resulting in reduced fuel cost and less firewood for cooking feed.
2. Improved forages
a) Selection of preferred forage varieties

The proposed forage varieties included 4 grasses (Mulato II, Mombasa guinea, Green elephant and Ubon paspalum), and 3 legumes (Ubon stylo, Arachis pintoi and rice bean). These varieties were selected as they are high-yielding, high quality and cold-tolerant, characteristics best suited to address feed challenges in the study area. Farmers were first given an overview of proposed forages then asked to fill in a checklist to select from the proposed forage varieties that best suit their needs and farming systems (Table 4).

Various planting methods were used for selected forages depending on the system and farmers’ preference. Examples include cut-and-carry mono-crop plots, grasses planted on contours, intercropping with annual or perennial crops, ground cover etc. Farmers applied varying amounts of fertilizers (NPK, urea, manure). Green elephant

Green elephant grass showed a high germination rate of >81% across all farming system types except in Type C1 with 79% (Table 7). Average yield ranged from 33.8 – 82.1 tonnes FM/ha with Type A and C2 recording the highest biomass of > 82 ton/ha after the second harvest while Type C1 reported the lowest yield as farmers did not apply any fertilizer. All farmers showed high preference (100%) and expressed interest to continue growing this variety as it is high yielding, grows fast, has soft leaves and stem and is liked by cattle and buffalo. However, when harvested too early or fed in large quantities, green elephant grass contains a lot of water which can cause bloating and diarrhea in cattle.

Germination rate ranged from 71-84% and was highest in Type C2 (84%) and lowest in Type A villages (71%) as it temporarily stopped raining after sowing. There were also issues with poor sowing and land preparation techniques and some seedlings eaten by chickens especially in unfenced plots. Biomass yield was lowest in Type C1 (11.8t FM/ha). Mulato II

Similar to green elephant grass, Mulato II also showed a germination rate of 74-86% in all system types except in Types A and C1 due to poor land preparation and sowing methods, high temperatures and also seedlings damage by chickens. Average yield after the second harvest was 41.9-51.1t FM/ha except for C1 (12.8t FM/ha). Highest preference for this variety was reported in Type C households. However, 48% of Type A households reported low preference for Mulato II due to low germination and yield in some farms as compared to green elephant, hairy leaves and not liked by cattle and buffalo were further factors contributing to low preference.
Mulato II Photo: Bùi Văn Tùng & Phan Huy Chương (NOMAFSI)
Ubon paspalum

Ubon paspalum recorded a high germination rate in Type A households (86%) and lowest in Type C1 and B (63-66%) attributed to poor land preparation and sowing methods, high temperatures and also seedlings damage by chicken. Type C1 also recorded the lowest yield of only 10.6t FM/ha. Most households reported high to medium preference while 50% of C1 had low preference for this variety. High preference was attributed to soft leaves and stem and liked by cattle when fed in moderate quantities. However, as with other grasses, cutting young Ubon paspalum and feeding large quantities caused digestion-related problems such as bloating and diarrhea in cattle.
Ubon paspalum Photo: Bùi Văn Tùng & Phan Huy Chương (NOMAFSI)
Ubon stylo

Stylo germinated well in Type C farms (80-84%), however the highest yield was reported in Type B after 2 harvests (26.4t FM/ha). Preference for Ubon stylo was medium to low as farmers complained about low yield, difficulties to manage, tough stem and not liked by cattle and goats even when fed in moderate quantities.

Rice bean

Rice bean had the highest germination rate out of the 7 varieties ranging from 82-100% with Type C1 reporting 100% germination of sown seeds. As rice bean was planted later in the rainy season, low yields were reported at the time of sampling with only 1 harvest. Most farmers reported high to medium preference and intend to continue growing rice bean because it is a multipurpose -purpose crop (seeds can be used as food, biomass as feed, and because of additional benefits of improving soil health) and has a high germination rate. One constraint reported is the slow regrowth after the first harvest.

Pinto peanut

Of all the 7 forage varieties, Pinto Peanut had the lowest germination rate (57-65%), lowest yield (2- 4t FM/ha) and lowest preference particularly in Type C1 (60%) due to low germination and yield, and slow growth. Surprisingly, Pinto peanut was expected to have a higher uptake and preference in C1 (extensive system) as it is best utilized as a ground cover under trees and tolerant to acidic soils

predominant in this area. However, the farmers who showed high preference for pinto peanut reported benefits of adopting this variety as they could feed it to pigs, chicken, and cattle, and for ornamental use because of its beautiful blossom.

d) Forage utilization and benefits of improved forages

- Forages are mainly fed for cattle and buffalo. Moreover, there is a small number of farmers who fed the promoted varieties to pigs and poultry (chicken, local goose and ducks). In this case, forages were often chopped and mixed with rice bran or maize meal.

- There was an increase in the number of forage varieties grown by farmers who previously relied on local Napier grass and to a lesser extent – Guinea grass, in addition to food-feed crops such banana, maize etc.
Increased amount of feed available for livestock was reported and animals had enough to eat.
- Cut-and-carry systems helped to increase the availability of forages near the farms and family house, especially during rainy days when grazing is difficult.
- Increased transition to intensive systems, from grazing to stall feeding especially in Type A households.

- Growing forages reduced the cost and time of collecting native grasses from paddy fields and forests and prevented harvesting grass contaminants such as herbicides. Farmers had more time for other on-farm and off-farm activities.
Increasing the availability of forages resulted in few farmers expanding their herd size.
IV. Farmers’ perceptions
1. Photovoice stories

In the frame of Li-chăn project, the photovoice method was used as a participatory monitoring and evaluation tool to document change stories from farmers’ perspectives (Wang & Burris 1997). Farmers gave their own reflections on livestock development including the benefits of growing improved forages, feed preparation and preservation for improved nutrition and productivity of livestock. These stories were featured in a virtual exhibition - Livestock Development in Vietnam from Artists’ and Farmers’ Perspectives - developed in collaboration with the Vietnam Fine Arts Museum (https://bit.ly/3BylpGr). Farmers shared stories on benefits of applying different methods of feed processing and preservation such as increased availability of feed, high preference of silage by cattle, increased weight gain of pigs fed with fermented feed. They also reported increased forage yields from selected varieties and availability of livestock feed, preference of their animals to different forages, challenges encountered when introducing new varieties to their animals, and plans to increase adoption of these forages. About SAPLING

CGIAR’s Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) is working in seven countries focusing on livestock value chains to package and scale out tried-and-tested, as well as new, innovations in livestock health, genetics, feed and market systems. SAPLING aims to demonstrate that improvements in livestock productivity can offer a triple win: generating improved livelihoods and nutritional outcomes; contributing to women’s empowerment; and, reducing impacts on climate and the environment. Its seven focus countries are Ethiopia, Kenya, Mali, Nepal, Tanzania, Uganda and Vietnam.
Acknowledgements

This work was conducted as part of the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity. CGIAR research is supported by contributions to the CGIAR Trust Fund. CGIAR is a global research partnership for a food- secure future dedicated to transforming food, land, and water systems in a climate crisis.
Background

The CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) initiative being implemented in Son La Province, Vietnam, aims to transform the livestock value chain in the Northwest Highlands of Vietnam towards greater livestock productivity, adaptation, equity, and sustainability. This aligns with the development goals of the agricultural sector in both Mai Son District and Son La Province. The work in the locality focuses on developing livestock value chains and commercially oriented cattle production initiatives (Resolution No. 75/2023/NQ-HDND dated 8 December 2023, Provincial People's Council) and encourages the implementation of sustainable agricultural practices, including scaling forages for livestock feed and reducing soil erosion (Official Letter No. 1587/UBND-NN dated 11 May 2024, People's Committee of Mai Son District).

During the implementation of SAPLING, Mai Son Agricultural Service Center (ASC) staff actively participated in technical training courses on feeds and forages, manure management, and animal health to gain knowledge and skills to introduce to local farmers.

With co-investment from the SAPLING initiative, Mai Son ASC organized and conducted 34 training of farmers (ToFs) sessions on feeds and forages, manure management, and animal health, applying SAPLING techniques and training materials to benefit livestock farmers in Mai Son District. The training took place from 11 – 22 June, 2024.
General information about the training
Trainers

The trainers for these courses were staff from the Mai Son ASC, who participated in SAPLING’s training for trainers (ToTs) on feeds and forages, and animal health. The trainers included Nguyen Thi Hien, Nguyen Thi Bich Hoai, Luu Thi Huong, and Lo Thi Hoa – all qualified veterinary officers.
Objectives of the training
The goals of the training were to:
1. train farmers in techniques on feeds and forages, manure management, and animal health.
2. provide farmers with hands-on practical sessions on feeding technologies, including feed preparation, preservations and feeding regime for cattle and pigs at different growth stages, and
3. prepare a monitoring plan to follow up on participating farmers in implementing technologies from the training.
Training content
The training used SAPLING’s materials including:
• Feeds and nutrition for cattle in Vietnam (https://hdl.handle.net/10568/134521);
• Feeds and nutrition for pigs in Vietnam (https://hdl.handle.net/10568/134553);
• Improved forages: establishment, management and utilization (https://hdl.handle.net/10568/137318 ).
Improving biosecurity and animal health in household-scale farms
(https://hdl.handle.net/10568/135986);
Feeds and nutrition for cattle and pigs

This covered classification of feed in cattle breeding including: raw feed (containing a lot of fibre, large volume including forage and dry forage), refined feed (energy-rich feed, protein-rich feed, mineral-rich feed).

Feeding cattle at different growth stages and fattening stages. Groups of pig feed ingredients: energy-rich group, protein-rich feed group, vitamin-rich feed group, mineral-rich feed group. Feed characteristics for ban-pigs, and feeding pigs at different growth stages.
Forages

Techniques for planting, managing, harvesting and utilization of forages: Mun River Guinea, Mombasa Guinea, Green Elephant Taiwan, Napier (VA06), fodder maize, Mulato II, Ubon stylo and rice bean. Recommendations on suitable planting season, fertilizers and seed treatment of forages.
Animal health
• Routine measures in pig and cattle farming:
• Feed management and watering
• Hygiene practices
• Regularly used medications and vaccines
• Biosecurity measures to prevent the spread of diseases and minimize pathogens on farm:
• Animal housing management and barn hygiene
• Control of people entering and leaving the farm
• Feed and water safety
Isolation/separation of animals
• Management of other animals on the farm
• Waste and dead animal management
Manure management and composting

Benefits of composting in manure management (helps in managing waste effectively; reduces negative environmental impact; improves soil health). Precautions in composting (maintain appropriate water level; ensure proper nitrogen levels provide adequate aeration etc.), and introduction of composting methods.
Training methods

Presentation: Trainers introduced training concepts and methods using engaging tools like posters and slideshows. After each session, trainers posed questions to encourage participants to share their local experiences. This created a forum for comparing practices, discussing challenges, and proposing solutions for improvement.
Conceptual thinking and sharing: Following each content section, trainers encouraged quick thinking exercises and discussions where participants could share their practical experiences.

Hands-on Practical exercises: Trainers guided participants through each step of the techniques. Trainers encouraged participation from households who did not implement techniques. Trainers spent time with participants who already use the practices to share their experiences and questions.
Time, location and number of participants

Mai Son ASC conducted 34 farmer trainings in 9 communes of Mai Son District: Chieng Luong, Chieng Chung, Muong Bon, Hat Lot, Chieng Kheo, Chieng Dong, Na Bo, Phiêng Cam, Chieng Mai, from 11–22 June 2024 (details in Annex 2). The total number of participants was 1,183 farmers, of which 775 were men (65.5%) and 408 (34.5%) were women. Most of the farmers were of Thai ethnicity (89%), Hmong (10.3%), and the rest were of Muong and Kinh ethnicities (Annex 2).

The participants came from 37 different villages. The total number of cattle owned by the participants were 2,879, the total number of pigs was 4,366, and the total area of plantedforage was 62,4 ha (Annex 3).
Evaluation of the training courses
Advantages
• The training classes achieved a participation rate of 98.5%, exceeding expectations.
• All planned training content was successfully delivered to the trainees.
• The majority of trainees demonstrated enthusiasm, proactiveness, and active participation in the activities led by the trainers.
• Most localities successfully organized full attendance for the training sessions. Following the course, trainees expressed commitment to implementing the knowledge and skills they acquired.
Challenges
• Some participants were hesitant and lacked initiative. During group discussions, not all group members actively participated.
• Participants' group discussion facilitation skills were limited, hindering maximum engagement from some members.
• Some participants lacked proficiency in Vietnamese, making it challenging for the trainers to convey the training content.
• The training took place during the harvesting season, which required significant time and support from local authorities to ensure adequate attendance.
Participants’ learning attitude
• Participants had a positive attitude and enthusiasm during the training sessions.
• After the training, participants expressed commitment to applying and implementing the knowledge they had gained.
Participants’ evaluation of the training
Regarding the level of meeting the expectations of the trainees:
• The trainers met the requirements of the training course in terms of knowledge and practical skills in animal husbandry.
• Regarding the training methods and the knowledge and experience of the instructors:
• The trainers participating in the training course introduced the most suitable training methods for the trainees, helping them to learn in the most effective and quickest way.
• The trainers possessed extensive knowledge and experience, allowing the trainees to acquire adequate knowledge and skills.
Regarding the organization of the training course:

The instructors organized the training course in a proper technical, methodological, and systematic manner, making it easy for the trainees to acquire knowledge (see detailed participants’ evaluation in Annex 4).
Some opinions shared by participants

Feed preservation: some households already practice silage preparation, but there have been instances of spoilage. This is due to some types of forages having high water content, and farmers do not dry them before ensiling. Some households have used sugarcane tops and corn stalks for silage. Limites skills on feed preservation for the dry season has affected livestock productivity.

The area for growing forages in some villages is still limited, mainly relying on naturally growing grass, or forages planted alongside gardens and fences. The main type of forage is Green Elephant (Napier), and limited diversity of other forage varieties. Forage planting on contour lines on sloping land to prevent erosion has not been implemented.
Farmers do not practice composting using animal manure; most just let it to decompose naturally. Many households do not collect manure, leading to unsanitary conditions and waste.

Local challenges in livestock production include limited land, insufficient space to build standard livestock barns. Market prices are low, animals are frequently get sick, leading to discouragement and lack of focus on livestock farming, especially for pigs. There are no disease prevention measures. When animals die, they are still slaughtered and shared with other households, causing the spread of diseases.
Outcomes and
activities
Outcomes and post-training activities

After the training, farmers were given detailed instructions on how to process forage biomass before ensiling to avoid mold and spoilage. They were also guided on methods for managing manure and isolating animals with diseases. Additionally, they were introduced to and taught how to plant a number of improved forages. The Agricultural Service Center, in collaboration with the local farmers' association and village leaders, will continue monitoring and encouraging farmers to implement different livestock production techniques. They will report monthly on the number of households applying the training content.

Farmers encountering difficulties during implementation can consult with the farmers' association, agricultural extension, or local veterinarians for support or report to the Agricultural Service Center.

The Agricultural Service Center encourages villages and communes, after receiving training, to organize sessions to share the knowledge gained with their families and neighbors through village meetings and the village and commune loudspeakers.
Conclusion

The training covered a range of essential topics in animal husbandry. Through a combination of lectures, demonstrations, and hands-on activities, participants gained practical skills in areas like composting, feed processing and preservation, and disease prevention in livestock.

The high participation rate and positive feedback from trainees indicate the program's effectiveness. However, the report also highlights some challenges, such as limited land availability for growing forages, inconsistent feed storage practices by farmers, and the need for improved disease prevention measures in animal husbandry.

Moving forward, ongoing monitoring and support through farmer associations and veterinaries will be crucial to ensure the long-term sustainability of these promoted practices. In addition, through village
meetings, ASC Mai Son will encourage farmers to share knowledge within their communities, thereby contributing to a more effective and sustainable livestock sector in Mai Son District.

Introduction

Pigs and cattle are vital sources of income for smallholder farmers in the Northwest Highlands of Vietnam. These animals have been identified as key value chains for enhancing livelihoods and ensuring food security. However, the productivity of these value chains remains low due to poor husbandry practices, disease risks, parasites, and the use of inappropriate technologies related to feed, breeds, and herd health. While advances in improved forages, animal breeding, herd health, and market access have demonstrated sustainable gains in on-farm productivity, achieving large-scale impact remains a challenge.
The Li-Chăn Project, implemented between 2019 and 2021 in the North-West Highlands, highlighted significant animal health challenges for livestock farmers in Sơn La Province:
• Most small-scale livestock farmers still rely on traditional husbandry practices, lacking the necessary knowledge of livestock management and biosecurity.
• High prevalence of infectious animal diseases, including African swine fever, foot-and-mouth disease, pasteurellosis, and lumpy skin disease.
• A shortage of qualified animal health workers and limited access to veterinary services.

The SAPLING Initiative, part of the CGIAR portfolio and known locally as Chăn-Hênh, focuses on sustainable animal productivity. Its goal is to transform livestock sectors in target countries to become more productive, resilient, equitable, and sustainable. The selection of key value chains under this initiative is based on:

• Building upon the achievements of the Livestock CRP (Livestock-led Interventions towards Equitable Livelihoods and Improved Environment in the North-West Highlands of Vietnam, also known as the Li-Chăn Project).
Stakeholder prioritisation, aligning with the provincial livestock development strategy, as determined during a virtual SAPLING consultation meeting in July 2021.
• Alignment with the interests of the Government and donors.

Under the Chăn-Hênh project, an Animal Health Model has been developed to promote the adoption of health innovations for cattle and pig farmers in Sơn La. This model encompasses a comprehensive approach to herd health, addressing biosecurity, animal management, housing, vaccination, parasite control, and the prudent use of antimicrobials, among other aspects. The model was piloted in Mai Sơn, Sơn La, where it led to significant improvements in animal health across the region.

The success of this model is a testament to its potential for broader implementation across Sơn La Province, offering a scalable solution to improve livestock productivity and the livelihoods of smallholder farmers

Approach of SAPLING

The SAPLING Initiative, or Chăn-Hênh project focuses on two value chains—pigs and beef—that offer significant potential for small-scale producers to capitalise on market growth. This goal will be realised through five key work packages:
1. Technologies and practices for sustainable livestock productivity.
2. Innovations and practices to ensure the safe consumption of livestock-derived foods as part of diverse diets.
3. Promoting sustainable livestock productivity for gender equity and social inclusion.
4. Developing competitive and inclusive livestock value chains.
5. Generating and consolidating evidence, models, and tools to support public and private decision- making for a sustainable and inclusive livestock sector.

The project is being implemented from 2023 to 2024 in four communes of Mai Sơn District, Sơn La Province (Figure 1). Within these communes, eight livestock farmer groups have been identified or established, with each group located in a targeted village. The members of these groups, who own cattle and/or pigs, have been selected for their readiness to adopt innovative techniques. These farmers are positioned to benefit from the project and serve as catalysts for change within their communities.

Eight training workshops on biosecurity and animal health were organised across eight core villages. The sessions were facilitated by experts from the National Institute of Veterinary Research (NIVR). Each workshop lasted half a day and covered four main topics: (i) biosecurity, (ii) vaccines and antibiotics, (iii) routine animal management practices, and (iv) practical sessions on disinfection.

Participants included livestock keepers from farmer groups, village and commune animal health workers, village heads, representatives of farmer groups, and members of the women’s union. In total, 207 livestock keepers (107 men and 97 women) attended the training.

The training employed a mix of presentations, group discussions, case studies, and practical demonstrations to engage participants and facilitate knowledge transfer. Trainers addressed numerous questions from participants about animal health throughout the sessions. Each participant received a training booklet and a bottle of disinfectant to encourage adherence to biosecurity practices.

In response to emerging diseases, posters on African Swine Fever (ASF), Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD), biosecurity, and antibiotics were developed. These were utilised during the training sessions and subsequently distributed to farmer groups.

Capacity Building for Animal Health Professionals

A two-day advanced animal health training course was organised for animal health professionals from four core communes in the Mai Sơn district. The training was facilitated by experienced experts from the National Institute of Veterinary Research (NIVR) and the Vietnam National University of Agriculture (VNUA).

The course comprised one day of theoretical instruction followed by a day of practical training, covering the following topics: (i) an overview of animal health, (ii) biosecurity, (iii) vaccines and antibiotics, (iv) animal diseases (ASF, LSF, and Pasteurellosis), (v) disease control, and (vi) hands-on practical training with animals. A participatory approach was employed, incorporating interactive brainstorming, case studies, and group discussions to engage participants effectively.

Establishment of demonstration farms

While training provides farmers with knowledge of biosecurity and animal health, practical demonstrations are crucial for understanding and adoption. To achieve this, the Chăn-Hênh team has agreed to co-select and co-implement demonstration farms to showcase best practices and technology. These demonstration
Page 9 of 12

farms will serve as learning sites in each village, aiming to inspire the community to adopt innovations from the Chăn-Hênh project. For the animal health model, interventions focus on biosecurity, animal housing, animal management, and animal welfare. Local animal health workers, along with the Sub-Department of Animal Health (Sub-DAH) and the Animal Husbandry and Aquaculture Department, were involved in this activity. Consequently, interventions from demonstration farms will be adopted and spread to the broader community.

A survey was conducted to select demonstration farms. The criteria for selection included: (i) being a member of a farmer group within the eight core villages, (ii) raising both pigs and cattle, and (iii) being willing to adopt interventions from the project. Eight demonstration farms were co-selected in the eight core villages across four communes: Chieng Chung, Chieng Luong, Hat Lot, and Muong Bon. Of the eight selected households, four were located in Chieng Chung and Chieng Luong, the study sites of the Li-Chăn project. Two households had already served as demonstration farms in the previous project but were revisited and re-enrolled. This approach allows the animal health model to build upon previous achievements.

All eight farms are smallholdings, primarily raising livestock for home consumption. The main income sources come from crop production, including coffee, rice, or sugarcane. However, all participating households are eager to apply the techniques from the project and share their knowledge with other farmers in the community.

Following the selection of demonstration farms, tailored interventions have been proposed for each farm based on survey results. From March 2024 to November 2024, project staff, with support from local animal health professionals, visited two demonstration farms at a time to establish the sites and carry out interventions. In addition, project staff contacted the farms monthly for monitoring. Our interventions include:
• Providing guidance and hands-on demonstrations of biosecurity, animal housing, livestock management practices, and animal welfare.

• Vaccination: Farmers were encouraged to vaccinate their animals according to the government’s schedule. In addition to these vaccines, we will provide supplementary vaccines as outlined in the following table.

• Providing subsidies for each demonstration farm: Subsidies were distributed based on the number of animals on each farm, including dewormer for pigs and cattle, iron dextran for piglets, disinfectant, sprayers, pesticide, booths, and clothing. Correct usage of each subsidised item was explained.

• Record keeping: A record-keeping template on biosecurity, vaccination, drug use, and details of sick and deceased animals will be distributed to each demonstration farm with instructions on how to use it.

• Technical support, if needed: Whenever farmers encounter difficulties in implementing interventions or need assistance with animal health, they are encouraged to contact project technical staff for advice.

Key indicators such as facilities, livestock health status, productivity, and biosecurity practices were closely monitored and recorded by technical staff through phone calls or monthly farm visits. Data were collected using questionnaires, checklists, and record-keeping.

To manage the risk of disease transmission, strict biosecurity protocols were followed whenever technical staff visited demonstration farms. This included providing disinfectant and sprayers and supplying visitors with appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), such as hand gel, boot covers, and coveralls if handling animals. The number of visitors to demonstration farms was also kept to a minimum, with visits only being made when absolutely necessary. These measures were implemented to reduce the risk of disease transmission during visits.

Support organizations

To expand the number of beneficiaries and enhance the project's impact, the Animal Health component collaborated with local partners in Son La province to replicate and scale activities. This included working with the Sub-Department of Animal Health, Animal Husbandry, and Aquaculture (Sub-DAH) to (i) organise training for 25 animal health professionals in Mai Son and Phu Yen, and (ii) establish three livestock demonstration farms.

Training materials for farmers have been shared with the Mai Son Agriculture Service Centre (ASC), enabling them to organise fifty-six training courses on biosecurity for livestock keepers independently, reaching approximately 2,000 participants. These training sessions have significantly increased the knowledge and practices of livestock keepers in relation to biosecurity and animal health. Training will continue to be organised in the future under the leadership of the ASC.

Lessons learned and recommendation

The animal health model implemented in eight core villages of Mai Son, Son La, has led to several significant positive changes in overall animal health. The impact of the model extends beyond the training participants, with other households in the area also adopting the recommended interventions. This demonstrates the effectiveness of the animal health model, which can be adopted at a community level through farmer-to- farmer knowledge sharing.
Knowledge and practice adoption levels were significantly better in practical sessions compared to theoretical ones. Information conveyed through hands-on demonstrations was more easily understood.
Page 11 of 12

Future training should prioritise this approach. Additionally, future sessions could include training on basic veterinary techniques, such as vaccine and drug administration, to help farmers manage animal health more effectively while reducing their reliance on veterinary services.

Advanced animal health professional training contributed to the prevention and control of prevalent diseases in the area, including African Swine Fever (ASF), Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD), and Pasteurellosis. Posters on ASF and LSD were also provided to farmers' groups, further supporting the control and prevention of animal diseases. We also provide technical support and guidance for group members in the event of animal diseases through Zalo groups. This highlights the importance of training tailored to the disease epidemiology in the area. Further epidemiological investigations are also essential to developing training content and interventions.

Demonstration farms have shown promising results, despite the short implementation time (e.g., improved visitor control, regular disinfection, and vaccine use). However, some challenges remain, such as the use of footbaths and animal quarantine. Ongoing support for these demonstration farms is critical to achieving desired outcomes and establishing successful models for other livestock keepers in the community.

Although the project lifespan is relatively short for observing long-term results, the initial outcomes are promising. More research and studies are needed to fully evaluate the positive changes and long-term sustainability of the interventions.

Collaboration with local partners is key to scaling up the successful model and ensuring long-term sustainability. Therefore, the project must continue collaborating with local partners to adapt and expand the successful animal health model.
By implementing these recommendations, the impact of the animal health model can be expanded and sustained, contributing to improved sustainable livestock practices in the area.

Strategic co-investment for sustainable livestock farming SAPLING, an initiative dedicated to promoting sustainable livestock practices in the northwest highlands of Vietnam, and ASC have pooled technical expertise and resources to develop a comprehensive training program designed to equip farmers with the skills needed to adopt more sustainable and productive livestock farming practices. The goal is to enhance productivity while minimizing the environmental impact of livestock farming. ASC aims to create a sustainable model that can be replicated across other communes in the region. Strategic recommendations: The ASC has recommended scaling the training programs to reach more farmers. This calls for additional resources in terms of training materials, follow-up support, and further adoption of sustainable practices. Report from Mai Son District Agricultural Service Centre to Mai Son People s Committee These trainings also address the environmental benefits of livestock production, particularly in terms of manure management and the planting of forages to reduce soil erosion. These practices not only enhance the productivity of livestock farming but also contribute to the broader environmental goals of the district, says Hang Dao, Vietnam s focal point for SAPLING s work packages 1 and 5 on feeds and forage interventions, environmental evidence, and scaling. The ASC s report is a critical document for securing the necessary support to sustain these initiatives. It highlights the importance of continued collaboration between the ASC, SAPLING, and local government stakeholders to ensure the long-term success of these programs. Building a sustainable future The partnership between the ASC and SAPLING has laid a strong foundation for sustainable livestock production in Mai Son District. By providing farmers with the knowledge and tools they need to adopt more environmentally friendly and productive practices, this collaboration is helping to transform the district s agricultural landscape. With continued support from SAPLING, the ASC aims to expand these programs, ensuring that even more farmers can benefit from the training provided. The success of these efforts will not only improve the livelihoods of local farmers but also contribute to the overall sustainability of the region s agricultural sector. This co-investment strategy, centered on training and practical application, serves as a model for other districts in Son La looking to enhance their agricultural practices while protecting the environment. ASC and SAPLING, with the backing of the People s Committee, are leading the way in promoting a more sustainable future for Mai Son District. About SAPLING

CGIAR’s Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) is working in seven countries focusing on livestock value chains to package and scale out tried-and-tested, as well as new, innovations in livestock health, genetics, feed and market systems. SAPLING aims to demonstrate that improvements in livestock productivity can offer a triple win: generating improved livelihoods and nutritional outcomes; contributing to women’s empowerment; and, reducing impacts on climate and the environment. Its seven focus countries are Ethiopia, Kenya, Mali, Nepal, Tanzania, Uganda and Vietnam.
