SUMMARY

Virtual and face-to-face trainings on DTREO, a digital genetic database, was organized in 2023 for research and development partners in Tunisia. A total of 11 participants, including five women from the National Research and Development Office of Tunisia, attended the training. The sessions highlighted the importance of a digital database for genetic evaluations and introduced the features of DTREO, such as offline data capture and quick feedback. The training covered data entry options, data configuration, and reporting capabilities and included a practical session on preparing the master file and loading data. Overall, the training aimed to equip participants with the knowledge and skills to use DTREO effectively in their small ruminant breeding programs. Following the training, significant progress has been achieved as 337 historic sheep pedigrees and performance data from three villages (Rahala, Sers, and Elles) have been successfully loaded into the DTREO system.

1 BACKGROUND

The Community-Based Breeding Program (CBBP) was introduced in Ethiopia in 2009 as an alternative approach to sheep and goat breeding, moving away from the conventional nucleus and using exotic breeds for crossing. The program's primary goal is to enhance the income and livelihoods of sheep and goat producers, improve market supply and food security, and establish a replicable genetic improvement framework within and beyond Ethiopia. Implementing a robust data capture and analysis system is crucial to achieving significant genetic progress. Without proper recording, identifying and culling unproductive animals becomes challenging, leading to poor-performing animals contributing to higher greenhouse gas emissions per unit of output. Thus, a digital database system enables informed decision-making regarding animal management, standard genetic evaluations, and mating selection and planning based on animal genotype estimates.

In collaboration with the Accelerating the Impact of CGIAR Climate Research for Africa (AICCRA) and the National Agricultural Research Systems (NARS), the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) has been working on expanding and sustaining a digital database system for ongoing and newly established CBBPs in Ethiopia and other countries. Various institutions, including Research Centers, Universities, and the Biodiversity Institute, have established numerous CBBPs across Ethiopia. Additionally, CBBPs have been implemented in countries such as Tanzania, Sudan, Uganda, Malawi and in other regions like Brazil, Iran, and Mongolia (Haile et al., 2019). Currently, there is a growing interest in expanding the CBBP approach and utilizing genetic databases in Tunisia. This training program has been organized to assist research and development partners in adopting the genetic database for their sheep CBBP flocks. The aim is to support their active participation in the use of the genetic database, thereby enhancing their CBBP initiatives and contributing to the program's overall success.
2 TRAINING CONTENT

The Small Ruminant Team of the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) conducted both virtual and face-to-face training sessions on DTREO – a digital genetic database in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, from 4-5 April 2023 and in Hammamet, Tunisia on 28 April 2023. Eleven from the National Research and Development Office participated; 5 were women. A total of 11 participants from the National Research and Development Office took part in the training, including five women.
2.1 Importance of digital database

The training highlighted the importance of a digital database for continuous genetic evaluations and animal ranking. It emphasized the limitations of manual data collection and the need for an efficient and reliable system to provide quick feedback to communities. Moreover, as data size increases, the manual data entry tasks become more complex, thereby necessitating the development of a central and automated digital database system to facilitate data capture, analysis, and timely feedback on animal rankings to communities.
2.2 Features of DTREO

The participants were introduced to the features of DTREO, which was described as a flexible and user-friendly platform. It allows offline data capture, enabling users to save and upload data to the database later when an internet connection is available. DTREO enhances the accuracy of estimated breeding values (EBVs) and

provides quick feedback to communities. It offers report generation, data analysis, and graphical representation capabilities.
2.3 Progress and Implementation

The training reported on the progress made in implementing DTREO in Ethiopia and Tanzania. The database has been successfully developed and tested in various regions in Ethiopia. Data collectors in Ethiopia have been trained and equipped with tablets to capture data since 2019. Historic data from Ethiopia since 2009 has been uploaded to the digital database. Data collection is ongoing in 60 community-based breeding sites across Ethiopia and Tanzania, with an additional 50 villages joining recently. The training included testimonials from users in Ethiopia who have experienced increased efficiency and reduced errors through DTREO. Researchers and enumerators mentioned the ease of accessing recent data, quicker information retrieval, and reduced errors due to the platform's functionalities.
2.4 Data entry options

Different data entry options were explained and discussed during the training. Participants were informed about direct entry via the mobile application, which allows data to be captured online or offline. They were also introduced to the web application for real-time data entry and analytics. Additionally, the use of importers for loading large datasets in standard file formats (.xls or .csv) was explained.
2.5 Data configuration and reporting

The training covered data configuration requirements, including various data sources and types. The platform allows users to configure data fields according to their specific collection practices and needs. Participants were informed about the available reporting options, including individual animal reports, reproduction reports, ranking reports based on EBVs and index values, certificate reports, and animal health reports. The platform offers flexibility for creating custom reports and integrating them with other data sources. The platform provides users with the ability to retrieve analytics. It reports through a user-friendly dashboard, enabling access and downloads of data files containing valuable information on all animals, including their performance and locations. The platform exhibits a high degree of flexibility, allowing for creating and integrating various reports and data types within the system. A series of planned modifications are scheduled to enhance user experience, functionality, and the generation of useful information for stakeholders. These improvements encompass the introduction of new events and reports, as well as the implementation of data capture capabilities for seamless integration with other data sources.
2.6 Practical session

The practical session provided hands-on training on using the DTREO digital genetic platform, including data preparation, loading, and exploring the various reporting features. Data loading can be initiated using baseline data or any data type that contains comprehensive information such as a village, owner, tag, sire, dam, dentition, parity, birth date, sex, body weight at different dates, coat color, disposal date, disposal reason, and more. To ensure accuracy and avoid duplications, it is recommended to prepare all the entries in a file known as the Master file. This Master file can then populate the templates for adding owners, animals, weights, and other relevant data. This approach helps in maintaining data integrity and streamlining the data loading process.

During the training session, the trainees were given an example data file to practice the steps in preparing a master file. They were guided on how to prepare and fill the master file with relevant information and prepare each event (e.g., add owner, add animal, growth, disposal events) for loading into the DTREO platform. The trainees downloaded the required event templates from the DTREO website and followed the instructions to ensure the data was properly organized and ready for loading. By working with the example data file and following the provided guidelines, the trainees gained hands-on experience preparing the master file and preparing events for loading into the DTREO platform. Detailed steps can be found at https://hdl.handle.net/10568/126192.

Following the training, significant progress has been achieved as historic sheep pedigree and performance data from three villages (Rahala, Sers, and Elles) have been successfully loaded into the DTREO system. The data collection process using DTREO is progressing smoothly, with 337 records uploaded to the database. Specifically, Rahala contributed 238 data entries, while Sers contributed 99 data entries. This achievement marks a significant step forward in establishing a comprehensive and valuable database for sheep breeding and performance analysis in the region.

INTRODUCTION

In 2010, sheep and goat community-based breeding programs (CBBPs) were initiated jointly by the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA), International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences in Austria (BOKU) in partnership with Ethiopia’s National Agricultural Research Systems (NARS).

Breed improvement requires continuous genetic evaluations and the ranking of animals based on their genetic merit. Pedigree and performance recording is crucial and is an important component of genetic evaluation. Until recently, common practice in Ethiopia had been to collect data manually in herd books, which do not offer an effective means of providing quick and reliable feedback to communities.

Manual data collection is prone to data loss and errors, which reduces the accuracy and limits the use of complex models to improve the accuracy of animal ranking and genetic parameter estimations. Moreover, as data size increases, the manual data entry tasks become more complex, thereby necessitating the development of a central and automated digital database system to facilitate data capture, analysis, and timely feedback on animal rankings to communities.

THE INNOVATION

ICARDA and Ethiopia’s NARS partnered with AbacusBio, an agribusiness technology firm, to use their cloud-based genetic database platform called Dtreo. The platform is designed to capture data (performance, pedigree, health and environment data), store and analyze it, and then send feedback to targeted communities for breeding and management decisions.

The main purpose of using Dtreo is to avail more accurate estimated breeding values (EBVs) and help provide quick feedback to communities. Higher accuracy of EBVs is expected due to reduced data errors and use of a sufficient data size. The database tool can run complicated models that help increase
accuracy of genetic evaluations. Dtreo can also build reports, provide analysis and create graphics.

Dtreo integrates well with smart device software designed for offline gathering of data in situations where internet connectivity is poor. Trained enumerators can easily choose event types, enter as much data as needed and save it all offline. Once internet connectivity is available, enumerators simply upload the data into the cloud by clicking the “send” button. When needed, the data is accessed by researchers, analyzed and ranking information is sent back to the selected community.

Increasing data collection efficiencies
Since 2019, research centers in Ethiopia have adopted a digital database platform called Dtreo to capture, manage and analyze their community-based breeding data.

Shenkute is a researcher at Debre Berhan Agricultural Research Center (BARC) overseeing five community-based breeding (CBBP) sites in Menz, in the Amhara region. Previously, Shenkute and his research team would travel every fortnight to project sites about 160 kilometers away to monitor data collection activities and retrieve a copy of the data from enumerators. Thanks to the functionality of Dtreo, however, Shenkute can now monitor and access recent data from all five sites from his office. He can also easily create summary reports and access more refined data for analysis.

Testimonials received from seasoned enumerators such as Adise from Menz and Asabu in Tamiru, Bonga, are likewise benefiting from the efficiencies provided by the digital platform. Whereas previously enumerators traveled with and entered data into herd books, enumerators are inputting data into digital tablets, which is making data collection easier. Retrieving farmer and animal information is much quicker and drop-down selections in data fields are helping reduce

errors significantly. Researchers are also appreciating the security afforded by data stored in the cloud. Floods that affected the Arba Minch Research Center and ongoing war in the northern part of Ethiopia have damaged herd books and computers.

CRITICAL FACTORS OF SUCCESS OF THE PROGRAM
• Efficient partnership among NARS and international partners is the main factor for establishing a digital database.
• Tremendous effort from committed researchers in NARS resulted in essential accumulated historic data being loaded onto the system.
• High levels of motivation to use an automated system.
• Ease and flexibility of the database system to accommodate any analytic system
• Long-term technical support, capacity development, follow- up and monitoring in the data capture, analysis and feedback system
IMPLICATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

In order to provide a more accurate picture of the genetic evaluation of small ruminants in the country, the database reach would need to be expanded to include more CBBP sites, particularly those established by national research institutions, universities, and the biodiversity institute in Ethiopia. To achieve this:
• A responsible national institution needs to take the role of coordination and ownership of the database system.
• All sheep and goat data in the national system needs to be moved to the central database system.

Contributing to SAPLING’s overall objective, SAPLING—Vietnam country programme aims to contribute to transforming two pig and cattle value chains in the Northwest Highlands (NWH) of Vietnam. In this region, pigs are the most important source of cash income from livestock of smallholder farmers. The region also leads in the number of buffaloes and cattle heads. However, these two value chains have low productivity due to different issues such as poor farming practices, disease risks and inadequate technology. Additionally, there is a lack of coordination and collaboration between different actors in the value chains, leading to inefficiencies and unequal distribution of benefits (Huyen et al. 2019).

To address productivity and competitiveness gaps in the value chain, it is necessary to introduce technical innovations and establish institutional arrangements for input delivery and market linkages. Farmer organizations, which can take various forms such as associations, cooperatives and farmer clubs, can play a crucial role in this process (Bizikova et al., 2020). These organizations help members pursue their individual and collective interests by facilitating communication, improving access to markets and services and enhancing knowledge and skills (Markelova and Mwangi 2010; Elly 2018; Gugerty et al. 2018; Vu et al. 2020). Farmer organizations have been shown positive impacts on smallholder agriculture, including increasing income, farm production and food security (Rahmadanih et al. 2018). Therefore, they have become increasingly important in developing countries, including Vietnam (Moustier et al. 2010; World Bank 2016).

A core component of SAPLING Vietnam’s overall strategy to strengthen the pig and cattle value chains, is the formation and support to farmers groups (inclusive of common interest groups, farmers clubs and cooperatives) for improved access of the farmers to input and output markets, for being a forum for capacity development and cocreate of solutions to issues pertaining to pig and cattle keeping. The objective of this study is to assess the existing farmers group (in terms of their governance, membership base, functions and strengths and weaknesses). The result of this assessment will underpin the design of SAPLING interventions around the farmers groups.
The assessment was conducted in four treatment communes of the project, Chieng Luong, Chieng Chung, Hat Lot and Muong Bon from 14–20 May 2023.

2. Materials and methods
2.1. Study area and target value chains

The study was conducted in Mai Son District, Son La Province and focussed on pig and beef cattle value chains. After consulting with local authorities, the team identified nine farmer groups involved in pig and cattle production and marketing in Mai Son District. These farmer groups were located in four communes, namely Chieng Luong, Chieng Chung, Hat Lot and Muong Bon. All these farmer groups were included in the assessment.
2.2. Methods for data collection
The data collection was divided into four parts:
a. Surveying groups’ management boards

● Objectives: To describe the integral functions of farmer groups. Five components are considered: i) democratic, inclusive and participatory management; ii) service offer and capacity building; iii) economic and financial sustainability; iv) administrative and managerial capacity; and v) market connections and trading capacity.

● Sample size (Table 1): Depending on the nature and scale of a farmer group, the management board could contain from 3 to 7 members. For each farmer group, one meeting was organized with these members. The collected information was filled in a semistructured questionnaire.

b. Surveying group members

● Objectives: To identify perceptions and opinions that encourage their engagement with these groups. The behavioral elements considered were perceived trust and member commitment to the farmer groups. Grouped in these behavioral elements we would get in deep into issues like service offers, technical/financial supports, market measures, decisionmakings etc. from the members’ perceptions.

● Sample size (Table 1): Key informant interviews (KIIs) were conducted with some representatives of members in each group. Given the number of regular members of the existing farmer groups (ranging from 5 to 15), around 1 to 4 members per group were selected for the interviews with consideration of gender, age group and ethnicity. A list of all members of the nine farmer groups were collected before the fieldwork to serve the random selection.
c. Surveying nongroup members
Nongroup members were classified into two types: (i) those who have never joined any farmer groups before and (ii) those who used to be members of a group but dropped out.

● Objectives: To capture the reasons why nongroup members refused to join or dropped out of a farmer group. Key issues must be explored including motivations, expectations, perceived benefits or challenges and constraints.
● Sample size (Table 2): nongroup members were not selected per group but per commune where the target farmer groups are operating.

- For nongroup members who have never joined any group, FGDs were used for data collection. A total of ten FGDs (two per commune, separately for men and women considering age group and ethnicity) were organized. Each FGD contained 4–9 participants based on their availability and willingness to join. Farmers who were invited to the FGDs must have pigs or cattle. Besides, to document the variation of perspectives, opinions, practices and livelihood situations, it was important to ensure some mix of participants along the characteristics such as ethnicity, age group, herd size (small, medium, large), market access (some participants from villages with good, some with poor market access).

- For nongroup members who used to be members of a group but dropped out, KIIs were used. A list of all nongroup members of this type in the four communes were collected before the fieldwork. Based on the list, participants were randomly selected for KIIs with consideration of a balance of men and women, age group and ethnicity. In total, 11 KIIs were implemented.

● Objectives: To hear voices from those at management level, explore their perceptions about the performance of these groups, any suggestions for improvement, support provided etc. The way they perceive the functioning of the group may be different from how the members and non members (farmers) see it.

2.3. Data analysis

The study utilized a constant comparison analysis method that is common for analyzing multiple focus groups and across group saturation (Anthony et al. 2009). The analysis was performed in three stages.
● Stage 1: Data from KIIs and FGDs were categorized by different organizations such as cooperatives, cooperatives groups and farmer groups (e.g. CIGs, farmer clubs etc.).

● Stage 2: The data and information of each group were sorted and categorized according to various factors such as background information, performance index, livestock activities (e.g. pigs, cattle), participatory management, service, capacity building, sustainability, administrative management, market access and trading capacity and behavior of members.

● Stage 3: Researchers and team members analyzed the thoughts and ideas of the groups and organized the information into different categories, including background information of the group, performance evaluation, technical details, management approach, services offered, financial sustainability, administrative capacity, market connections, member behavior and recommendations for improvement.
3. A short state of art of farmer groups
3.1. Normative framework of farmer groups

In Vietnam, there are various types of farmer organizations such as farmer union/association, cooperatives, cooperative groups, farmer/producer groups (common interest groups—CIG) and farmer clubs. Definitions, main activities, membership, structure and operations of these forms are summarized in Annex 1.
3.2. Evolution of farmer groups over time
a. Vietnam Farmers' Union

Vietnam Farmers’ Union, originally known as the Red Farmers’ Union, was established in 1930. It has undergone name changes over the years and is currently referred to as VNFU. As a social- political organization, the VNFU is involved in activities that support the development of agriculture and the overall socio-economic progress of the country. Its main tasks include mobilizing and organizing farmers' movements for various aspects of development, as well as implementing government policies and programmes in rural areas. The Union also takes care of the wellbeing of its farmer members (VNFU 2023).
b. Cooperatives
According to Wolz (2000), collectivization in Vietnam began in the North in the late 1950s. The process involved cooperatives playing a significant role in a centralized party-state system.
Page 9 of 66

Members and management boards had limited decision making power as they were required to follow central plans. There were two types of cooperatives: lower-level ones where members still owned the main means of production and higher-level ones where the main means of production were collectively owned (Prime Minister 1959). The cooperatives consisted of various production teams.

The first cooperative in Vietnam was established in 1948. By 1986, Vietnam had a total of 73,470 cooperatives, with 17,022 (23%) of them involved in agriculture. The rapid growth of cooperatives before 1986 was because they were seen as one of the main economic components in Vietnam, alongside state owned enterprises and replaced household based economies. Cooperatives eliminated private ownership of production materials, allowed members to be employees without individual performance responsibilities and distributed benefits equally among members (MPI 2022).

The ""Doi Moi"" or Renovation in 1986 brought about a shift in the way production was organized, particularly in terms of cooperation. Cooperatives and production teams started functioning as service links during and after the production process (Turley and Selden 1993). The Lan Law in 1998 and amended in 1992 had a significant impact on farm households and cooperatives by ensuring the land use rights of farmers. This allowed individuals and households who were given land by the state to have the freedom to exchange, transfer, rent, inherit and mortgage their land use rights, contributing to the re-emergence of private farming and a household based economy (Wolz 2000). The traditional operation of cooperatives was not suitable for supporting farm households in changing economic conditions (Harms 1995). As a result, agricultural cooperatives began to change their structure in the 1990s to improve efficiency and transition into service cooperatives, known as new style cooperatives (Wolz 2000). Members could voluntarily join these reorganized cooperatives and purchase shares. The authority of decisionmaking within the cooperatives was enhanced as all members of the management and supervisory boards were elected directly by the members (Wolz 2000). However, not many new style cooperatives were successful and there was a decrease in the number of cooperatives overall during the period 1990–94. Their performance was unsatisfactory, leading to the collapse of many cooperatives (Harms 1995).

The first Cooperative Law was approved in 1996 and took effect in 1997. Accordingly, a cooperative was an independent economic organization formed by employees who shared common needs and interests. They voluntarily contributed capital and resources to enhance the collective and individual strength, improve their businesses and services and ultimately contribute to the socio-economic development of the country (Vietnam Parliament 1996). Accordingly,
Page 10 of 66

cooperatives were no longer controlled by the state and instead focussed on supporting and serving their members. They operated based on principles of self reliance, self responsibility and equal and democratic management (MPI 2022).

In 1997, Decree 16 was released regulating the transformation of former cooperatives into new style cooperatives (Vietnam Government 1997). The Decree redetermined the position and role of cooperatives. In 2010, there were a total of 11,924 cooperatives (Figure 2). However, there were several issues with cooperatives, including a decrease in their contribution to the economy, low and inconsistent growth rate, poor financial and management capabilities and around 20% of cooperatives being inactive. These problems were attributed to farmers' understanding of cooperatives, the legal framework, inadequate enforcement of the Cooperatives Law and ineffective support policies (Tu 2011).

The development of cooperatives in Vietnam underwent a significant change after implementing the Cooperative Law in 2012. This Law defined cooperatives as socio-economic organizations that were formed voluntarily by members for their mutual benefit, allowing them to function similarly to businesses by providing various services to members, including input provision and marketing of agricultural products (MPI 2022). The number of cooperatives in Vietnam in 2020 was 15,306, with approximately two-thirds of them being agricultural cooperatives (Figure 3).

c. Cooperative groups

In Vietnam, cooperative groups were formed to improve productivity in activities that individuals or households couldn't do alone. These groups, originally known as labor exchange teams, were created by local authorities during the period of collectivization from 1945 to 1955 (VCA 2022). The collectivization process was divided into three stages: LETs, low-level cooperatives and high- level cooperatives. This allowed farmers to become familiar with collective production. Later, the process could be shortened by developing LETs directly into high-level cooperatives or by organizing farmers directly into low-level cooperatives (VCP 1959).

LETs included farmers who exchanged their labor with each other for daily production tasks (Trung Dang 2018). LETs promoted mutual assistance among farmer members, but the operation and performance were different among regions (North, Central and South). According to VCP (1959), about 65% of farmers joined LETs during the period of June to December 1968, while only 5% joined cooperatives.

A cooperative group is a more advanced form of LETs. According to the Civil Law 2005, cooperative groups were created through cooperation contracts certified by the People's Committees of communes, wards and townships. These groups consisted of three or more individuals who contributed assets and efforts to complete specific tasks and shared the benefits and responsibilities (Parliament 2005). Cooperative groups were small in scale (10–13 households), had a simple organizational structure, engaged in practical activities and were suitable for people's capabilities (Vietnam Parliament and UNDP 2012). They typically operate through mutual assistance, flexible partnerships and short-term connections. Cooperative groups serve as a foundation for the development of cooperatives. As of 2022, Vietnam had a total of 123,240 cooperative groups (Figure 4).

d. Farmer self help groups and common interested groups

The collectivization movement in North Vietnam saw a significant growth in cooperatives between 1960 and 1980, while the same movement in South Vietnam was not successful. Many cooperative members in the South continued to farm individually and relied on informal self help groups for support. These groups were particularly prevalent in areas without agricultural cooperatives or where they were not functioning effectively. In the Mekong delta region, around 80% of agricultural households were part of these mutual self help groups (Wolz 2000). In the North, the number of
Page 12 of 66

self help groups grew as the number of active cooperatives declined (Thayer 1995). Since 2017, strong emphasis on formal farmer organizations and private services in Vietnam led to less discussion about self help groups. However, self help groups continue to function in rural areas of Vietnam, albeit in various forms (Bui Minh 2016; Minh Thai 2022).

Several international organizations have adopted the approach of forming farmer groups for projects in Vietnam. These groups, known as common interest groups (CIGs), receive support and interventions from the projects and can serve as production or business models for expansion. An example of this is the ""Commercial Smallholder Support Project"" funded by (IFAD 2020) in Bac Kan and Cao Bang provinces. Under this project, a total of 1,400 CIGs were created in two provinces and 1,092 of them received financial support (IFAD 2022). The CPRP or Commodity oriented Poverty Reduction Programme in Ha Giang created and financially supported 477 CIGs, consisting of 5,218 members, the majority of whom were poor and near poor households, ethnic minorities and women, focussing on 30 agricultural products. Another project, LPS/2015/037, also followed a similar approach by establishing CIGs.

Under the new regulations, the old cooperative model became obsolete, which led to the disintegration or stop operation of numerous organisations. This gave way to a developing process of new forms of association in agricultural production, a field open to exploration. Within an evolving economy with greater exposure to international markets, adopting a scheme based on collective voluntariness reveals a challenging path for agricultural production s social organisation, even more so if the individual perspectives of stakeholders on the performance and convenience of these groups are considered. Previous interventions have promoted the creation of farmer groups in Vietnam s Northwest Highlands (NWH) to foster associativity, facilitating connection to markets and economies of scale for services, technologies, and knowledge transfer to livestock farmers. This research thus provides an assessment of the functioning and capacities of farmer groups engaged in cattle and pig production. This approach integrates the analysis of behavioural elements from members, non-members, men, women, and local authorities on the perceived trust and commitment to participate in existing forms of cooperation. Information was collected through focus groups discussion and key informant interviews. The findings are currently being analysed and will allow researchers to design interventions aimed at strengthening farmer groups. They will too serve as input for current efforts to develop innovative models to deliver and scale innovations towards sustainable livestock production, replicable in other regions. Objective
Introduction

The recent transformations of cooperative laws in Vietnam have led to the disintegration of old cooperative models, giving way to new associative schemes for agricultural production that are yet to be explored.
Assess the functioning and capacities of farmer groups engaged in cattle and pig production in the Mai Son district, Son La Province of Vietnam.
Methodology

Within an economy in constant evolution and open to international markets, the associative model offers an opportunity for the social organization of agricultural production to respond to market demands of quality and volumes, as well as to generate economies of scale, connecting small producers with input networks, extension services, capacity building, and credit.
9 farmer groups of all types (cooperatives, farmer clubs, common interest groups, etc.) in Mai Son district currently active in cattle and pig production were identified and evaluated.

Sample size: Depending on the nature and scale of a farmer group, the management board can contain from 3 to 7 members. For each farmer group, one FGD has been organized with between 2-3 of these members, with consideration of gender, age group, and ethnicity.

This approach promises to be an alternative for strengthening livestock production (cattle and pigs) in the Northwest Highlands in Vietnam due to the opportunities for sustainable market connections in a scenario of cattle oversupply that has dropped the prices and has increased uncertainty among small producers.
The collected information was filled in a semi-structured questionnaire.

A Likert Scale was used to measure the functioning of the groups based on five components, as well as open questions to provide greater detail on the topics. The topics included were: 1) democratic, inclusive, and participatory management, 2) service offer and capacity building, 3) economic and financial sustainability, 4) managerial and administrative capacity, and 5) market connections and trading capacity.

Public policies and previous interventions have promoted the establishment of farmer groups to generate economies of scale. However, the functioning and cohesion of these groups are still weak and highly dependent on external support and the functioning of the beef and pork market.

In general terms, the formation and functioning of farmer groups highly depend on the support of development programs and market dynamics.

Strong cooperative dynamics based on communal and ethnic ties are identified, especially within producers located in the most remote and mountainous areas of Hmong ethnic minorities. The links around livestock productivity are manifested in the joint purchase of inputs for production due to the high costs of mobilization, the free grazing production system that makes it difficult to control and monitor the animal’s consumption of resources, the use of joint funds to support members when facing calamities such as bovine deaths, and the tradition in which the elderly people of the villages play an essential role in monitoring and evaluating the functioning of the groups.

Conclusions
CIG Oi village
Economic and financial sustainability: Most farmer groups do not have the economic resources necessary to carry out their activities.
CIG Buom Khoang village

Farmer group improvement and formation still require institutional support to strengthen the foundational bases of resources management and administration and to make alliances with key partners to support activities and capacity development of the cattle and pig producers.

Service offers and capacity: Neither group offers any service support to its members. However, it is possible to identify cooperation efforts in the joint purchase of inputs and information exchange network. The latter is particularly notorious in those farmer groups where some members implement genetic improvement.

Strengthening the marketing network within farmer groups is essential, especially in facing macro situations in the beef market. It is possible to take advantage of the links established with traders who are members of the groups so that information about market conditions and prices will spread and allow producers to organize themselves in terms of quality, breeds, and volume requirements.

Market connections and trading capacity: Despite the farmer groups are an alternative for sustainable connection to markets, none of the groups have had the opportunity to establish alliances for the commercialization of cattle. The macro situation of the beef market deepens the crisis since groups recently formed through development projects based their activity plans on the expectation of a thriving market that, in the last two years, has changed, leading producers to retain cattle or even migrate to other production systems.

Adapt and integrate social cohesion tools for groups of producers in the most remote areas. Likewise, rely on the lessons learned from the operation of other groups, such as the Women's Unions, that have successfully offered services and support to community members.

About SAPLING

CGIAR’s Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender inclusion (SAPLING) is working in seven countries focusing on livestock value chains to package and scale out tried-and- tested, as well as new, innovations in livestock health, genetics, feed and market systems. SAPLING aims to demonstrate that improvements in livestock productivity can offer a triple win: generating improved livelihoods and nutritional outcomes; contributing to women’s empowerment; and, reducing impacts on climate and the environment. Its seven focus countries are Ethiopia, Kenya, Mali, Nepal, Tanzania, Uganda and Vietnam.

Context

SAPLING is one of the CGIAR Initiatives focusing on sustainable animal productivity. This Initiative aims to contribute to transforming livestock sectors in 7 target countries to make them more productive, resilient, equitable, and sustainable. Contributing to SAPLING’s overall objective, SAPLING - Vietnam country project, also known as Chăn-hênh, aims to contribute to transforming two livestock value chains (pigs and cattle) in the Northwest Highlands of Vietnam. This work is led by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT and is implemented in collaboration with various national partners from 2022-2024.

SAPLING Vietnam is implemented in two districts (Mai Son and Phu Yen) of one northern upland province (Son La). 9 out of 22 communes in Mai Son District and 12 out of 27 communes in Phu Yen District were approved for SAPLING implementation. In the early stages, the work is primarily implemented in Mai Son District, specifically in four core communes (Chieng Luong, Chieng Chung, Hat Lot, Muong Bon), to test and validate innovation packages. Phu Yen District will be joined in the later stages for upscaling purpose drawing on lessons from Mai Son.

A core component of SAPLING Vietnam’s strategy to strengthen the pig and cattle value chains is the formation or support to livestock farmers groups for both improved access of the farmers (women, men, youth and ethnic minorities) to input and output markets, as well as being a forum for capacity development and co-creation of solutions to issues regarding pig and cattle raising.

In November 2023, the project supported the assessment of six new livestock common interest groups (CIG) for group strengthening and development. Based on the assessment, four livestock farmer groups (three CIGs established by the Li-chăn project and one cooperative) were added to the project as part of capacity building for livestock keepers from the end of November to December 2023. An indepent consultant and project staff conducted training and provided technical support to the 10 farmer groups on the following topics:
1. Production and business planning, capital management and utilization at the household level;
2. Business planning and market access, capital management and utilization at the group level; and
3. Collecting information on middlemen and trading companies for livestock outputs
The objectives of these trainings were to:
- Ensure that each member household (including husband and wife) creates a production plan that fits their capacity and aligns with the group's business plan;
- Introduce some circular agricultural economic techniques that can lower livestock production costs and minimize environmental pollution;
- Develop an effective business plan and market access for each group, aligning with their capabilities to ensure a market for their products;
- Finalize and share a list of livestock traders at various levels (village, commune and district) with the groups to develop a plan for selling cattle and pigs before the Lunar New Year;
Explore existing sources of capital for farm production;
Finalize the cooperation contracts for the groups; and
- Create Zalo groups for offering online technical assistance to the farmer groups.
Implementation time, location and participants

The consultant arranged a training course lasting 2–3 days for each group. Held at the community house, the training sessions took place during the day or in the evening, to accommodate the schedules of the farmers and maximize attendance. Participants were drawn from the groups and local authorities (communes/villages).

Results achieved
1. Instructions on production and business planning, capital management and utilization in households
a. After participating in the training, farm households acquired knowledge and skills in production and business planning, as well as in mobilizing and managing capital sources

❖ Household representatives who took part in the business planning training were able to identify and list four key costs related to a product in order to calculate the selling price effectively and prevent any financial losses. These include the cost of depreciation of assets, raw materials, labour, and others.

• The training participants admitted that they had only been keeping track of the costs related to purchasing breeds, animal feed and fertilizers, while neglecting other costs. As a result, they lacked sufficient data to accurately determine the selling price of their products, resulting in a situation called ‘fake profit, real loss’ and a tendency to hold onto livestock in hopes of a future price increase.

• Once households have calculated their costs accurately, they can figure out how much it costs to produce each kilogram of their product at any stage. By comparing the cost of production to the market purchase price, they can determine if they will make a profit or loss and decide the most opportune time to sell their product. This practice will also discourage households from holding onto livestock or crops for extended periods in hopes of higher market prices.

❖ The training participants changed their perception of the market and market-oriented livestock farming.
• The participants understood that market prices are determined by supply and demand, and fluctuate constantly. No one can control or manipulate market prices.
• Competition exists in the market at various levels, including between production villages, communes, provinces, countries and regions.

Thus, to remain competitive in the market, simply waiting for prices to rise is not a viable strategy. Instead, farmers must actively monitor and manage production costs and utilize scientific and technological advancements in livestock farming. These include:

- Regularly updating production techniques that focus on utilizing local resources and reusing raw materials to reduce production costs, for example by growing elephant grass, making silage and creating concentrates from crop residues;
- Converting unproductive land into areas for growing feed sources like grass and corn, which helps reduce the cost of agricultural materials; and
- Staying informed and building relationships with companies, units and networks of purchasing traders to ensure a market for livestock products.
❖ After receiving training on business planning, households assessed their livestock farming practices and identified key areas for improvement in order to enhance productivity and profitability.

- Many households engaged in cattle farming do not consider the costs involved and believe that it is not expensive to raise cattle. As a result, they keep cattle for extended periods, hoping to sell them for a higher price in the future. However, after calculating the various costs, they realize that the longer they raise the cattle, the more losses they incur. Even if the selling price increases, the costs of raising the cattle increase at a faster rate. This newfound understanding is valuable for households in this sector.

- After calculating the profit and loss, cattle farmers are interested in cattle breeds that grow quickly and have high economic efficiency. For example, the Lai-Sind breed can be sold commercially at 6 months of age and reach a slaughter weight of 300 kg within 24 months, while local grass-fed cattle typically only reach 120–150 kg. The 3B breed reaches a weight of 140–150 kg at 4–5 months and can gain 0.8–1.2 kg/day when fattened for 8–9 months, resulting in a weight of approximately 500 kg after a year.

Farm households are looking forward to recommendations from the Chan-Henh project on reputable suppliers of hybrid cattle (specifically Lai-Sind and 3B) so they can make informed decisions on switching breeds.

- After analyzing the production costs, pig farming households discovered that a significant portion of their investment went towards purchasing commercial feed. On average, households spend VND 3,500,000–5,000,000 per pig on various costs such as breeds, feed and vaccines. These costs primarily focus on raw materials for production and overlook other costs. Many households end up facing losses in pig farming, leading them to abandon the practice despite investing heavily in infrastructure.
Farm households are depending on the Chan-Henh project for training on producing their own animal feed, in order to lower the costs associated with pig farming.
- Households do not prioritize nutrition in raising cattle, primarily feeding them raw materials like straw and grass. Some households give cattle concentrate, but it is insufficient.

- Cattle farmers are not fully utilizing the potential of fodder grasses as a valuable resource for feeding their livestock. Leaflets are distributed in village community houses, introducing high-yield fodder grass varieties suitable for local weather and soil conditions. With proper planting and care, an average of 250–350 tons per hectare per year can be achieved. However, the current utilization of fodder grasses is not maximizing their productivity.

- In addition to limited planting area, farmers are worried about the costs of purchasing fertilizer for grass cultivation, resulting in limited investment in fertilizer for maximizing grass yields. For example, VA06 grass is a hybrid variety with a high yield potential of 330– 360 tons/ha/year, but it requires a significant amount of manure and fertilizer for optimal

growth (13–15 tons of manure or 600 kg of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, NPK, fertilizer per ha). However, many households only invest in 100–200kg of NPK fertilizer and do not fully utilize the source of manure due to grazing habits. As a result, the harvested volume of VA06 does not meet the demand for livestock farming, with only 80–100 tons per hectare being harvested. Farmers typically reserve VA06 grass as a backup for when natural grass is scarce, without realizing that its nutritional value decreases over time, making it inadequate for cattle diets.

Improper use of manure is a concern for households that raise cattle and pigs. Instead of properly composting it, they opt to use dry manure, leading to nutrient loss and the need to purchase additional NPK fertilizer for grass growth. This practice also causes environmental pollution and community conflicts.
Farmers are looking to the Chan-Henh project for training in circular agricultural methods to manage livestock waste, minimize pollution and produce affordable natural fertilizer for crops.

2. Instructions on business planning and market access , capital management and utilization in farmer groups

Upon initial assessment, it was found that there is a lack of close cooperation between the group management board and member households. Households often sell products independently without involving the groups. After conducting analysis, the groups identified several key issues that need to be addressed.
- The groups lack a record-keeping system for storing information about purchasing units, agricultural supplies and delivery units.
- The groups lack sufficient supply to engage professional distribution agents in big cities, who typically require a large number of cattle and pigs. This shortfall might harm the groups' standing.

- The lack of understanding about roles and responsibilities among the management board and members prevents them from working closely together. Currently, they operate independently without clear guidelines or focus on developing skills for future staff. If this issue is not addressed, the departure of a key person could potentially lead to the group falling apart.

- The groups’ activities are currently irregular and do not prioritize meeting the needs of the market. In order to be successful, groups must produce goods or services that are in demand, connect with the market, handle various tasks such as collecting, processing, transporting and delivering, and provide excellent customer service. It is important for the
group to have trained and skilled individuals who can effectively coordinate these tasks, rather than relying solely on the group leader.

- Currently, households can obtain capital from different sources, such as agricultural banks and trust funds of the policy bank for farmers' associations, women's associations. This capital is mainly used for major expenses, but there is a lack of access to small loans for short periods. Livestock groups also do not have their own funds to quickly meet the capital needs of their members for production.
To address these challenges, the management boards and members of the farmer groups gained knowledge on various aspects, including:
Setting the group's revenue goals and developing plans to achive the goals;
- Developing a market access and sales plan;
- Compiling lists of buyers, producers, collections and freight units;
Improving the group’s operational structures; and
- Reviewing and adjusting the group's operational regulations.

With the help of the consultant, the groups evaluated the members' ability to form bonds, the resources available to the group and the necessary actions to improve the group's activities, including the following:

The groups decided to meet again in order to reorganize the group members into different teams based on their expertise. These teams include: (i) market research and sales, (ii) production, (iii) collection and processing, and (iv) transportation and delivery. The general manager will be the group leader and will oversee the groups’ efficiency regularly.
- The groups plan to update their regulations to provide more clarity on the responsibilities and benefits of the staff in the teams above.
- The groups will create a sales plan and track revenue targets on a weekly, monthly, quarterly and yearly basis to build trust among members and expand production in the future.

- The groups decided to work together to reduce costs and increase profits by using agricultural by-products, producing their own feed, and sharing disease prevention and vaccine sources. They also need to learn how to set wholesale and retail competitive prices in order to reach more customers in different markets.
- Some groups will further study the VSLA model to increase their production capital. This will:
i. assist producers in effectively managing their cash flow and planning their production, determining when it is necessary to borrow money;
ii. attract new members in the community to participate and contribute to creating a larger capital pool;
create more opportunities to expand the production area for raw materials; and
limit borrowing money from external sources (e.g. banks and black credit).

By proactively establishing a fund, the group can increase its capacity to generate capital. Additionally, by using the VSLA fundraising model, the group can cover the expenses for market development activities, product promotion and product branding using its own funds. This resource contributes to the long-term growth and sustainability of the groups.

At the end of the training, the groups developed cooperation contracts that outline their operations, membership numbers and management board roles. Each group also established rules regarding the contribution of shares to ensure smooth operations.
3. Survey of information of livestock middlemen and trading companies

At present, the groups primarily concentrate on livestock production and do not have a designated sales plan for specific time periods (week/month/quarter/year). Sales are done on an individual basis, depending on the immediate needs of households.

Member households reported that selling their livestock products is easy. They simply need to post pictures on social media platforms like Facebook and Zalo, after which traders inquire about the products, visit their homes to assess the quality, negotiate prices and complete the transactions. However, farmers often believe that traders are responsible for lowering prices, which leads to a lack of trust and a failure to establish a mutually beneficial relationship.

For example, as of November 2023, the purchase price of live cattle fluctuated only around VND 60,000–65,000 per kg, much lower than the price of VND 90,000–120,000 per kg in 2021–2022. The purchase price of live cattle significantly decreased, while the price of beef in the market remained high at VND 190,000–220,000 per kg, causing farmers to believe that traders are profiting unfairly. NEXUS highlights
New Nexus Capacity Scorecard

Researchers from the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) in Pakistan have developed a ‘Nexus Capacity Scorecard’ – an innovative survey tool to capture institutional capacity for implementing systems solutions across three domains: knowledge, awareness and skills; enabling an institutional environment; and institutional learning, collaboration and knowledge sharing. The tool will be used as part of a capacity assessment to establish a baseline understanding of government and institutional capacity and needs. The data collected will help track capacity scores throughout the three planned phases of the Initiative. A similar tool has been developed specifically for academic institutions. In addition, the team is conducting focus group discussions with female government professionals working in water, energy, food and environmental agencies to learn more about the experiences of women in these sectors.
Groundwater governance workshop in Nepal
A workshop on groundwater governance in Nepal, organized by the Groundwater Resources Development Board in collaboration with NEXUS Gains and IWMI, took place

on January 13, 2023. The objectives of the workshop were to engage with relevant stakeholders on the governance of groundwater in the federal context of the country, and discuss resulting challenges and opportunities for policy, jurisdiction and implementation. The workshop brought together government officials, development partners, and research and civil society organizations to discuss the future direction of the formal groundwater governance structure in the country based on preliminary research findings.
Early career researchers discuss food systems challenges

A workshop for early career researchers was held from November 7 to 11, 2022, in South Africa. Organized by NEXUS Gains in partnership with the University of KwaZulu-Natal’s Centre for Transformative Agricultural and Food Systems, the event brought together researchers from various disciplines and institutions around the world to discuss their work on sustainable and healthy food systems. The workshop aimed to promote knowledge and skills sharing to support participants’ research and professional growth. Mentoring sessions covered self-awareness, publishing and career paths, and enabled discussion of the challenges faced by women in science. After fruitful discussions at the workshop, participants decided to develop a common understanding of the capacities and duties of food systems researchers and the resilience of food systems with the aim of publishing an opinion piece in a peer-reviewed journal.
Rice–fish systems illustrate the benefits of integration

Though rarely acknowledged, agricultural intensification can undermine fisheries. The use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides pollutes water and can kill fish and other flora and fauna if applied inappropriately. In rice–fish systems, which integrate rice production with aquaculture, it is necessary to manage for both the rice and the fish. If done properly, such systems can increase water productivity, bring economic and nutritional benefits for communities and, because less agrochemicals are used, increase biodiversity and other environmental benefits. While not a new idea – rice– fish systems have been around for over 2,000 years – this is a neat example of managing in an integrated way to achieve multiple benefits.

Definitions

The water–energy–food–ecosystems (WEFE) nexus is a cross-sectoral concept offering a holistic perspective of the interconnections among water management, energy production, food/agriculture, and ecosystem health.

Nexus thinking has emerged as a way of conceptualizing and addressing trade-offs, compromises and potential synergies among water, energy, food, and ecosystems. A WEFE nexus approach integrates management and governance across sectors and considers each sector as equally important and closely connected in planning (FAO 2014).

WEFE institution refers to any institution that works within the water, energy, food, and ecosystem/environment sectors, including public (governmental), private, non-governmental, research, civil society organizations, etc.

1. Introduction

The Water–Energy–Food–Ecosystem (WEFE) nexus approach represents a holistic and interconnected perspective for addressing the complex interdependencies among water, energy, food, and ecosystems (Simpson and Jewitt 2019). WEFE frameworks recognize that changes in one sector can have cascading effects on others, emphasizing the need for integrated and sustainable solutions. In WEFE nexus thinking, water, energy, food, and ecosystems are viewed as interconnected systems, with links and feedback loops. This integrated perspective highlights the importance of managing WEFE resources collaboratively to achieve social, economic, and environmental sustainability.

Nexus approaches involve the application of integrated strategies to optimize resource use, enhance resilience, and mitigate potential tensions across sectors that use and depend on shared resources. By adopting a nexus approach, stakeholders can develop comprehensive solutions that address multiple challenges simultaneously, promoting synergies and minimizing trade-offs. Key principles of nexus approaches include fostering cross-sectoral collaboration, considering the social and gender dimensions, and incorporating sustainable practices. These approaches aim to enhance efficiency, reduce environmental impact, and promote the equitable and resilient use of resources.

Efficient management of WEFE systems and the adoption of comprehensive, sustainable approaches requires robust stakeholder capabilities. Understanding institutional and individual capacities of actors involved in implementing WEFE nexus approaches is a critical, but often overlooked, first step.

This ‘Nexus Capacity Scorecard (NCS) – Education and Research’ is intended to gauge nexus capacities within and/or across academic institutions conducting research in or teaching courses related to the water, energy, food/agriculture, and environmental sectors (henceforth referred to as ‘WEFE academic institutions’).

This version of the scorecard is part of a toolkit that includes the original Nexus Capacity Scorecard (NCS) to capture nexus capacities within and/or across WEFE institutions or organizations in government, the private sector, or civil society. The NCS supports the self-assessment of institutional processes, readiness, and capacities in relation to WEFE approaches. The purpose is to identify opportunities, possible gaps, and inform the planning of tailored WEFE nexus capacity-building efforts, programs and interventions, and/or their monitoring over time.

The NCS – Education and Research is a complementary tool that can be used by WEFE academic institutions in tandem with the original NCS or on its own. Like the NCS, it can be used for monitoring capacities over time and as a launching pad for discussions on where capacity support is most needed within academic institutions conducting WEFE research or teaching WEFE-related courses. It is designed for use by WEFE academic institutions (faculty, department heads, etc.) to self-assess institutional capacities, opportunities, and gaps to engage in WEFE research and train future WEFE nexus researchers.
The NCS – Education and Research aims to answer the following questions:
1. Is there evidence of a WEFE nexus perspective at the institution (in terms of curricula and research carried out by senior faculty/professors)?
2. Is there an interest or demand for WEFE-related research and evidence-building?
3. Is there an enabling environment for WEFE nexus thinkers?

The scorecard is designed for use in multiple contexts and as such is adaptable to different program needs. Institutions should ask participants for their informed consent (using e.g. the template provided in Section 3, or by a local Institutional Review Board (IRB) for research ethics). They are also encouraged to tailor the introductory texts for the survey tools according to their specific requirements.

Note: The NCS – Education and Research is a rapid self-assessment tool based on the perceptions and context of individuals from academic institutions using them. As such, the ‘capacity score’ derived should be understood as a nuanced and institution-specific metric. The primary use of the tool is to serve as an internal compass for universities, stimulating dialogue and guiding targeted capacity-building efforts within the specific context. If the tool is being disseminated across multiple universities as part of a larger research initiative, questions should be standardized and scores can be compared across institutions to understand their relative capacity rankings.

The NCS was initially developed and pre-tested for the Pakistan context. The questions aim for universal relevance, but certain questions or phrases may require adaptation to the local context to ensure relevance.

This is the first edition of the NCS – Education and Research, and it has not undergone validation across countries. Feedback from those implementing the tool is encouraged to enhance its effectiveness. This will help in refining and improving the scorecard for future iterations.

Data collection
Data can be collected using the scorecard in several ways:
• Via an online survey: the link can be sent to respondents via email. This is the fastest way to reach many respondents, but there is a risk of a low response rate.

• Through interviews: interviewees respond to the scorecard questions and the interviewer asks follow-up questions along the way. This approach is more time-consuming than the online survey but yields richer information.

• During a relevant workshop or event: participants respond individually or in a group, online or using a hard copy of the scorecard. Results can be discussed in real time, as a launchpad for dialogues and planning on WEFE nexus capacity strengthening.

Optional: After each question, in online and in-person options, respondents may provide evidence or any additional comments that explain their chosen score or suggestions for building capacity on the specific
indicator.
Analyzing the Scorecard results

The total score will be the sum of the values assigned to each question. The overall score can range from minimum 0 (if the respondent consistently selects the Level 0 option) to a maximum score of 80 (if the respondent consistently selects the Level 4 option). The ‘Don’t know/Unsure’ (DK) answer choice is counted as ‘0’ and included in the overall analysis. Given that respondents are presumed to be knowledgeable faculty, department heads, and higher education students, minimal ‘DK’ responses are expected.

Researchers using the NCS can decide whether to establish a cut-off for excluding ‘DK’ choices (e.g., if there are 5 or more ‘0’ scores (25%), the respondent may be considered deficient for the survey and excluded from the analysis to ensure the analysis is reflective of informed opinions). The decision to include or exclude ‘DK’ responses should consider the specific context, sample size, and objectives of the survey.
Note: Researchers should consider the specific goals and context of the use of the NCS when deciding whether to include or exclude ‘Don’t know/Unsure’ responses from the analysis and scoring.

There is an important distinction between a respondent selecting ‘No Capacity’ (1) and ‘Don’t know/Unsure’ (0). A respondent indicating ‘No Capacity’ recognizes that there is a lack of capacity, suggesting an awareness of a deficiency in capacity for the given indicator. In contrast, a 'Don’t know/Unsure’ response indicates a lack of knowledge or uncertainty about the specific indicator, suggesting that the respondent may not have sufficient information or understanding on the topic. This distinction is critical for a nuanced interpretation of results, allowing for a more accurate assessment of awareness levels related to the selected indicators and guiding researchers and organizations on areas where capacity is needed.

Including ‘Don’t know/Unsure’ responses in the analysis is important for maintaining data integrity and reflecting honest uncertainty among technical expert respondents. Excluding these responses may introduce bias and overlook areas where knowledge is lacking or uncertain. By including this response in the analysis, the results can offer a more accurate representation of participants’ expertise and guide future efforts to address knowledge gaps.

Definitions

The water–energy–food–ecosystems (WEFE) nexus is a cross-sectoral concept offering a holistic perspective of the interconnections among water management, energy production, food/agriculture, and ecosystem health.

Nexus thinking has emerged as a way of conceptualizing and addressing trade-offs, compromises and potential synergies among water, energy, food, and ecosystems. A WEFE nexus approach integrates management and governance across sectors and considers each sector as equally important and closely connected in planning (FAO 2014).

WEFE institution refers to any institution that works within the water, energy, food, and ecosystem/environment sectors, including public (governmental), private, non-governmental, research, civil society organizations, etc.

We expect that along with the use of this framework, more formative research will be conducted to understand food system actor experiences, constraints, and opportunity spaces. We expect the impact of this approach to research and action will be to more effectively achieve agency and behavior change targets, and resulting agri-food system transformations. Executive Summary

Systems-level transformation is increasingly recognized as necessary to improve the sustainability, equity, and resilience of agri-food systems. The CGIAR Initiative on Agroecology uses a systems transformation approach in alignment with Gliessmann (2014) and the 13 principles of agroecology outlined by the HLPE (2019). This approach requires new understandings of actor agency and behavior change processes that enable systems change. To provide these new understandings for approaches and investments in agroecological transitions, our study presents a novel framework and lessons from past experiences in similar transitions that required changes in behavior and agency of food system actors.
The specific objectives of this study were to

1. Understand how agroecology-relevant projects, government and/or donor programs, community initiatives, and social movements (collectively referred to as “initiatives” in this report) have approached behavior change and agency of food system actors for agri-food systems transformation;
2. Identify common assumptions on behavior change and agency that underpinned the initiatives’ design; and

3. Recommend adjustments to the Theories of Change, assumptions, and processes in initiative design and implementation to enhance the roles of actor agency and behavior change processes in systems change.
Methods

To address the study objectives, we drew upon initiatives that involved agroecology-relevant projects, government or donor programs, community initiatives, and social movements (henceforth called “initiatives”) from five countries: Tunisia, Zimbabwe, Peru, India, and Kenya. We developed an inventory of initiatives through a review of published and gray literature, such as websites and reports. We then characterized these initiatives in terms of the type of initiative, time period of implementation, and the focal agroecological principles addressed.

To further investigate approaches to changing behavior and agency, we selected a subset of initiatives from each country as case studies based on the following criteria: engagement with multiple and diverse agroecological principles, geographical scale of reach, diverse representation of initiative type and objective, relevance or impact as reported by local experts, and some country-specific criteria. We interviewed the designers and/or implementers of these case study initiatives to collect additional data, including the perceived factors that enabled or impeded the intended behavior changes.

We developed and applied a framework for behavior change and agency of actors in agri-food systems to synthesize across the case studies:
i. Targeted actor groups, targeted behavior changes, and intervention modalities (behavior change approaches) applied

Individual behavioral factors were most targeted by case studies. Technical assistance, training, and demonstrations were the most common approaches used to shape producer knowledge, attitude, and behavior. All cases applied multiple approaches to target behavior, for instance, improving productive infrastructure in addition to providing technical assistance and training.
ii. Whether and how actor diversity and power asymmetries were addressed
iii. Common assumptions made about achieving change and how these played out in practice

After identifying the key assumptions underlying the Theory of Change in each case study, we analyzed whether these assumptions were supported by the initiative results, primarily the factors reported as enablers of or impediments to change, or needed refining.
Key results

The inventory included a total of 239 past initiatives that had pursued agroecological transitions, often by addressing a range of the 13 HLPE agroecological principles. Sixty-five percent of these initiatives had begun within the last 12 years (although dates were unavailable for 25% of the initiatives) and 88% were government- or donor-supported projects or programs. Nineteen community initiatives and ten social movements were also identified.

These initiatives most often applied agroecology principles related to resilience: biodiversity (71% of the initiatives), soil health (67%), economic diversification (60%), and synergy (49%). The exception was animal health, which was among the least applied (19%) of the 13 principles. One principle related to social equity was also frequently applied (co-creation of knowledge, 44%), while other social equity principles were given lower priority: connectivity (31%), social values and diets (31%), and fairness (25%).

From the 29 case studies, food system actors whose behaviors were targeted for change included producers (farmers, fishers, pastoralists, and other food producers) as individuals and groups, other value chain actors (retailers, input sellers, and actors in postharvest activities), extension and education actors (national agricultural extension agents and researchers), communities (women and groups of natural resource users), governance actors (policymakers and donors), and food consumers.

All case studies targeted the behavior of farmers and/or other producers, most often related to on-farm activities (such as changing or diversifying the farm production portfolio, 45% of cases) or value chain engagement (such as collaborating/ negotiating with value chain actors, 41% of cases). When the behavior of other actor groups was targeted, it was usually to reinforce influence on producer behavior. For example, 52% of the cases targeted the behavior of extension/education actors. Other commonly targeted behavior of non-producer actors involved improving natural resource management practices in communities (28% of cases), engaging governance system actors to encourage agroecology- friendly policies (24% of cases), and changing diets of consumers (21% of cases).

Facilitating actor interactions was also common. Seventy-six percent of the cases supported collaboration through producer organizations or multi-stakeholder platforms to create opportunities for collective action toward change. Designers and implementers of initiatives frequently perceived factors related to these interactions as enablers of change, such as the scope and quality of partner engagement or a codesign process that included target actors and led to buy-in. However, poor stakeholder coordination was sometimes perceived as an impediment to change, even among cases that applied approaches to address producer and stakeholder interactions. Many of the case studies also sought to expand actors’ opportunity spaces by addressing external forces influencing
behavioral outcomes:

Economic drivers: Fifty-five percent of the cases sought to expand actor opportunity spaces by addressing economic drivers of behavior, through facilitating market relationships, expanding credit mechanisms, and/or strengthening value chains. Cases addressing these drivers more frequently reported that market opportunities and engagement with value chain actors and other diverse stakeholders helped to achieve intended changes. However, these cases also more frequently noted that inadequate market linkages contributed to ongoing challenges.

Resource system drivers: Fifty-two percent of the cases approached resource-related drivers of behavior beyond the level of individuals’ resources, for example, by improving infrastructure related to water management, food production, storage, and processing. Many of these cases also facilitated social learning and networking, and their frequently reported enablers of change, such as wide stakeholder involvement, reflected these approaches.

Social and relational drivers: Fifty-five percent of the cases addressed these drivers using approaches such as promoting agency, entrepreneurship, and/or inclusion and equity. Forty- one percent of the cases had a specific focus on inclusion and equity for women or other marginalized groups. Cases that did not address such social and relational dynamics more often reported poor codesign and poor alignment with stakeholder needs as challenges to achieving intended outcomes. Governance drivers: Only 38% of the cases addressed governance (including institutional and policy-related) drivers of behavior; of these, only one case reported success in achieving institutional reform. Cases that did and did not address governance drivers commonly reported institutional and policy challenges to achieving behavior change. At the same time, cases that did address governance drivers more often reported success in achieving intended outcomes through partner engagement and collaboration, market and value chain opportunities, and/or wide stakeholder involvement.
