In Murewa, 95 participants engaged with the display, with eight potential service providers expressing interest in acquiring the peanut butter-making machine, manual groundnut sheller, and peanut roaster. Groundnut production is high in Murewa, so farmers were especially intrigued by the value addition machinery, which opens new opportunities for processing and marketing. As groundnut farmers, these machines will give us a business opportunity, to sell peanut butter in large quantities, explained Colleta Nzara. We used to lose so much money by just selling unshelled groundnuts because very few could manually process into peanut butter, but with these machines, the whole process is so much easier added Florence Mutize of Murewa district. In Mbire, where 57 participants visited the stand, the basin digger was a major attraction. This is the first time I am seeing this machine that can ease our labor burdens when making our Pfumvudza plots, shared Jennifer Nyatande from Mbire district. I m eager to invest in one to both reduce costs on my farm and offer services to others, she added. The 2024 Agroecology Fairs provided an opportunity to demonstrate how mechanization can be both accessible and transformative for smallholder farmers. With growing interest from local communities, the Mechanization and Extension activity continues to work toward sustainable agricultural development across Zimbabwe s rural districts. Executive summary

The main objective of this action was to co-identify other technological and institutional innovations that can be implemented within the agroecology living landscapes (ALLs) to facilitate the agroecological transition with specific reference to pre-selected value chains. The action also aimed to co-develop the action to be implemented in the ALLs by the farmers. This co-development capacitated all stakeholders and built confidence to use local resources to solve local problems. This was done through ALLs thematic working groups, which produced detailed information on quantities and protocols to be used for the application of local technologies within pre-selected value chains. Plenary sessions were held to validate various innovative technologies and to come up with the desired action plans for the 2023/24 farming season. Detailed quantities of various ingredients and protocols for the various local technologies were discussed and validated. Discussions recommended the use of local resources that are less expensive and readily available and further research on technologies that were not validated with little evidence. For the future sustainability of the ALLs, we recommend the development of a Local Farmer Innovation Guide/Manual as a reference for future farming activities.

Introduction

The pursuit of research and innovation in food, land, and water systems is paramount in the quest for a sustainable and climate- resilient world where the spectres of hunger and malnutrition are effectively banished. As the global community strives to meet the ambitious targets set by the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030, there is a growing recognition of the need for innovative approaches to address the complex challenges facing agriculture and food systems. Within this context, the CGIAR, a global research partnership for a food-secure future, is stepping up to the challenge with a comprehensive and relevant portfolio of initiatives, one of which is the ""Agroecology Initiative.""

The Agroecology Initiative is conceived as a transformative force across food, land, and water systems, seeking to demonstrate and advocate for the applicability of agroecology. The initiative recognizes the pivotal role that agroecology can play in fostering sustainability and resilience, particularly in low-income countries where small-scale farmers form the backbone of agricultural practices. By collaborating with diverse stakeholders, including farmers and other actors in the food system, the initiative aims to promote the investment and adoption of agroecological practices. In the pursuit of the Agroecology Initiative's objectives, it is crucial to consider Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) as an integral component. Indigenous knowledge, developed over generations within local communities, embodies a wealth of understanding about sustainable agricultural practices, biodiversity, and ecosystem management. Incorporating IKS into agroecological transformations ensures that the initiatives are culturally sensitive, socially inclusive, and adapted to the specific needs of local communities. The significance of IKS in sustainable agroecology transformation lies in its ability to offer context-specific insights and solutions. Indigenous communities often possess a deep understanding of their local ecosystems, plant varieties, and traditional farming techniques that have evolved in harmony with nature. By acknowledging and integrating IKS into the Agroecology Initiative, there is an opportunity to co-create knowledge and build inclusive relationships among various actors in the food system. This approach not only respects cultural diversity but also enhances the effectiveness and acceptance of agroecological innovations at the local level.

Furthermore, the consideration of whether technological innovations are indigenized or wholly indigenous to a community is essential for several reasons. First, indigenization refers to the adaptation of technologies to suit local contexts and needs. Understanding whether technological innovations have been indigenized ensures that they align with the specific requirements and cultural nuances of the community, fostering greater acceptance and sustainability. Second, ensuring that innovations are not only adopted but also adapted to local conditions enhances the resilience of the implemented solutions. Additionally, acknowledging whether technological innovations are wholly indigenous is crucial for issues of ownership, intellectual property, and equitable distribution of benefits. It ensures that communities retain control over their traditional knowledge and resources, preventing the exploitation of indigenous wisdom without due recognition or compensation. The Agroecology Initiative's emphasis on integrating Indigenous Knowledge Systems and understanding the indigenization of technological innovations reflects a holistic and inclusive approach to sustainable development. By embracing the diversity of knowledge and engaging with local communities, the initiative strives to create a transformative impact on food, land, and water systems, contributing to the realization of a more sustainable and resilient global food future.

Which other technological or institutional innovations – based on local knowledge - can be implemented to facilitate communities in the agroecological transition based on the constraints and opportunities identified earlier? Methodological approach
World cafe approach

BHT adopted the World Café methodology, a simple, effective, and flexible format for hosting a large group of farmers' dialogues (Agroecological Living Landscapes - ALLs). Another reason for this adoption was that the approach has several elements, each element of the method having a specific purpose and corresponds to one or more of the design principles:
Introduction and reconnaissance

BHT and AEI TEAM personnel began with a warm welcome and an introduction, setting the context and re-capture of their last activities on value chain selection and putting participants at ease. The discussion also went on to explain the issues of the value chains and the importance of understanding various stages in the production process from inputs, production, processing, marketing and governance issues and a further link to the various value chains that had been identified by farmers in previous activities in addition to other additional ones.
Small-Group Rounds:

The farmer participants were categorized into distinct groups based on demographic criteria, specifically, older men (40+ years), older women (40+ years), younger men (youths below 40 years), and younger women (youths below 40 years). The stakeholders from the districts constituted the fifth group. These groups were tasked with engaging in discussions pertaining to various stages of the pre-identified and prioritized value chains, encompassing inputs, production, processing, marketing, and governance within their respective ward. To facilitate these discussions, the five groups were strategically positioned at different posts, each assigned to focus on a specific component. Initially, each group was allotted 45 minutes to deliberate on the designated aspects, document key points, and transcribe these onto charts. Following this initial session, the groups were instructed to transition to a different post, where they were given an additional 15 minutes to contribute to another chart. During this phase, group members had the option to either remain stationed with the chart as a ""table host"" for subsequent rounds or move to a different post.

This structured process ensured that each group had the opportunity to examine and provide input on all five components. At the conclusion of each 15-minute interval, group members rotated to different charts until all groups had actively contributed to every chart. The outcomes of these discussions were visually represented in diverse formats, often employing various colours on the charts to highlight additional information contributed by different groups. In addition to the insights garnered from individual groups, supplementary information from the collective assembly, including stakeholders, was actively sought and recorded for each component across the distinct value chains. This methodological approach allowed for a comprehensive and inclusive exploration of the various dimensions of the value chains, fostering a holistic understanding of the perspectives and inputs from the diverse stakeholder groups involved.
Plenary sessions
After the small groups (and/or in between rounds, as needed), individuals were invited to share insights or other results from their conversations with the rest of the large group in plenary.

Results
Mbire district

In the Agroecology Living Landscapes initiative, farmers and stakeholders have strategically prioritized the sorghum and livestock value chains for the agroecological transition. Collaboratively identifying and integrating Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) within these value chains is crucial for their success. This prioritization stems from the recognition of sorghum as a vital staple crop and livestock as an integral component of sustainable farming. By incorporating IKS, which encapsulates traditional, locally adapted practices, the initiative seeks to enhance resilience, optimize resource utilization, and promote ecological balance, ensuring a holistic and culturally relevant approach to agroecological transformation in these key agricultural sectors.
Livestock value chain
Animal Health

In Mbire, farmers are grappling with the challenges of managing livestock health in an environment marked by the absence of veterinary clinics and extension services, coupled with the prohibitive costs of pharmaceutical drugs. In response to these constraints, farmers in Mbire have turned to their indigenous knowledge systems (IKS) to combat pests and diseases affecting their livestock. The reliance on IKS is driven by factors such as the potency and cost-effectiveness of ethnoveterinary medicines, the local availability of resources, and the sustainability of these practices amidst the unpredictable backdrop of climate change and variability (Table 1). The farmers have developed a repertoire of practical solutions rooted in their traditional knowledge to address common issues plaguing their livestock.

For instance, in dealing with the challenge of ticks, farmers employ a variety of methods such as handpicking, the application of warm ashes, smearing snuff on affected areas, utilizing Karemerapewa (a climber found on Mopani trees), employing chilli spray, and using thorns to prick ticks (Table 1). Similarly, for foot and mouth disease, farmers resort to practical measures such as salt and soap solutions, salt soil (Mutyora), Sodom Apple (Nhundurwa), and wild cucumber. The management of more severe ailments like Heartwater and Redwater involves the application of Karemerapewa, Murunjurunju, Bambamupani (a climber found on Mopani trees), a small green shrub (Kasviswa), Aloe vera, Rubber hedge (Katsvotsvo), and soot. Lambskin issues are addressed with salt water, while anthrax necessitates the drastic measure of burning the affected animal, and blackleg is managed through the application of hot water on the affected legs (Table 1).

The practicality of these methods lies in their affordability, accessibility, and sustainability, making them viable alternatives in the absence of conventional veterinary services. However, challenges persist, notably in the lack of scientific evidence on the efficacy of these indigenous practices and the absence of precise dosages, which raises concerns about potential toxicity. To enhance the sustainable use and adoption of IKS in livestock health management, there is a pressing need for comprehensive documentation, research, and scientific validation of these traditional practices in Mbire.

Human-Wildlife conflict

In the agricultural landscape of Mbire, farmers have ingeniously incorporated traditional methods to effectively minimize human- wildlife conflicts, particularly with lions, foxes, and hyenas. Recognizing the threat these predators pose to livestock, farmers have implemented improved livestock enclosures to create a protective barrier (Appendix 1, 2 and 3). For crocodile management, the strategic placement of thorny branches at water holes serves as a deterrent, mitigating the risk of livestock falling prey to these aquatic predators. In the case of baboons and wild dogs, herding practices and the confinement of young livestock play a crucial role in preventing conflicts. Moreover, to counter the challenge of stock theft, farmers have turned to the use of juju—an indigenous spiritual practice—to either fix the thief (reversing the process if the thief admits guilt) or to safeguard the entire livestock herd. This intricate blend of traditional wisdom involves herding practices and daily enclosure of livestock, showcasing the adaptability and resourcefulness of Mbire's farmers in navigating the complexities of coexisting with wildlife while safeguarding their livelihoods. Through the incorporation of these practical measures rooted in indigenous knowledge, farmers in Mbire are not only fostering harmonious relationships with the surrounding wildlife but are also exemplifying the potential of IKS in addressing contemporary challenges in the realm of agroecology.
Water shortages

In Mbire, farmers actively address water shortages in livestock by employing practical and sustainable measures, such as digging wells to tap into underground water sources (Appendix 3). They also fence water sources with tree branches or reeds (Kusosera Murwizi) to prevent contamination and preserve water quality. Leveraging wetlands (Makambwe) and strategically digging water holes along riverbeds, farmers enhance water availability for their livestock. These practices not only mitigate the impact of water scarcity but also align with agroecological principles by promoting resource efficiency, ecosystem health, and the resilience of farming systems in Mbire.
Technologies of interest and suggested action plan

Farmers in the community have identified innovative approaches in livestock management, aiming to address challenges and enhance animal health while reducing costs. One such innovation involves dipping livestock using a combination of katunguru and karemerapewa. The objective is to minimize expenses associated with traditional dipping methods. Activities include the collection of raw materials and the implementation of dipping procedures. Individuals within the community will spearhead these efforts, supported by a collaborative network including veterinarians, AEI TEAM (International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center), Agritex (Agricultural Extension Services), local leaders, and researchers. The timeline for testing this innovation is set for November 2023, and the required resources include katunguru and karemerapewa. The expected output is improved livestock health resulting from the application of this cost-effective dipping technique.

1.0 Introduction

The Agroecology Initiative (AE-I) acknowledges context-specific technologies to enhance the sustainability and resilience of food systems. It is hinged on interconnected agroecology principles. In low-input systems, improving the connectivity of these principles can be used to enhance, re-model and optimize productivity. These efforts require co-designing socio-technological innovations that reduce environmentally disruptive inputs and enhance resilience. Local stakeholders and food system actors (FSA) play a crucial role in this co-creation, testing and evaluation process to promote culturally relevant innovations and ensure natural resources are managed responsibly and inclusively.

In the Mbire and Murehwa districts of Zimbabwe, the AE-I is working with 4 Agroecology living landscapes (ALLs). Most of the ALLs members rely on crops and livestock as a source of livelihood and are active in the associated value chains (Output 3.2 Value chain Mapping). In Murewa, the value chains identified include horticultural crops (tomatoes, onions, carrots, butternuts - we can select), poultry (indigenous), livestock (cattle and goats), maize, groundnuts and sweet potato. Mbire's value chains included cotton, livestock (goats and cattle), honey, sorghum and sesame. However, they face several challenges (Report 1).

The main challenges relating to crop production were increased pest and disease incidences (namely fall armyworm), crop failure, increased incidences of drought and, at times, long dry spells and low access to improved seed varieties. For animal production, challenges were related to poor quality grazing lands, fodder and feeds, the prevalence of several pests and diseases and poor livestock breeds. Our first entry point was the crop production aspects, which we hope can also assist with alleviating some of the issues of poor fodder and feed quality. The following interventions were co-identified: (i) introduction of appropriate scale mechanization, (ii) Push-pull (PP) for insect pest control, (iii) Conservation agriculture (CA) for improved resilience to drought, (iv) Seed and livestock fairs to improve access to inputs, markets and, showcase and promote crop and livestock diversity, and (v) Haymaking and Feed formulation for improved animal health.

In our concerted effort to foster co-creation and empower farmers in driving sustainable agricultural practices, we have strategically incorporated their invaluable feedback and input into the development and testing of co-identified technologies, particularly geared towards supporting agroecological transition. Recognizing the significance of addressing challenges related to seed availability, we introduced seed and livestock fairs just before the growing season commenced. To assess the effectiveness of CA and PP technologies, the research team and extension officers collaborated to design and establish demo plots. In response to labour issues, the members of the ALLs actively participated in identifying fellow members to serve as mechanization service providers. Working in tandem with extension officers, these individuals underwent comprehensive training and were equipped with cutting-edge machinery to implement and showcase the identified technologies. Field days were organized to broaden the outreach, inviting local Food System Actors (FSA) and other stakeholders to engage actively in the evaluation process. During these events, participants were not merely passive observers; they were encouraged to actively rate, rank, and propose adaptations to the technologies on display.

The commitment to co-creation extended further as farmers, in collaboration with extension officers, undertook thorough pest and disease assessments at various stages of crop development, culminating in hands-on harvesting experiences. This allowed farmers a first-hand opportunity to assess the technologies. Subsequent to this intensive engagement, farmer feedback played a pivotal role in prompting collaboration with BioHUB to identify local technological innovations that could complement and enhance the existing technologies aligned with the identified value chains. The culmination of these efforts materialized in the incorporation of both adapted and locally sourced technologies into the meticulously planned demonstration plots for the upcoming 2023/24 season. Acknowledging the dynamic nature of agriculture and the unique challenges faced by individual farmers, a consultant has been engaged to implement decision choice experiments (DCE). This Initiative aims to gain profound insights into farmers' decision-making processes concerning the identified technologies.

The insights garnered from the DCE will be instrumental in informing the design and implementation of baby trial experiments scheduled for the forthcoming 2023/24 growing season. This innovative approach ensures that the farmers involved in the baby trials are not just passive recipients but active participants, as they will be provided with inputs and empowered to adapt the

2.2.1 Seed and Livestock Fair

Objective: In response to challenges related to the lack of appropriate seeds and eroding agrobiodiversity and, as a way to transition prevailing food systems to more sustainable ones, farmers, government stakeholders, and other FSA participated in locally organized seed and livestock fairs. The seed and livestock fair aimed to enable farmers to access improved and locally adapted seeds and livestock breeds. In addition, the seed and live fairs provided a platform for learning about agroecological practices and principles, namely participation, connectivity, soil and animal health, economic diversification, biodiversity, synergies, and fairness. Farmers were also allowed to see different machinery that could aid land, food, and feed preparation and address their labour shortage challenges.
The fairs were also used as a platform to give feedback on the initiative activities to communities and participating FSA.

Approach: The researcher team, with extension officers, farmers and other food system actors, collaborated on planning and implementing the seed and livestock fair. After the first fair in 2022, we had several feedback sessions with stakeholders and communities to report on what worked and what did not. Suggestions, such as including livestock and feed and fodder section, were then incorporated into the 2023 fair and the inclusion of the ALL exchange visits between the two districts.
Lessons learnt, achievements and challenges:

• In 2022, 1058 FSA participated; in 2023, we had 701. Farmers displayed over 40 food and fodder crop species and around ten livestock species. Over 300 farmers could access improved seed varieties, while nearly 100 exchanged local landraces.
• By adopting a multi-partner approach, these fairs bring local food systems actors together to ensure household food and nutrition security and improved income streams for farmers.

• Stakeholders, partners and other projects and initiatives, including the RAIZ project, LIPS, Grasslands research station, various seed companies, Hamara Chicks, PHI Commodities, International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), BioHUB Trust (BHT), Kurima Machinery and Technology, and Zimplow Limited participated in these fairs promoting collaboration and synergies.
Farmers hold a high regard for their landraces, possessing a diverse array of seeds.
• The participation of seed companies and other FSAs in Mbire seed and livestock fairs is limited, primarily due to the considerable distance involved.

Objective: Farmers within the ALLs identified drudgery associated with farming operations as a challenge. The objective was to set up service providers of different machinery to improve production efficiencies and ease processing and transportation burdens.

2.2.3 Crop-related technologies
2.2.3.1 AE technologies for IPM and CSA

Objectives: Farmers in the Murehwa and Mbire districts face several production constraints, including low resource use efficiency, insect pests and diseases, low synergy across farm domains, and poor food and feed quality. In view of the challenges, ALL members and the WP 1 team have identified technologies that can address some of these challenges. These technologies include push-pull, intercropping and conservation agriculture.
Approach: To demonstrate

usefulness of these technologies, ten demonstration plots were established across the district and within wards where the ALLs have been established. The objective of the demonstration plots is to compare and benchmark the performance of conservation agriculture, push-pull, and conventional practices on productivity, rainwater use efficiency, and pest biocontrol. The treatments will be as follows –
1. Push-pull treatment: maize or sorghum intercropped with cowpea or bean under strip-cropping, with Brachiaria as a border crop under conventional tillage as a biological control to fall armyworm
2. Conventional treatment: maize or sorghum is the sole crop under conventional tillage (control treatment)
3. Conservation Agriculture (CA) treatment: maize or sorghum under no-tillage with residue retention (water retention)

The research team designed a protocol detailing how the different plots will be established in the different plots (See Appendix 2.2.3.1). Demo plot holders were selected randomly across the list of farmers participating in the baseline survey. Care was taken to select farmers across the different typologies. As such, we used a stratified sampling strategy to select demo plot holders. After the selection process, farmers were asked if they were willing and would consent to host a demo plot. All the selected farmers were willing and consented. Following the protocol, facilitators, extension officers, and farmers were then trained to set up the demo plots based on the different treatments using the established protocol. Crops were monitored and managed by the demo plot holders with the help of field facilitators stationed in each district and ward. Farmers were trained on record keeping to ensure every management practice employed was captured. A demo plot characterization survey was developed in KoboCollect and administered by the facilitators together with the farmer. This tool was meant to understand the management employed by the farmer. Local facilitators were trained to train farmers on pests and disease scouting and assessment. A survey was developed in KoboCollect and deployed twice during the life of the crops to monitor pest incidence and damage severity across all treatments. Harvesting protocols were also developed in KoboCollect; two sets of tools were developed for each crop and plot, the first ones for collecting fresh weights soon after harvesting, while the others were for collecting dry weights after the crops had dried up. The protocols detailed step-by-step processes for the harvesting. For instance, in all plots, two rows of the outer crops were treated as boundary crops to eliminate the other effects that might have affected the crop. Additional management data was also captured by the harvesting tool. Data was then analyzed using the R software. Data was first assessed for normality, which then informed the use of scatterplots and bar graphs to present data.
Lessons learnt, achievements and challenges:
• The initial germination of brachairia in Murehwa was very low, leading to several replantings. In Mbire the germination was around 80 – 90%.
• Bettles and aphids severely attacked cowpeas
Farmers have knowledge of biopesticides, farmers who applied chilli sprays and blue cherry bush liquid sprays managed to harvest both sorghum and maize.
• Dry beans did not perform well owing to the excessive rainfall received in Murehwa

Technologies performed differently depending on the district, agroecology and farmers, suggesting that spreading the demo plots across different farms and typologies would give a good indication of technology performance.
Planting of the demo plots was done after many farmers had already established their crop fields.

Objective: A rating and ranking exercise was conducted to solicit farmers' views and initial uptake or adoption of the tested technologies for the 2022/23 farming season

Approach: A participatory approach to understanding farmer perceptions and choices was used for this exercise. The rating and ranking exercise was embedded in field day activities in both districts. 3.0 Methodological considerations

• Farmers faced pest issues, with beetles and aphids attacking cowpeas that were used in the push–pull technology, but some successfully applied biopesticides to salvage the cowpea harvests. While the design of the push–pull technology was that the main crop of interest was cereal and the cowpea and brachairia were not to be harvested, the application of the biopesticide shows that farmers also prioritized cowpea as a food crop in the system.
Issues such as excessive rainfall affecting dry bean performance in Murehwa and concerns about the push-pull system's impact on sorghum were raised by farmers.
The multi-partner approach fostered collaboration among stakeholders, projects, and initiatives, promoting synergies.

Training initiatives resulted in increased awareness and participation, with women increasingly operating machinery. Mechanized technologies were well-received for livestock care and transportation. Ongoing efforts include linking environmental institutes with service providers for fireguards.

• The delayed planting of demo plots after farmers had already established their fields underscored the importance of aligning interventions with local agricultural timelines. Plans to repeat studies incorporating socio-economic innovations for a holistic understanding of agroecological preferences. We have started with discrete choice experiments for better contextual considerations, as technologies performed differently across districts, agroecologies, and among farmers.
• In the initial stages,a deliberate inventory of past and existing technologies and innovations was not conducted; this could have helped to improve already existing technologies in the communities
4.0 Results
4.1 Inventory of technologies

We have developed an inventory of existing technologies. First, through the challenges and opportunities exercise (See Appendix 2.1), then through the baseline survey (See Appendix 2.1) and dialogues with ALL members on existing alternative technologies (Appendix 2.2.4.1).

For the baseline suvery, Intercropping, conservation agriculture, crop rotation, use of manure and biopesticides were noted. During detailed FGD, several alternative technologies were highlighted. For instance, the biopesticide made from the leaves of katunguru (blue bush cherry plant) was identified as an existing practice that will be tested in demonstrations alongside push- pull techniques, offering manageable scale testing. Meanwhile, the application of manure from chickens, goats, and cattle in sorghum fields was common. However, scientific validation has been suggested for testing of the composition and optimal quantities of technologies such as manure and biopesticides. Furthermore, considerations for potential ecological impact are raised, urging awareness of raw material destruction and reduced biodiversity, necessitating a balance between technology adoption and environmental preservation.

Cultural aspects emerge as potential conduits for behavior change, as Biohub discovered during engagements where certain practices, such as witchcraft, were linked to institutional arrangements, reflecting the community's intention to address issues like theft. Drawing inspiration from cultural behaviors, such as observing elephants' feeding patterns for zero tillage, suggests a holistic approach to innovation by aligning with existing practices. The discussion on convergence or divergence of technologies and innovations vis-a-vis existing practices underscores the importance of aligning indigenous knowledge and so called improved technologies. Technologies that seamlessly integrate with local practices demonstrate convergence, while those deviating from the norm indicate divergence or parallel implementation. This nuanced approach ensures a thoughtful and context-specific implementation of alternative technologies within the broader Agroecology Initiative in Zimbabwe.
4.2 Description of technologies being tested

The visioning process was instrumental in delineating the envisioned future context, facilitating the identification of key priorities and goals, and fostering trust and collaboration among the FSA. Following this, an in-depth exploration of challenges and opportunities within the identified value chains was undertaken. These findings were subsequently validated in successive meetings to solidify the outcomes of the visioning exercise. In the course of addressing challenges and leveraging opportunities, a collaborative effort led to the identification of potential technologies aimed at mitigating the identified issues ( Table 1 and Table 2). A subset of farmers was then given the opportunity to field-test these technologies. Subsequent to this phase, a broader group of farmers engaged in a collective evaluation, providing valuable feedback and suggesting alternative technologies and features. In parallel, extensive consultations with ALLs were conducted to gain insights into both existing and alternative practices

Introduction

In mid-2024, the Hom and Thamaleuy communities, with facilitation support from WorldFish Cambodia and IWMI Laos, co- developed a management plan for the Nonglom wetlands. By November, they secured official endorsement from the Samakhyxai district government for the plan and the proposed management committee to lead its implementation.

One of the key actions proposed under the management plan is to establish a Fisheries Conservation Group and Sao Baan (Villager led action research). Their role will be to collect data on current fishing access, facilitate an improved regulation of fishing activities, and enhance fishing practices through the creation of fish conservation zones and the improvement of aquatic habitats. The purpose of this action is to manage fishing access by regulating efforts and practices, while also ensuring the ecological requirements for fish and other aquatic animals in the Nonglom wetlands are met.
Objective

The purpose of the checklist is to guide the collection of information on current fishing access and its contribution to local livelihoods. The data and information generated will inform the Nonglom Management Committee’s decisions on regulating fishing access, establishing fish conservation zones, and defining how aquatic habitats and their connectivity can be reestablished. Iterative data collection will help establish trends in access, resources, and needs for aquatic habitat enhancement.
Potential Users of the Checklist

The Nonglom Wetlands Management Committee and its four thematic groups are composed of local stakeholders, including the chiefs of the participating communities, the village-level Lao Women’s Union, the Village Youth Group, the Village Land Use Unit, and local fishers from the Hom and Thamaleuy communities. Potential applicants are local individuals with limited education but should have the capacity to understand and record data and information with minimal prior orientation or introduction.
Structure of the Checklist

The checklist collects data on various aspects of fishing, including the population structure involved, fishing grounds, fishing efforts, gear types, target species, and the amount of catch by season and gear type. It also examines how fish contribute to local livelihoods and food nutrition. This exercise will provide data to assess the state of the fisheries and the ecological health of the wetlands.
Application of the Checklist

The checklist must be translated into Lao and reviewed for ease of use. Hard copies should be made available for applicants to use directly when collecting information from fishers in the wetland areas surrounding the lake and in Sekong. In the future, with adequate support and access to smartphones, the checklist content could be incorporated into mobile applications like KoboCollect to facilitate easier and more accurate data recording.

Introduction

In mid-2024, the Hom and Thamaleuy communities, with facilitation support from WorldFish Cambodia and IWMI Laos, co- developed a management plan for the Nonglom wetlands. By November, they secured official endorsement from the Samakhyxai district government for the plan and the proposed management committee to lead its implementation.

One of the key actions proposed under the management plan is to establish a Fisheries Conservation Group and Sao Baan (Villager led action research). Their role will be to collect data on current fishing access, facilitate an improved regulation of fishing activities, and enhance fishing practices through the creation of fish conservation zones and the improvement of aquatic habitats. The purpose of this action is to manage fishing access by regulating efforts and practices, while also ensuring the ecological requirements for fish and other aquatic animals in the Nonglom wetlands are met.
Objective

The purpose of the checklist is to guide the collection of information on current fishing access and its contribution to local livelihoods. The data and information generated will inform the Nonglom Management Committee’s decisions on regulating fishing access, establishing fish conservation zones, and defining how aquatic habitats and their connectivity can be reestablished. Iterative data collection will help establish trends in access, resources, and needs for aquatic habitat enhancement.
Potential Users of the Checklist

The Nonglom Wetlands Management Committee and its four thematic groups are composed of local stakeholders, including the chiefs of the participating communities, the village-level Lao Women’s Union, the Village Youth Group, the Village Land Use Unit, and local fishers from the Hom and Thamaleuy communities. Potential applicants are local individuals with limited education but should have the capacity to understand and record data and information with minimal prior orientation or introduction.
Structure of the Checklist

The checklist collects data on various aspects of fishing, including the population structure involved, fishing grounds, fishing efforts, gear types, target species, and the amount of catch by season and gear type. It also examines how fish contribute to local livelihoods and food nutrition. This exercise will provide data to assess the state of the fisheries and the ecological health of the wetlands.
Application of the Checklist

The checklist must be translated into Lao and reviewed for ease of use. Hard copies should be made available for applicants to use directly when collecting information from fishers in the wetland areas surrounding the lake and in Sekong. In the future, with adequate support and access to smartphones, the checklist content could be incorporated into mobile applications like KoboCollect to facilitate easier and more accurate data recording.

Objective

The purpose of this document is to provide a concise guideline on organizing a meeting of the Nonglom Management Committee. It does not cover how to facilitate the meeting itself, which will be addressed separately. This guideline is intended to inform the meeting convener, moderators/facilitators, and rapporteur of the steps and action points to be performed before, during, and after the meeting.

This will ensure that the issues to be addressed are clearly identified and well-articulated beforehand, allowing participants to come to the event adequately prepared. Additionally, it will ensure that necessary details are discussed during the meeting, and key actions are noted and shared for post-meeting implementation.
Potential Users of the Guideline

The Nonglom Wetlands Management Committee and its four thematic groups consist of local stakeholders, including the chiefs of the participating communities, the village-level Lao Women’s Union, the Village Youth Group, the Village Land Use Unit, and rice and cash crop farmers and fishers from the Hom and Thamaleuy communities. Potential applicants are local individuals with limited education but should have the capacity to understand and record data and information with minimal prior orientation or introduction.
Structure of the Guideline

The checklist collects data on various aspects of fishing, including the population structure involved, fishing grounds, fishing efforts, gear types, target species, and the amount of catch by season and gear type. It also examines how fish contribute to local livelihoods and food nutrition. This exercise will provide data to assess the state of the fisheries and the ecological health of the wetlands.
Application of the Guideline

The guideline follows the natural progression of a meeting process, starting with defining the purpose and goals. It then moves on to preparing an agenda and identifying the targeted participants, ensuring that necessary resources are available for the event. Additionally, the guideline emphasizes the importance of effective facilitation, capturing action points, and outlining follow-up actions.
1. Define the Meeting’s Purpose and Goals
5. Facilitate the Meeting Effectively
Clearly outline the objectives of the meeting. What specific progress do you want to check? What decisions need to be made?
Start on Time: Respect everyone’s time by starting and ending the meeting as scheduled.
2. Prepare a Detailed Agenda
List Topics as Questions: Frame agenda items as questions to focus discussions and outcomes.
Prioritize Topics: Ensure the most critical issues are addressed first.
Encourage Participation: Create an inclusive environment where everyone feels comfortable sharing their views.
Stay Focused: Keep discussions on track and avoid going off-topic.
6. Use Visual Aids and Tools
Allocate Time: Assign realistic time slots for each agenda item to keep the meeting on track.
Utilize charts, maps, and other visual aids to illustrate progress and challenges.
3. Invite the Right Participants
Ensure that key stakeholders, including community leaders, local government officials, and representatives from relevant organizations, are invited.
Consider the roles and responsibilities of each participant to ensure productive discussions.
Consider using digital tools for real-time data sharing and collaboration.
7. Document Decisions and Action Points
Record key decisions, action items, and responsibilities. Ensure that everyone knows what is expected of them after the meeting.
8. Follow Up
4. Distribute Materials in Advance
Share the agenda and any relevant documents or reports before the meeting. This allows participants to come prepared with questions and comments.
o Send out meeting minutes and a summary of action items promptly.

The purpose of the action is to manage access to using the water for irrigation against the current increasing demand for water to irrigate more and more watermelon farms.
Objective

The purpose of the checklist is to guide the collection of information on current dry season cash crop farming and the inherent demand for their irrigation. The generated data and information will inform decisions by Nonglom management committee to benchmark the maximum area for dry season cash crop farming and the withdrawal of water for their irrigation and for reallocation to achieve multiple purposes. The checklist gathers data and information on the location and size farmlands, the sources of water used for irrigating the lands and how they are used, current irrigation practices and potential challenge with access to the water and recommendations from the users on their improvement management. Research Protocol
Nonglom Wetlands Management Planning
a5 come SZ Agroccology CGIAR
Context/challenge/ALL vision, what research questions will this innovation aim to answer

The Nonglom wetlands are located in the agricultural landscape of Samakhixay, where resources such as water, land, and fish have been heavily exploited to support local livelihoods. Currently, there are few, if any, management actions in place to regulate resource access and use, let alone efforts to restore or re-establish the wetland ecosystem functions and the goods and services provided by the once natural habitats.

The purpose of the wetlands governance and management innovation is to restore, as much as possible, the wetland ecosystem functions—such as water provision, water purification, and habitats for biodiversity, fish, and other wildlife—along with their associated goods and services. This will be achieved through the application of relevant agroecological principles and the re-establishment of the area’s natural habitats. This initiative will also provide a roadmap and springboard for realizing other proposed innovations for agroecological transitions.

The research question for this innovation is: How do agroecological innovations perform in restoring wetland ecosystem functions across the landscape, and how should they be adapted to the local context.
Justification (why is there a need and how has this need been articulated or).

The Nonglom wetlands are crucial for local livelihoods, serving as an important fishing ground, a water source for farming, and providing various other environmental services. However, these wetlands and their surrounding areas face increasing threats from persistent degradation and fragmentation of natural habitats. This is due to the area’s long-term conversion to agricultural production, increased water abstraction for dry season crop irrigation, indiscriminate fishing, and the discharge of agricultural tailwaters.
What is your innovation (trial)

This innovation aims to address the sustainable management and governance of wetland resources by engaging local Food System Actors (FSAs) in designing and implementing actions to regulate resource access and management, and to restore and maintain the ecosystem. The innovation involves relevant FSAs in a co-design process and joint implementation to optimize the livelihood benefits for local people. It seeks to engage local villagers in conducting action research to inform regulations on resource access and to build local ownership in both planning and implementation processes. An evidence-based approach will be applied to document lessons and generate interest among FSAs for their engagement.
How has this been co-designed (this will be consolidated across trials into a co-design report

Consultations with relevant Food System Actors (FSAs) are integral to the design and implementation of this innovation. The process began with visits to selected government sectoral departments in the relevant provinces, as well as civil society and private FSAs, to understand current agroecological (AE) practices and scope the potential Agroecological Learning Landscape (ALL). An inter-provincial multi-sector workshop was then held to generate interest in AE concepts and identify the relevant FSAs for the ALL.

Local FSAs, including rice and other crop farmers, fishers, and gatherers of Other Aquatic Animals (OAA), were introduced to the innovation and its potential benefits, as well as the requirements for their commitment to participate in delivering the tasks. They were then consulted along with other stakeholder groups, such as the heads of the participating villages (Hom and Thamaleuy), leaders of specialized village groups like the Lao Women’s Union (LWU), the Village Youth Group (VYG), and the Village Land Use Unit (VLUU), as well as the district and provincial Departments of Agriculture and Forestry. Selected participatory tools and processes were used during these consultations.
The outputs from this consultative process were compiled and presented back to the FSAs for validation.

How will this be implemented (approach…e.g., action research, salaphoum, farmer field school also mechanisms such as water user groups, management committees etc.

While the management plan is being drafted through a participatory process involving the innovation team, local FSAs, and representatives from local authorities and the district and provincial Departments of Agriculture and Forestry, the roles in its implementation will vary. A local management/coordination committee will be formed, comprising members from the provincial and district Departments of Agriculture and Forestry, village heads, and representatives from village groups such as the Lao Women’s Union (LWU), the Village Youth Group (VYG), and the Village Land Use Unit (VLUU), among others. This committee will guide and coordinate the implementation of the plan.

Initially, at least two interest groups will be organized, consisting of local resource user groups—the water user group and the fisher group. These groups will implement and conduct selected village-led action research to inform the development and compliance of local regulations. They will participate on a voluntary basis in implementing the actions outlined in the plan.

The primary goal is to deliver the management and action plans. Alongside this, the Nonglom Management Committee will be established to coordinate and facilitate the plan’s implementation. Consultation and validation meetings with local FSAs will provide key indicators and milestones for the plan development process. The committee’s effectiveness, including the frequency of meetings, decisions made, and connections with higher authorities, will be the main indicators of progress.
Transition pathway (maybe here, maybe in the context section?)

The transition from a lack of awareness or initiative for managing Nonglom to having a structured plan and a functioning local management committee is a significant agroecological innovation. This committee will coordinate deliberations, facilitate collective actions, and conduct village-led action research to implement local resource use and management strategies.
Interlinkages between trials and between initiatives

This innovation is closely linked to other initiatives, such as rice-fish farming, underground water solar irrigation, and soil testing. It engages complementary subjects, like establishing a farmer water user group, with overlapping participants including DAFO/PAFO staff members, residents, and local authorities. This shared perspective ensures that objectives and methods across all innovations are synergized. The innovation builds on past and ongoing projects and local practices, such as the UNDP/GEF efforts since 2006 on sustainable use and management of the Lower Mekong Wetlands, to maintain long-term engagement and ownership.
What research outputs / deliverables are expected (technical reports, journal articles, etc.)

The key deliverable is a management plan for the Nonglom wetlands. Additional outputs include the establishment of a local management/coordination committee with defined duties, and the formation of resource user groups, such as a fishery group and a farmer water user group. The process and lessons from their engagement and deliberation will also be documented.

Introduction
Management plan

The Nong Lom (NL) wetlands contain approximately 20 ha of a permanent freshwater lake that are mainly used for fishing and irrigating rice and seasonal crops in the lake’s immediate surroundings. However, the lake is no longer sufficient to meet the increasing demand for irrigation, and there are now very little fish in it because of unsustainable fishing practices and the degraded and fragmented habitat. No written management plan has ever been put in place for the wetlands. In mid-2000, a regional project extended limited financial and advisory support for management actions on the ground. But when the project ended in 2007, management was ceased, and no management has taken its place since.
1. Promote more sustainable multiple use of NL water: 3 actions and 14 activities.
2. Mitigate potential pollution from agriculture run-off: 3 actions, 14 activities.
3. Ensure sustainable fishing practices: 3 actions, 14 activities.
4. Restore ecological functions of the NL lake and its surroundings: 2 actions, 10 activities.
5. Develop and operationalize local management mechanisms: 3 actions, 10 activities.
Rationale

Transformational Agroecology across Food, Land, and Water Systems is a CGIAR Initiative that aims to harness nature’s goods and services while minimizing adverse environmental impacts and improving knowledge co-creation and inclusive relationships among food system actors. To that end, improved management for the NL wetlands was selected to pilot some agroecological principles in different components of the local food system.
Relevance to the Initiative’s principles

Recycling; input reduction; soil health; biodiversity protection; synergy among plant, soil, animals and water; co-creation of knowledge; land and natural resource governance; participation of all relevant stakeholders, both state and non-state actors, including a balanced representation of men and women.
Approach
The Initiative used a demand-led participatory approach to the co-design and co-development of the management plan.
INITIATIVE ON
Agroecology CGIAR
Process

Relevant stakeholders were engaged to identify relevant components of the food system for the innovation. Both government and non-government actors shared their knowledge on the resources, issues and challenges, and ultimately proposed options for the management objectives and actions. The Initiative’s team from WorldFish Cambodia and the International

Water Management Institute in Laos play primarily a facilitating role in steering the process and getting the outputs written up and presented back to them for validation. The development process for the plan took stakeholders/communities 9 months to develop, even as stakeholders were busy with their regular activities.
Outputs
The draft management plan consists of two main parts:
1. Nong Lom: Its resources and environment
2. The Nong Lom management plan.

The first parts provides an overview of the biophysiological environment, socioeconomics, and resource use and governance (both past and present) of Nong Lom. The second part includes a long-term objective and five management objectives, as well as an implementation arrangement that includes annual actions, a budget breakdown, evaluation and adaptive planning.

Progress
September 2023:
• Presentation and video screening to raise understanding and interest of the need for improved management of the NL wetlands
• Village chiefs (Hom and Thamaleuy), Lao Women Union (LWU), Village Youth Group (VYG), Village Land Use Unit (VLUU), local fishers, and local rice and cash crop producers
• Consultation started to understand the resources at stake and also threats and challenges
December 2023:
• Presentation and validation to the co-design team on progress made since the previous period
• Samakhysai District Office of Agriculture and Forestry (DAFO)
• Consultation on past management and challenges, and overall governance in place
• Attapeu Provincial Office of Agriculture and Forestry (PAFO)
• Co-design and co- development team of 15–20 people
• More than 60 participants in the initial awareness and consultation
February 2024:
• Presentation and validation to the co-design team on progress since the previous period
• Consultation to formulate management objectives and actions, a proposed management structure and teams, prioritization of actions, and budget estimates
• Presentation and validation to the co-design team on progress made since the period
• Elaboration on duties and responsibilities for the management committee and thematic groups
• Selected activities implemented, including providing initial capacity building and establishing a management committee and four thematic groups

1. Nonglom and its Environment
1.1 Description of Nong Lom and its surroundings
1.1.1 Overview

The Nonglom (NL) wetlands feature a permanent lake surrounded by agricultural and residential areas. During the dry season, the lake’s open water spans about 20 hectares, measuring approximately 350 meters by 2,400 meters, with water depths ranging from 0.5 meters in the dry season to 1.5 meters in the wet season. A dirt road encircles the lake, particularly to the northeast, where rice paddies and cash crop fields lie beyond the road’s perimeter.

Two rural residential areas are situated on the southeastern side of the lake, with National Road #18A skirting the villages further southeast. The agricultural land around the lake is primarily used for growing cash crops such as rice, watermelon, and cassava. Only a few trees remain scattered throughout the agricultural areas, with small patches of vegetation mostly found towards the southern end of the lake.

Despite its limited water storage capacity, the lake is a crucial source of water for irrigation and fishing. Fishing occurs year- round in the lake and seasonally in the surrounding agricultural landscape, providing a vital source of livelihood for the local community.
1.1.2 Location

Nonglom is located in Attapeu province, which lies in the transition zone between the Annamite Mountain Range to the east and the Mekong Plains to the west. It is adjacent to the Bolaven Plateau, bordered by Sekong to the north, Champasak to the west, Vietnam to the east, and Cambodia to the south. Sixty percent of the province is mountainous, with seventy percent of these areas classified as ‘very steep’. The capital town, Samakhyxai, is situated in a large valley surrounded by mountains.

Geographically, the Nonglom area is positioned in the middle of a flooded plain, between a mountain range to the northwest and the Sekong River to the southeast. Central to the Nong Lom wetland is the Nong Lom lake, with approximate coordinates as follows:
Nonglom is about 20 km west of Attapeu provincial town. It is situated approximately 2,000 meters from the mountain range to the northwest and 700 meters from the Sekong River to the southeast.

Running parallel to the lake, about 350 meters to the southeast, is National Road #18A. The two nearest villages along National Road #18A are Hom (14.780128, 106.743108) to the southeast and Thamaleuy (14.787119, 106.747953) to the northeast of the lake, east of the road. The lake and its surroundings are largely vegetation-free, with only small shrubs scattered randomly, particularly on the western shore near Hom village.

1.2 Landscape and ecology
1.2.1 Geology and Pedology

Nonglom is part of the lower Sekong basin, which reaches its highest elevation at 576 meters. This area features rugged topography with high peaks in its upper regions, a large plain in the central area, and flat valleys extending from Attapeu through Cambodia to the confluence with the Mekong River.1

Three main soil types have been identified in the Nong Lom wetlands: Alisols, Luvisols, and Acrisols. Luvisols, which have high nutrient content, are suitable for a wide range of agricultural activities if well managed. In contrast, Alisols and Acrisols are highly acidic, poorly drained, and prone to aluminum toxicity. Liming and fertilization are essential for their agricultural use, making them less productive compared to Luvisols.

The Sekong River flood plain is composed of a mixture of alluvial sediments and sedimentary rocks, which enhances its fertility due to regular flooding that deposits nutrient-rich sediments. However, current soil management practices, such as monocropping, are causing a decline in soil fertility over time, making the soil less productive.
1.2.2 Climate

The climate is dominated by monsoons, resulting in distinct wet and dry seasons. Most rainfall occurs from May to September when prevailing winds blow from the southwest. Annual rainfall varies from 1,000 mm in the extreme south to 3,000 mm in the north. Mean temperatures range from about 10°C in January to 38°C in July, with cooler temperatures in the north and warmer temperatures in the south. The climate in Attapeu is significantly influenced by the Annamite Mountain Range, which acts as a barrier. Areas of the Annamite with lower crests receive more rain over a longer season.

1.2.3 Water and Hydrology

The Sekong River Basin is one of the most significant tributaries of the Mekong River. Its watershed, covering 28,815 hectares, spans the entire Attapeu province as well as parts of neighboring provinces in Laos and Cambodia. The Sekong River valley includes sections of the Samakkixay, Xaysetha, and Sanamxay districts.1

Nonglom lake and its surroundings receive water primarily from the catchment area to the west during the wet season, rather than from the nearby Sekong River. Several small seasonal creeks flow from the foothills through the plain before reaching Nonglom. Refer to the map for details on the water channels running through the plain.

The map highlights the channel flowing out of the lake but does not show a clear channel feeding water directly from the foothills to NL. Instead, much of the lake’s inflow comes from surface runoff spreading across the low, flat fields to the west of NL. To manage excess water during the wet season, farmers install PVC pipes in their paddy field bunds. These pipes allow excess water to flow across the bunds and also serve as fish traps. Numerous water inlets are visible along the dirt road to the west of NL.

1.3 Biodiversity

There is no record of any past biological study of the lake and its surroundings. Local people have recounted the many different plant and animal species, including fish and waterbirds, that once inhabited the area. However, this knowledge of biodiversity has not been documented, and most of these species are no longer present. Given the important ecological functions provided by the vegetation to sustain the wetland and lake environment, and the significance of fish for local livelihoods, it is crucial to conduct extensive studies of the local species of plants and animals and to reestablish relevant habitats. Understanding the local biodiversity, including the species and their habitats, is critical for effective management and conservation.

Direct observation reveals that there is almost no aquatic vegetation, or plants present in the lake itself. In the immediate surroundings of the lake, particularly in the paddy and cash crop landscape, there is no vegetation that could support regeneration. A few shrubs can be seen between 5 and 10 meters from the lake shore during the dry season, scattered haphazardly in the southwest and behind the villages to the east of the lake. Although the communities reported a dozen species of aquatic plants, most of these are not currently sighted.

1.4 Resource and land Use

The Sekong River valley, which flows through the middle of the province, is considered the “rice bowl” of Attapeu. It is one of the larger rice-growing areas in Lao PDR, although yields are low. Paddy rice and watermelon farming have been the major agricultural crops around the lake, while livestock grazing and the utilization of non-timber forest products from the mountains and wetlands have been the most common land use practices in the larger area. Recently, cassava planting has become a major cash crop on the newly cleared land on higher ground.

Many of the paddy fields and surrounding areas along the channel between NL and the Sekong are privately owned, mainly by residents. However, large plots of land used for teak and other plantations mostly belong to people from outside the communities. A field trial site belonging to the provincial Department of Agriculture and Forestry is located to the east of NR18A, between Hom and Thamaleuy villages.

Like the lands along the channel between NL and Sekong, much of the land immediately around the lake is privately owned by community members and has been used mostly for dry season rice and watermelon production. Hom village is situated very close to the southeast of the lake, and Thamaleuy is to the northeast, mostly on the other side of NR18A. A narrow strip of land close to the lakeshore in the south, west, and northeast of the lake is also used for planting watermelon, mainly after the rice is harvested. According to the village chiefs of Hom and Thamaleuy, 80% (about 24 ha) of farmland around Thamaleuy belongs to Hom, and only 20% to Thamaleuy.2

Current uses of NL include water for rice irrigation in the dry season, animal drinking and wallowing, and fishing all year round. The proximity of paddy fields to the lake makes it easy to access irrigation. A few households next to the lake also use the water for home gardening but not for domestic consumption due to its high turbidity from excessive fishing in the dry season.

The lake is subject to open access fishing by local villagers in the surrounding areas. Some fishers claim private access to small segments of the lake with established brush gardens to attract fish, and harvesting is done either with nets or by the pumping dry method. This traditional fishing practice has been inherited for generations but lacks legal recognition by any authority. The lake is heavily fished, with no areas reserved for protection or as dry season refuges, and the fishing methods include destructive practices such as pumping dry and electrocution.

PVC pipes are fitted to the bunds of paddy fields to facilitate water flow across the fields, and fish are reported to use these pipes to cross between fields. Where water channels leading to the paddy fields are present, fish traps, some fitted with fences (locally known as “lee”), are not uncommon. These traps appear to target fish on their way back to the main water body in the late wet season. However, fishing with traps and associated fences is banned in the main channel/creek.

A few fishponds are also present next to the creek, about 1,400 meters northeast of the lake, where the channel outlet from the north of the lake meets the creek. These ponds are privately owned and could be managed to provide dry season refuge ponds as well as for fish production. Given the frequent sighting of fish traps, it can be assumed that fishing is quite important, especially in the wet season, and fish migration across the landscape in the wet season is also significant. A few borrow pits can be seen right beside the southeast shore of NL, behind Hom village.
1.5 Socioeconomics of Nong Lom Communities

Nonglom Lake is surrounded by two small villages, Hom and Tamaleuy, with populations of 2,137 and 971, respectively. While Tamaleuy has an almost equal number of males and females (485 males and 486 females), Hom has a higher male ratio, with 1,111 males to 1,086 females.

No information is currently available on their level of education. However, both communities appear to have relatively weak access to higher education due to their remoteness from large cities, aside from Attapeu. Attapeu is the third smallest province in terms of population and the second smallest in population density in Laos (source: Wikipedia).

The two communities can be categorized as agrarian, heavily dependent on farming as their primary source of income to support their livelihoods. The charts below illustrate how each village relies on different income sources.

Rice cultivation has been the backbone of local livelihoods, typically occurring between June and December, with an average yield of 1.5 tons per hectare. Unlike their counterparts in selected villages from Sanamxay district, where organic rice production is practiced with support from Indochina Development Partner (IDP) – a private sector entity exporting rice to Europe – rice farming practices in this area follow traditional methods. However, some changes have been reported recently, with more farmers applying chemical inputs to their rice production, ranging from fertilizers to pesticides.

Since 2009, the government has raised awareness among farmers about reducing the use of chemical fertilizers and turning to composting, providing training on making compost. Despite this, adoption levels were low. In 2020, many villagers turned to multiple cropping for their cash crops, planting watermelon, sugar cane, and vegetables. While much of the land surrounding NL is dedicated to rice farming during the wet season, 5-6 hectares of land, particularly areas close to NL where water access is easy, are used by 17 households for watermelon farming. In 2024, watermelon farming covered an area of 5-6 hectares. Farmers grow watermelon on an alternating year basis on the same plot of land, allowing a year for the soil to rest and regenerate its fertility.

Fishing is an important secondary activity for many farm households, providing extra income or supplementing the family’s food supply. Two-thirds of farm households in Lao PDR engage in capture fisheries. Of these, 92% fish in rivers, 40% in lakes, and 37% in rice fields. Capture fisheries are widespread across the country, with 74% of farm households in Attapeu participating in fishing. Fishing is usually carried out for household consumption. Only about a thousand aquaculture producers rely on aquaculture as their main source of income, with a third selling some aquaculture products.

1.6 Governance of Nong Lom area
1.6.1 Existing legislations and institutions
Lao PDR has implemented various laws and regulations to govern its agricultural sector. Key agencies with relevant mandates include:
o The Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry: Oversees several departments, including:
o Department of Agriculture: Responsible for the development and promotion of sustainable agriculture practices, crop production, plant protection, and agricultural extension services.
o Department of Irrigation: Handles the planning, construction, and maintenance of irrigation systems to support agricultural production.
o Department of Agricultural Extension and Cooperatives: Provides advisory services, training, and technical support to farmers and promotes the development of agricultural cooperatives.
o Provincial and District Agriculture and Forestry Offices: Implement and monitor agricultural and forestry activities at the local level.

Article 4 of the Law on Agriculture (01-98/NA, 10 October 1998) protects the rights and interests of farmers with relevant policies and regulations to promote agricultural production. Article 5 protects agricultural land from inappropriate modification without prior approval from the ministry. Article 25 of the Land Law (No. 70/NA, 21 June 2019) states that land use conversion can only be made if necessary to maximize benefits and improve livelihoods, in line with the Land Allocation Master Plan, land use strategy, and sectoral and local land use plans. Article 6 ensures that thirty percent of the overall land nationally is set for use and development, with forest land covering not less than seventy percent.

The Government of Lao PDR recognizes wetlands as important natural resources providing ecosystem services such as water regulation, biodiversity conservation, and carbon sequestration. The Law on Environmental Protection and Management (No. 07/NA, 2019) and the Law on Water and Water Resources (No. 06/NA, 2019) provide the legal framework for the protection and management of wetlands in Lao PDR. These regulations are crucial for managing NL lake.

The Department of Livestock and Fisheries of the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, along with its sub-national offices under the Provincial Agriculture and Forests Office (PAFO) and District Agriculture and Forest Office (DAFO), is responsible for the management and development of the Lao fisheries sector. The first comprehensive national law governing fisheries in Laos was the Fisheries Law 2009 (No. 03/NA, 09 July 2009). There is no local-level law or regulation governing fisheries management; local practices must refer to national law provisions. The law regulates the management, conservation, and development of fisheries resources in Laos, including the protection of aquatic biodiversity, the prevention of illegal fishing practices, and the promotion of sustainable fishing practices.

1. Nonglom and its Environment
1.1 Description of Nong Lom and its surroundings
1.1.1 Overview

The Nonglom (NL) wetlands feature a permanent lake surrounded by agricultural and residential areas. During the dry season, the lake’s open water spans about 20 hectares, measuring approximately 350 meters by 2,400 meters, with water depths ranging from 0.5 meters in the dry season to 1.5 meters in the wet season. A dirt road encircles the lake, particularly to the northeast, where rice paddies and cash crop fields lie beyond the road’s perimeter.

Two rural residential areas are situated on the southeastern side of the lake, with National Road #18A skirting the villages further southeast. The agricultural land around the lake is primarily used for growing cash crops such as rice, watermelon, and cassava. Only a few trees remain scattered throughout the agricultural areas, with small patches of vegetation mostly found towards the southern end of the lake.

Despite its limited water storage capacity, the lake is a crucial source of water for irrigation and fishing. Fishing occurs year- round in the lake and seasonally in the surrounding agricultural landscape, providing a vital source of livelihood for the local community.
1.1.2 Location

Nonglom is located in Attapeu province, which lies in the transition zone between the Annamite Mountain Range to the east and the Mekong Plains to the west. It is adjacent to the Bolaven Plateau, bordered by Sekong to the north, Champasak to the west, Vietnam to the east, and Cambodia to the south. Sixty percent of the province is mountainous, with seventy percent of these areas classified as ‘very steep’. The capital town, Samakhyxai, is situated in a large valley surrounded by mountains.

Geographically, the Nonglom area is positioned in the middle of a flooded plain, between a mountain range to the northwest and the Sekong River to the southeast. Central to the Nong Lom wetland is the Nong Lom lake, with approximate coordinates as follows:
Nonglom is about 20 km west of Attapeu provincial town. It is situated approximately 2,000 meters from the mountain range to the northwest and 700 meters from the Sekong River to the southeast.

Running parallel to the lake, about 350 meters to the southeast, is National Road #18A. The two nearest villages along National Road #18A are Hom (14.780128, 106.743108) to the southeast and Thamaleuy (14.787119, 106.747953) to the northeast of the lake, east of the road. The lake and its surroundings are largely vegetation-free, with only small shrubs scattered randomly, particularly on the western shore near Hom village.

1.2 Landscape and ecology
1.2.1 Geology and Pedology

Nonglom is part of the lower Sekong basin, which reaches its highest elevation at 576 meters. This area features rugged topography with high peaks in its upper regions, a large plain in the central area, and flat valleys extending from Attapeu through Cambodia to the confluence with the Mekong River.1

Three main soil types have been identified in the Nong Lom wetlands: Alisols, Luvisols, and Acrisols. Luvisols, which have high nutrient content, are suitable for a wide range of agricultural activities if well managed. In contrast, Alisols and Acrisols are highly acidic, poorly drained, and prone to aluminum toxicity. Liming and fertilization are essential for their agricultural use, making them less productive compared to Luvisols.

The Sekong River flood plain is composed of a mixture of alluvial sediments and sedimentary rocks, which enhances its fertility due to regular flooding that deposits nutrient-rich sediments. However, current soil management practices, such as monocropping, are causing a decline in soil fertility over time, making the soil less productive.
1.2.2 Climate

The climate is dominated by monsoons, resulting in distinct wet and dry seasons. Most rainfall occurs from May to September when prevailing winds blow from the southwest. Annual rainfall varies from 1,000 mm in the extreme south to 3,000 mm in the north. Mean temperatures range from about 10°C in January to 38°C in July, with cooler temperatures in the north and warmer temperatures in the south. The climate in Attapeu is significantly influenced by the Annamite Mountain Range, which acts as a barrier. Areas of the Annamite with lower crests receive more rain over a longer season.

1.2.3 Water and Hydrology

The Sekong River Basin is one of the most significant tributaries of the Mekong River. Its watershed, covering 28,815 hectares, spans the entire Attapeu province as well as parts of neighboring provinces in Laos and Cambodia. The Sekong River valley includes sections of the Samakkixay, Xaysetha, and Sanamxay districts.1

Nonglom lake and its surroundings receive water primarily from the catchment area to the west during the wet season, rather than from the nearby Sekong River. Several small seasonal creeks flow from the foothills through the plain before reaching Nonglom. Refer to the map for details on the water channels running through the plain.

1.3 Biodiversity

There is no record of any past biological study of the lake and its surroundings. Local people have recounted the many different plant and animal species, including fish and waterbirds, that once inhabited the area. However, this knowledge of biodiversity has not been documented, and most of these species are no longer present. Given the important ecological functions provided by the vegetation to sustain the wetland and lake environment, and the significance of fish for local livelihoods, it is crucial to conduct extensive studies of the local species of plants and animals and to reestablish relevant habitats. Understanding the local biodiversity, including the species and their habitats, is critical for effective management and conservation.

Direct observation reveals that there is almost no aquatic vegetation, or plants present in the lake itself. In the immediate surroundings of the lake, particularly in the paddy and cash crop landscape, there is no vegetation that could support regeneration. A few shrubs can be seen between 5 and 10 meters from the lake shore during the dry season, scattered haphazardly in the southwest and behind the villages to the east of the lake. Although the communities reported a dozen species of aquatic plants, most of these are not currently sighted.
